This watch is a serious upgrade and, yeah, it’s the priciest one on the list, but here’s why it’s worth the investment: It’s a timeless classic with next-level features that will last a lifetime. It’s powered by the Chronometer 8806 movement, so it’s super accurate, and it comes with a 5-year warranty, just in case. In all honesty, it's the kind of watch that'll make you look like a million bucks at an upscale gala or extravagant dinner party. Pair it with a tailored suit and some slick dress shoes for a look that means business.

The movement is the engine of the watch—it's what keeps it ticking. Below, we've broken down the main three types and their benefits.

Powered by a battery and known for being super accurate, quartz movement is low maintenance, lightweight, and affordable. It's a great option if you just want a reliable watch without the fuss. Quartz watches will only require the replacement of the battery every few years, which is a simple task and costs fairly little.

Backed by the motion of your wrist—no battery required. The gears that make up the movement wind themselves when the watch moves. Automatic watches feel a little more special, sometimes like high-end brands Rolex or Omega, but they'll need to be worn regularly or placed in a watch winder to stay powered. They'll also require consistent maintenance and servicing to keep them optimally running. Automatic watches typically cost more than most quartz watches, but there are many great options that are affordable these days.

You wind it yourself, usually every couple days. Instead of the movement rotating automatically with motion, the gears need hand-winding to keep the movement running. These watches require attention and typically harken back to the era of vintage, throwback timepieces like pocket watches. Manual watches usually cost more than quartz watches and are on par in price with some automatic watches. They tend to be a little less affordable though.

Think of the case as the body of the watch—it's the shell that houses everything important, like the movement (the engine that makes it tick) and the dial (the thing with the numbers and hands). Cases come in different shapes, sizes, and materials. Below, we break down the most common materials used for cases.

Durable, versatile, and scratch-resistant. It's the most common and works for everyday wear.

Lighter than steel but just as strong, making it perfect for sports watches.

Scratch-proof and sleek but can be a bit pricey. It has a modern, luxurious feel.

A strap is any flexible band—made of leather, rubber, nylon, or fabric—that secures the watch to your wrist. Straps can change the entire vibe of the watch. A bracelet, on the other hand, is made of metal—stainless steel, titanium, or sometimes gold—linked together. Bracelets usually feel sturdier and add a bit of weight to the watch, giving a more premium, polished look. The good thing is many watches allow you to swap between a strap and a bracelet, so you can switch up the style depending on the occasion.

Classic, comfortable, and stylish. Perfect for dress watches but less durable for heavy-duty activities.

Stainless steel or titanium bracelets are durable and versatile for both casual and formal occasions.

Great for sports and water activities—comfortable and easy to clean.

When shopping for the best men's watch, features and complications can make all the difference in terms of functionality and style. Ultimately, these details should match your lifestyle. We've broken down some important specs to keep an eye out for, but these are by no means an exhaustive list of everything you could find in some complex watches.

This is the ring around the watch face, and when it rotates, it actually serves a purpose (beyond looking cool). On dive watches, for example, the bezel is used to track elapsed time—turn it to line up with the minute hand before you dive, and you'll know how long you're underwater. Some bezels work for other things, like GMT watches, where they help track a second time zone. But in everyday life, most people just fidget with them because it's oddly satisfying with a ratcheting sound.

Water resistance tells you how well your watch can handle moisture. There are two equivalent measurements you will typically find when it comes to this rating. Meters (as in depth) is the first and atmosphere (designated as ATM and measures the pressure of every 10 meters. So the first rating is 30m, which is rated at 3 ATM. This is splash-proof, which means your watch can handle occasional hand-washing or light rain, but don't submerge it. 50m (5 ATM) is good for shallow water activities like light swimming, but no diving. 100m (10 ATM) can handle swimming, snorkeling, and most water sports. 200m+ (20 ATM) is built for diving and serious water activities. Watches like the Omega Seamaster are built specifically for this sort of pressure.

A chronograph is a type of complication added to the watch movement that essentially gives the watch a stopwatch functionality. It's great for timing events, workouts, or even laps around a track. You'll typically see sub dials for seconds, minutes, and sometimes hours. While it adds functionality, it also gives the watch a sporty, complex look. The most famous example of a chronograph is the Rolex Daytona, made famous by watch icon Paul Newman.

A date window adds convenience—you won't have to check your phone or calendar to know the date. It's a small but handy detail, especially for busy schedules. Watches such as the Seiko 5 or Tudor Black Bay makes this feature feel seamless by blending it into the design.

Luminous markers or hands are a must if you plan on wearing the watch in low-light situations, like at night or in darker environments. Watches with Super-LumiNova or tritium tubes glow brightly and for extended periods and make the dial easier to read when overhead light is sparse.

Pay attention to case diameter and thickness. Case diameter is the main number you'll see alongside watches. Generally speaking, around 38-42mm diameter is ideal for most wrists, but larger or smaller watches can suit personal taste. The diameter of cases tends to ebb and flow with watch trends. For the first part of this century, case sizes gravitated over 40mm for lots of watch makers. But in 2026, smaller watches (even down to 32 and 34mm) are en vogue. We like to find a happy medium and suggest trying on different sizes to see what's most comfortable for your wrist.

If you’re rough on your gear or are looking for an everyday wear, opt for a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal (the transparent covering that protects the dial), shock resistance, or robust designs for long-lasting wear.

Our style team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, continually tests almost every watch known to man and put them through their paces for everything they’re designed to handle: marathon training, cycling, traveling, hiking, sleep tracking, daily fitness routines, and dressy occasions. To identify the most ubiquitous watches, we relied on our previous experience testing and owning various models, as well as prior expert coverage on Men’s Health.

We considered features such as case material, comfort, battery life, accuracy, dial design and aesthetics, water resistance, and magnetic resistance. Bonus points were given for unique specs that added functionality like a date window or sub dials. Our picks aren't just utilitarian though—they're seriously stylish, making them the perfect accessory for everything from the gym to date nights. In the end, we narrowed it down to 7 standout watches that tick all the right boxes and can provide a timepiece for any type of guy.

#4686. Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

Every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting new gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the company has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

The new S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

The other big piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

The clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

There’s an important caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T says it is currently fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a company to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

The analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Real Motors plans to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The company has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The company showed off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The company also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

Both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The new models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha showed off its new NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the new model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s new compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway showed off a new vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

The company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The new Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

NIU showed off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company showed off several new models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push new tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the company has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

With its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up new possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely new types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no announced production plans, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Vespa showed off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A new Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Micah Toll is a personal electric vehicle enthusiast, battery nerd, and author of the Amazon #1 bestselling books DIY Lithium Batteries, DIY Solar Power, The Ultimate DIY Ebike Guide and The Electric Bike Manifesto.

The e-bikes that make up Micah’s current daily drivers are the $999 Lectric XP 2.0, the $1,095 Ride1Up Roadster V2, the $1,199 Rad Power Bikes RadMission, and the $3,299 Priority Current. But it’s a pretty evolving list these days.

#4685. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4682. Pottery Barn Jake Leather Sofa Review, Tested by AD (2026)

I’ve wanted a leather sofa for many years, but I could never find a color I liked—a detail just as important to me as the material. I wasn’t interested in the usual black, brown, or cognac options, instead preferring something less traditional but not squarely trendy. And then I discovered Pottery Barn’s Jake Leather Sofa in Vintage Hunter, which hit my sofa sweet spot, exuding a deep confidence that reads as rich, grounded, and classy. Its sophisticated presence anchors my living room without overpowering the space.

If you don’t love the stately green hue as much as I do, that hardly means the Jake isn’t your room’s match. The sofa’s customization options—another major selling point—are robust: In addition to being able to choose from a broad range of leathers and upholstery colors, I could also select the style of the seat and back cushions, adding up to a piece of furniture that feels more personal than an off-the-sales-floor purchase. With its slim arms, low profile, plush cushions, and bronze-finished metal legs, it strikes a balance between streamlined and inviting.

How much does it cost? Are there payment plans available?

The cost of the Jake depends on the size, material, and cushion configuration you choose, falling somewhere between $2,000 and $6,000 for most designs. To save yourself from shopping-cart sticker shock, price out the exact model you want, since the leather grade and sofa width can meaningfully change the total. For instance, my 86-inch-wide, 36-inch-deep model in Vintage Hunter retails for $3,999, but a 70-inch-wide, 36-inch-deep loveseat in a Chocolate Performance fabric costs $3,099, and is sometimes on sale for less.

What are the upholstery or customization options? Did you choose any?

There’s little you can’t choose with the Jake. Available in an extensive selection of leather colors and finishes, you can also pick the number of back cushions you’d like (two or three) and style of seat cushion (two separate or a single bench). For my vintage leather sofa in Hunter, I decided on one bench-style seat cushion and three back cushions.

What is the lead time for customization, manufacturing, and delivery?

It took about six weeks for my sofa to arrive at my home after I ordered it, which felt reasonable for a piece with customized upholstery and cushion selections.

What kind of couch or seating arrangement did you have before, and what drew you to your new couch?

My previous sofa was a smaller turquoise felt sleeper from Mopio that I bought on Amazon; its blue undertones made it feel brighter and more casual. I loved the feel, but dog hair got caught in it easily and was hard to vacuum. This Hunter shade is deeper, moodier, and much closer to the sophisticated design I had envisioned for the room.

What was the delivery process like? What was the assembly process like? How long did it take, and how many people did it require?

Receiving the sofa could not have been easier, thanks to Pottery Barn’s included white-glove delivery service. Two people brought the sofa into my home, placed it where I wanted it, and assembled it on the spot. The entire process took about 10 minutes. For a substantial piece of furniture like this sofa, the luxury delivery experience was a major advantage.

What are the dimensions? How does it fit in your space? Would it be better suited for a certain type of home?

I chose the 85-inch-wide version, which measures 36 inches deep and 32 inches high, and it fits my apartment almost perfectly. It feels generous enough to function as the room’s main seating option without commandeering the full focus of the room. I would recommend this size for a midsize living area, provided that the access points can accommodate its width. As always, measuring the doorway, elevator, stairwell, and turning radius before you click “buy” is just as crucial as measuring the piece’s final spot.

Sit test: Is it comfortable? Does it feel well-made? Does the couch have a tendency to sag?

Comfort is where the Jake has exceeded my expectations. It feels supportive and substantial, and the cushions have held their shape without developing an obvious sag. In the four to five months I’ve had the Jake, several visitors have already stayed over and shared that they’ve experienced restful nights on this couch.

The only recurring quirk I’ve experienced is that the seat cushion occasionally slides forward a smidge. It is easy to nudge back into place and has never become a serious annoyance. It’s also entirely possible that this funky detail has more to do with my sitting tendencies than the sofa’s construction.

Is the sofa suitable for particular decor styles and if so, which?

The Jake naturally fits with modern and contemporary interiors. Its low, linear profile, narrow arms, and metal legs provide a clean architectural quality, while the Hunter leather adds depth and character. However, with the right design elements in place, the sofa would also look at home in decidedly relaxed spaces, with warm woods, woven textiles, vintage pieces, or more traditional accessories.

Is it durable and practical in a modern home?

Despite its sophisticated appearance, this sofa isn’t your grandfather’s precious showpiece that exists for looking at and not sitting on. Rather, I’ve found it to be durable, practical, and comfortable to actually use daily.

But that’s just for humans; pets are the bigger consideration here. I have a dog, and a few scratches have already appeared on the leather. My current remediation system is to cover the sofa with a sheet when we are home and remove it before guests arrive. It works, but anyone hoping for completely carefree pet ownership should be realistic about the care needs of a leather sofa before purchasing this polished piece.

The Jake might fare better with children than with a dog, since typical spills are often easy to address quickly, while claw marks are harder to reverse (if possible to do at all). I am planning to try a leather conditioner to soften the appearance of the scratches, though I have not tested it yet. Before applying any product, I would follow Pottery Barn’s care instructions to spot-test it in an inconspicuous area first. Ultimately, the Jake is probably better suited to a pet-free home, or to any owner willing to go whatever lengths necessary to protect and maintain the leather.

Do the photos do this product justice? Was there anything you were surprised to see IRL?

The sofa looks remarkably similar in person to how it appears online, including the depth of the Hunter color and the overall proportions. There was no unpleasant reveal on delivery day; the sofa I had spent weeks picturing was essentially the sofa that arrived.

Would the couch be easy to move into another room? Would it be easy to move to another apartment or home by yourself?

While it’s more manageable to move than other full-size leather sofas may be, largely in light of its removable legs and loose cushions, I wouldn’t call the Jake a portable sofa. It’s not modular, but rather comes in a single piece, so moving it to another room or home is certainly not a single-person job. However, assuming the doorways and corners cooperate, rehoming its 85-inch span should be possible, so long as you have help on hand.

Comfort: A+Value: ADelivery and assembly: A+Style: A+Overall couch rating: A

#4681. The 6 Best Brooks Shoes for Walking, Tested By Style and Fitness Editors

The Adrenaline GTS 26 and the Ghost 18 topped our list.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ve been known to have questionable standards in some areas of life—like my preference for boxed wine post-grad or my ability to convince myself that cereal counts as dinner. But when it comes to what I put on my feet, the bar is high. I used to think a good walking shoe just meant something that didn’t give me blisters. Now, as a style writer with a pile of sneakers so high it rivals Everest, I expect a lot more. I’m talking support, tons of comfort, and yes, style. That’s exactly why Brooks has become my go-to. The brand’s secret sauce: a perfectly balanced, firm-yet-plush cushioning that makes long days on my feet feel like a walk in the park.

Brooks has been around for over 100 years, and the brand has perfected its walking (and running) shoes. It’s no wonder that Brooks sneakers also come highly recommended by our team of active editors and podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM. “Brooks has always been one of my go-to shoes, especially for walking,” says Schaeffer. That’s thanks to their ideal balance of comfort and support, extensive sizing, secure laces, and breathable, sturdy mesh uppers. You need a shoe specifically for walking because it offers the necessary cushion to take the impact off your joints and give your foot the support it needs to propel forward. These features help prevent aches and injuries.

There’s a seemingly endless amount of sneakers to choose from, but don’t stress: I’ve put in the work to try out the best Brooks shoes for walking. I log (at least) 10,000 steps per day between walking my energetic Jack Russell terrier all around Long Island and commuting into Manhattan for work. Our team of editors also tested every Brooks sneaker through power walking, long days at the office, and leisurely strolls. Our favorite shoe of the bunch is the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, but many others came close for their cushion and stability.

After testing dozens of shoes, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 26 takes the crown as my go-to for walking (and tbh, everything else). The latest Adrenaline GTS iteration still nails the balance between cushion and support, keeping my stride steady without feeling stiff or squished—which is exactly what I loved about the 25.

What really seals the deal? The firm-yet-cozy midsole hugs the foot just right, offering a secure, locked-in feel that still stays comfortable mile after mile. The 26 has about the same amount of cushioning as the previous version (maybeee a tinge more). It’s the perfect amount of cushion to keep feet comfy without sacrificing stability. The mesh upper got an upgrade too, with even more perforations to keep things cool even on the hottest days. I also love that Brooks kept the 10mm heel-to-toe drop (as opposed to the GTS 24's 12mm drop), which helps reduce the potential for strain in the hips and knees. I just snagged the 26 two weeks ago, but so far, I’ve racked up 15+ walking miles and 5 running miles, pain-free.

The previous Adrenaline iteration actually took home the top spot for walking shoes in our 2026 Fitness Awards for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. And so far, the Adrenaline GTS 26 is looking like a superb contender, keeping all of our favorite details of its younger sibling while improving breathability.

My favorite thing about both versions is the shoe’s GuideRails tech, which uses firm foam on either side of the heel to keep feet locked in. The foam is infused with nitrogen, making it super comfortable and lightweight without being overly plush. Bonus: The (did I mention breathable?) mesh upper keeps things comfy without too much stretch (key for stability while walking), Schaeffer says.

One heads-up: the Adrenaline GTS 26 is one of the heavier shoes on this list at 9.6 oz., so if you like a super lightweight shoe, you may want to consider the Glycerin Flex. However, I actually find this sneaker feels way lighter thanks to the mesh upper.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review

If versatility is your priority, the Brooks Ghost 18 delivers. With its nitrogen-fused cushioning, the latest version of the shoe packs in the same amount of plush padding that we loved in the Ghost 17 (it was a 2025 WH Sneaker Award winner for a reason!). Impressively, the moderately high stack height at the heel doesn’t feel too squishy or wobbly. It’s a great do-it-all shoe for long walks, standing all day, and running.

Upgrades from the previous version include a new sockliner that makes for a comfy, snug fit and a flat tongue (the old one was a more classic padded option). “It does a good job of hugging the shape of your ankle without rubbing or chafing,” says fitness writer and WH contributor Korin Miller. “I like the smooth, seamless feel it creates, but I noticed that the edges start to curl in with repeated use.” I’ve noticed the same, but it’s definitely not an issue once your foot is in the shoe—just something to double-check when you slide your foot in.

I’ve worn these for long walks with my pup, all-day errands, a Costco shopping spree (IYKYK), and a full day on my feet at a music festival—and my arches stayed happy through it all. The soft midsole offers that just-right level of give that absorbs impact without feeling too soft or marshmallowy. The knit mesh upper is even more breathable than in the last version, adding to the barely-there feel, as does the plush ankle collar, which doesn’t chafe or rub at all.

One of my only gripes about the Ghost 17 was the slightly narrow toe box, but thankfully, the Ghost 18 solved this issue for me. It’s much more spacious now, both in terms of width and height.

If you’re after a walking shoe that’s super cushy, the Brooks Glycerin 23 is it. I’ve tested these on nearly 10-mile walks through nature preserves and standing for hours at the DMV (ugh). I never once felt like my feet were sore or that I needed to rush to sit down—these things felt like walking on pillows.

But the cushioning isn’t the only win here. The Glycerin 23’s knit upper gives this shoe a sock-like feel that hugs your foot without squeezing. It’s smooth, stretchy, and breathable, making it one of the most comfortable shoes I’ve worn on long walks. The shoe has a mild heel drop that helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot and reduces foot fatigue, which I sometimes experience with other walking shoes. While I wouldn’t quite describe the shoe as sleek or minimalist, it balances its plush cushioning with a more understated silhouette (aka it doesn’t veer into chunky dad shoe territory).

I also appreciate how well this shoe performs on uneven surfaces thanks to its wide platform and ample traction. The durable outsole covers plenty of ground, and the traction has a complex, winding tread pattern. I never feel like I’m going to slip, even on slick pavement.

So far, the Glycerin 23 does a great job of keeping my feet locked in despite its super thick cushioning—but it’s not designed for max stability. Those with specific foot problems, like plantar fasciitis or issues with overpronation, may want to pick a slightly less cushioned, more supportive shoe, like the Adrenaline GTS 25.

Read More: The Best Shoes For Standing All Day

The Brooks Ghost Max 3 took home the top spot in our guide to the most comfortable sneakers for its perfect balance of maximum support and cushioning. It keeps my feet comfortably locked in, even after hours of wear, and my ankles never feel wobbly, which often happens with plush shoes like this one.

“Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!),” says style contributor Lily Wohlner. I agree. That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it almost feels like walking on a moving runway at the airport.

Even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s super stable thanks to its signature Guardrails tech (the same found in the Adrenaline GTS 25). The outsole also has a broad base, which reduces rolling of the foot inward and outward and cradles the foot in place without interfering with your stride. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton says these features are great for high arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel one ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options.

During testing, we did notice some wear and tear on the upper pretty early on (after a few months). While it was a bit of a bummer, the elite combo of cushion and support keeps this kick high on my list of Brooks sneakers.

Think of the Glyceric Flex as Glycerin 23’s lighter, more flexible counterpart. The upper and outsole are both made from super bendy materials that give the shoe an almost barefoot feel.

I’m a big fan of this shoe for walking, long periods of standing, running, and plyometric workouts. It's incredibly versatile, thanks to ample nitrogen-infused cushioning and a flexible midsole. The FlexZone technology—a strategically placed groove in the center of the shoe’s outsole—helps enhance the shoe’s flexibility and allows the foot to move naturally. Combined with the pods under the front of the foot (which reminds me of On’s signature CloudTec system you see on most of the brand’s outsoles), the shoe has a super bouncy feel without feeling wobbly.

Bonus: at only 8.0 ounces, it's the lightest shoe on this list, so your feet won’t feel bogged down. But it still falls in Schaeffer’s recommended weight range (eight to 10 ounces), so it's hefty enough to keep your foot locked in. Plus, the flat knit upper is super soft, breathable, and—yes—flexible, which adds to its airy feel.

But the shoe’s lighter weight means it offers less heft and a less supportive feel. If you need more structure or have specific stability needs, these might not be your best bet. But, if you’re into a flexible, responsive shoe that doesn’t weigh you down—this one’s tough to beat.

The Brooks Ghost Max L offers a super plush, easygoing stride. The high-stacked cushioning is next-level—soft but stable, like walking on a marshmallow. It has an outsole with a curved bottom, like a rocking chair, to help propel you forward so each step takes a bit less energy.

I didn’t expect to notice the rocker bottom that much, but I totally get the hype. Schaeffer says he actually prefers rocker-bottom shoes for walking, especially as we get older, because they help take pressure off joints. That said, the same rocker technology makes me feel a little off-balance when I try to run or power walk in them, so I keep these strictly for leisurely walks and casual wear.

Looks-wise, I’m team Ghost Max L all the way. Some might say the stacked foam gives grandma shoes, but I think it strikes that perfect balance of chunky and cool—especially when styled right. I like to wear mine with a wide-leg pant and a blazer on top. It’s got just the right amount of bulk to feel trendy without being clunky, and pairs well with everything from athleisure to workwear.

However, this shoe runs small. Definitely size up if you’re in between sizes or like a little wiggle room. I could have used a half size larger than what I wear in the rest of my Brooks shoes for a little more comfort, but I still get a lot of casual wear out of them regardless.

First things first, you want a good mix of comfort and stability in your walking shoe, says Schaeffer. He recommends looking for a pair that cups your heel in a way that isn’t too snug or too loose. This feature will keep your feet from wobbling with every step you take. That sort of stability keeps your foot aligned as you walk, which is key for overpronation (foot rolls in too much) or underpronation (foot rolls out), helping prevent strain on your joints and maintaining balance. You want a shoe that’s comfortable on your feet, but Shaeffer says to avoid any that are overly cushioned, and instead look for a shoe that is a bit sturdier to keep your feet in neutral alignment to avoid foot fatigue and prevent sprains or strains.

The front of your sneaker (aka toe box) should never be too snug because it can pinch the nerves and inflame the ball of your foot (aka metatarsalgia). One way to know if your toe box is wide enough? Make sure your foot lies one thumb width from the side of the shoe and one thumb width from the front of the shoe. Tip: If you have a longer second toe, a larger toe box is even more important, Schaeffer says.

Brooks is famous for its incredible arch support, which is exactly what Schaeffer says to look for in a walking shoe. However, if your arches need a little extra TLC, Schaeffer suggests getting insoles that cater to your specific foot needs. He recommends Dr. Scholl’s Multipurpose Insoles or custom orthotics. "The insoles help with alignment and keep you balanced," he says, which is especially important if you suffer from chronic pain, plantar fasciitis, or issues with your feet rolling inward or outward while you walk. If this sounds like you, we def recommend scheduling a visit with a podiatrist to make sure your feet get the care they need.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer says to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Schaeffer says most people love a lightweight shoe since it's nice to feel like there's nothing down there. Just make sure the shoe has a supportive feel, and it holds your foot with every step you take. "In this case, I'm okay with the shoe being light," he says. "But, if the shoe is too light (under four ounces), you sacrifice function and stability." All of the Brooks sneakers on this list are between eight and 10 ounces, so they're the perfect weight in Schaeffer's book.

Over the past two years, the Women’s Health team has undertaken a comprehensive approach to curating the ultimate guide to the best Brooks walking shoes by testing nearly every new pair as it drops. Along with insights from Brad Schaeffer, DPM, board-certified foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City, we’ve put more than 30 Brooks sneakers through their paces.

As the associate style and reviews editor, I led the testing process with support from fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi, NASM-CPT, associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, and fitness and reviews editor Charles Thorp, NASM. Our evaluation involved multiple phases, consulting runners and walkers on the Women's Health team, and most importantly, testing the shoes firsthand. We subjected each shoe to everything from fast walks to long travel days to leisurely strolls. The narrowed-down list above includes the six shoes we were most impressed by

#4680. The 8 Best Weight Benches, Tested by Editors and Certified Trainers

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Expand your training possibilities at home with one of these picks.

A TRUE NECESSITY for any real home gym, a great weight bench opens the door to a ton of exercise possibilities. The best weight benches are sturdy and reliable, allowing you access to a whole range of exercises, and the ability to target nearly every muscle in your body.

The best weight benches can be used for way more than just the classics that bear its name, like the bench press. "They're good for everything from chest presses, dumbbell bench presses, incline bench supersets, skull crushers, glute bridges, incline rows to hit your back, ab moves, quad and leg moves like split squats, and more biceps moves than you can imagine," explains Men's Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS Neither flat nor adjustable weight benches occupy as much room as bulkier equipment, such as a hefty power rack, either. And for those that are adjustable, you can easily change the angle on your presses.

Whether you prefer to do your weight work with barbells or dumbbells (or even adjustable dumbbells), the best weight benches are compatible. Plus, many of the best weight benches include attachments and hidden features that allow for an even wider range of workouts, like a leg developer or squat rack.

We've gathered a selection of top-notch weight benches after rigorous testing and research to elevate your training and home gym experience. Keep reading, because you can't go wrong with any of these eight benches.

This model from Hammer Strength was originally introduced in 2016 exclusively for athletics and clubs, and was designed to be a versatile bench with an Olympic rack system. We're such a fan of this brand, we've got quite a few pieces in our own Men's Health gym. It's American-made and sold around the world due to its high-quality, durable construction.

With seven different back pad positions (from −10 degrees for decline lifts and up to 75 degrees for overhead presses), it packs more multi-functionality than most benches out there. Plus, it has built-in wheels, making it great for home gym spaces that require moving a bench around during workouts to accommodate space.

From Samuel's point of view, this is one of the sturdiest benches he's ever used. "Its tough surface lets me create a great base for bench presses," he says. An underrated thing he loves: the comfort of the seat portion of the bench, which allows for locking in a good position during overhead presses and incline curls.

It's more expensive than other options in this guide, but if you're looking for a bench that can keep up with your biggest reps and hardest lifts, this pick has got your back.

REP Fitness nailed it with this piece. This is the bench that I choose to lift with at home. The assembly is as easy as you could hope for with a heavy-duty bench like this. A few separate parts connect with screws and an Allen key. Everything was put together and ready for my workout in less than half an hour (just enough time for you to feel accomplished but not tired).

This bench shines in that it is as comfortable as it is durable. Few benches combine sturdiness, comfort, and versatility like this one from REP Fitness. It offers six different incline angles and a three-post design that anchors it to the floor no matter the exercise. It can also support up to 1,000 pounds, making it a solid option for novice to intermediate lifters.

"The backrest feels way more cushioned than other benches in its class, yet still manages to deliver rigidity when I drive my shoulder blades down for a set of bench presses," explains Samuel. This bench has only a minimal gap between the seat and back, which has never interfered with any of our lifts. It's also not ridiculously heavy (less than 100 pounds), so it's easy to move around my home gym when needed.

It's also a total breeze to adjust from fully flat up to a 90-degree incline. I've never had an issue with either of the two adjustment mechanisms getting stuck. Three seat positions add to its versatility, too. And the roller pads help secure your lower body with decline sit-ups and decline presses.

Read More: Our REP Fitness AB-3000 Review

Bowflex's flagship 5.1S Collapsible Bench is a good mid-range weight bench for small spaces and beginners. What we love most about this bench is its stowable design—when not in use, it can be stored vertically to reduce its footprint by more than 50 percent. For those who only use a bench at home from time to time and aren't pushing hundreds of pounds per exercise, this transformable option is a great choice.

"This bench is rated to support up to 600 pounds, but keep in mind that it's considerably lightweight," says Samuel. "Meaning if you line up on there for, say, incline rows or preacher curls, it may slip. I find it works best for me for bench presses and seated exercises like press, biceps curls, etc."

The position of the leg bar is not perfect, especially for those moving heavy weight, and we found it can act as a roadblock to setting up lifts properly. That being said, there is a good number of exercises that you can do properly with this bench not possible with others. It features six adjustable settings, including 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees, flat, and more decline range than most similar benches we've tested (−20 degrees).

Flat benches often support more weight than their adjustable counterparts, but the REP Fitness FB-3000 tops the charts with the best weight capacity and comfort features of any flat bench we've tested. Grippy vinyl upholstery prevents slippage on its surface when setting up for a lift, and firm, high-density foam cushioning makes driving down feel as stable as benches double its price. There's even an optional wall hanger for stowing it away when not in use.

It stands 17 inches from the floor to the top of the pad, and features a three-post design equipped with wheels and a handle to make moving it around easy. Its dimensions are largely consistent with benches used in powerlifting competitions, ensuring powerlifting users a training experience that closely aligns with professional standards. Talk about setting up for success, right?

"For less than $200, there isn't a better flat bench on the market. Especially for simple, foundational lifts like the bench press," explains Thorp. "I'm a big fan of how simple this bench is, with even padding throughout, making it a solid option for weighted step-ups as well."

The FB-3000 distinguishes itself with incredible value, but it does come with the same limitations as any flat bench: You miss out on a range of exercises that incline positions on adjustable benches provide. A flat bench is great for most powerlifters, but limiting to the rest of us lifting at home. Beyond its performance, this flat bench comes in various colors, including glossy black, red, blue, and textured versions, allowing users to personalize their gym setup.

Following extensive testing over the years, we've determined this bench to be the most versatile, and a standout in this guide of solid choices, which is why it made our Men’s Health Fitness Awards. This adjustable bench from Prime Fitness USA earned its spot primarily due to its stability—unlike lighter benches, it stays put during exercises on nearly any surface we've tested. Boasting a weight capacity of 1,000 pounds when flat and 600 pounds in an incline position, it can handle substantial weights for various fitness levels.

Seven adjustable backrest positions provide more flexibility than most benches, and the cushioning strikes a perfect balance between comfort and stability. The bench's quick switch between incline settings is also ultra smooth and efficient. Our Fitness Director Samuel enjoys this piece so much he wishes it was an option in the commercial gyms he frequents.

Heavy lifters will love how immovable this bench is: Unlike some lighter benches, it won’t slide away from you with exercises like chest-supported rows—regardless of the surface. With the substantial weight capacity, we felt confident and stable pushing heavy weight on this bench. The trade-off is that it's heavy itself, and while it has built-in wheels for transport, we wouldn't plan on taking it up and down the stairs a lot.

The cushioning manages to be comfortable while still providing a stable, sturdy base. Speaking of bases, the footprint on this bench is more sizable than most, so consider dimensions carefully if you're tight on space.

For those in search of a better-looking bench fit for your living room or guest room, this new offering from Matrix is a great option. The build is commercial-grade, and fit for most heavy lifts. This bench is part of a set the manufacturer offers that includes adjustable dumbbells and a storage rack, for those who are seeking a sleek-looking package.

"I like how easy it is to move and store this bench for how stable and sturdy it is," says Thorp. "Combined with the adjustable dumbbells, it brings everything that I need for a solid workout to my basement, with an aesthetic that elevates the room."

As sturdy as the bench is, it lacks the weight capacity of the Prime or the Hammer Strength benches. Able to handle up to 650 pounds, it should withstand the majority of training scenarios, but if you're a bodybuilder looking to move some real weight, there are probably better places to look in this guide.

The versatility of this bench is another highlight, with five different angles of incline and the ability to reverse the backpad to better support individuals with different body types or other comfort demands. The wheels and handle make it easy to move, and storing against the wall for additional floor space is simple.

This flat bench from Flybird is a suitable option for beginners who are tight on space, offering good value at right around $100. While there are higher-quality flat benches available at a higher price point, the foldable legs make it a standout choice for storage when not in use. The pin and lock system for the folding legs is efficient, taking less than a minute to set up or break down.

The bench is also extremely lightweight, making it easy to move and store as needed. However, for those performing lifts with dumbbells over 50 pounds, a heavier option is preferable for more stability. Despite its lightness, we found it reliable for various exercises like light dumbbell presses, curls, and skullcrushers at home.

According to Samuel, this is a very solid entry-level bench. "It's more on the cushioned side and actually very comfortable," he explains. "It's obviously not going to do incline and is prone to sliding, so you definitely want a yoga mat under it." It's a budget-friendly option suitable for novice and intermediate lifters, as long as precautions are taken to stabilize the bench.

This bench has become Amazon’s top-selling option because it comes almost fully assembled and seems easy to store. It isn’t the lightest option out there but, for the bench’s advertised versatility, the weight isn’t too bad and it folds up neatly.

We have reservations about this bench though, as it isn’t as stable as it appears—while having a 660-pound capacity, that doesn’t mean you can count on security for all of the movements you might do with it. The padding separation that makes it possible to fold may cause some discomfort when doing decline presses or sit-ups.

While it won’t be at the top of our recommendations for serious lifters (it will shift on you), it seems to be a decent budget option for beginners who aren’t sure how much they’re going to spend on home gym equipment. Though there is a little added peace of mind coming at the hands of Amazon’s classification, indicating that it’s a product “customers usually keep.”

First and foremost, you'll need a weight bench strong enough to handle your training regimen—and even if you're not doing heavyweight moves, you'll want it to support a decent amount of load. That's because it's about more than your bodyweight and the weight you're training with; each time you set up on the bench, there's potential for additional impact. In general, aim for a bench that can support at least 500 pounds; that'll set you up for success in nearly all your training and support more advanced exercises that bring even more impact (such as step-ups and plyometric Bulgarians).

The right balance between stiff and cushioned padding is essential to ensure your bench will stay in good condition with use. Highly cushioned benches might feel nice, but they tend to deform over time, creating an uneven surface. This can also compromise your form during workouts, especially when your spine or shoulders are required to stay in alignment. While most padding is stitched to the bench, some is stapled, which tends to lift away from the bench’s frame eventually. Not enough padding isn't good either, as you'll feel like you're lying on a plywood board.

If you plan on using your adjustable bench for flat bench variations, be mindful of the distance between the back pad and seat pad (otherwise known as the ‘pad gap’). Anything larger than 2 inches will be noticeable and may feel uncomfortable during certain lifts.

In general, the three types of weight benches are flat, adjustable incline, and adjustable incline/decline. The first two are pretty self-explanatory and the latter, of course, adds versatility for decline-angle exercises. "If you're unsure which bench to get, opt for a bench with incline-angle options. Sure, this may cost slightly more initially, but it'll set you up with a bench that can grow with you," explains Samuel. "In general, most website workouts and app workouts assume that, if you're training with a bench, it has incline options. So not having incline options can set you up for frustration. It'll also heavily limit your ability to vary your workouts in fun ways. The incline bench is the most future-proofed purchase option."

If you're a powerlifter, or you're buying a bench for a particular program, a flat bench might be perfect. Decline-angle benches open up new movements (especially when it comes to core training), but they're generally unnecessary. Think of that as your luxury option.

Like all home gym equipment, weight benches can take up a lot of room. If you’re tight on space or just appreciate being able to move your equipment out of the way, consider a collapsible weight bench or, at the very least, one with wheels. If you’re after an adjustable weight bench, wheels should be a top priority. Because they’re on the heavier side, this will make stowing away and setting up tremendously easier. You don't want setting up your bench every session to be a part of your workout.

Return policies and warranties represent the manufacturer’s confidence in its product. And with most home gym equipment manufacturers, the better the quality, the better the warranty. In the case that something goes wrong with your bench, it’s important to know your investment is protected, so look for benches that come with at least a one-year warranty.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, my job is to evaluate the latest and greatest training equipment available. I've had extensive experience with weight benches in both the training facilities I've worked out of and the home gyms I've built. I also consulted with Men's Health fitness experts, editors, and writers on the top weight benches they’ve experienced firsthand. The experts included our own Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. The team has tested dozens of weight benches over the years, from high-end, commercial-grade models to budget options.

Our extensive testing process involved a comprehensive evaluation of multiple factors—including size, durability, performance, suitability for different fitness levels, and value—to ensure that we recommend only the best. We tested each weight bench through exercise routines that included flat and adjustable bench moves, covering a wide range of motions and use scenarios. To determine stability and structural integrity, we tested benches at both comfortable and near-maximum capacities, allowing us to assess performance under varying loads.

To gather diverse perspectives, we consulted with our MH Advisory Board and Strength in Diversity trainers, who provided valuable feedback on the top weight benches based on their expertise and experiences. The result is the picks for the best weight benches you can buy right now.

You don’t necessarily need a weight bench to get strong and build muscle, but having one gives you access to a host of exercises (regardless of fitness level), especially when it comes to upper-body training.

Most basic exercises that beginners should master, like dumbbell presses and single-arm dumbbell rows and hip thrusts, are much easier to execute with a bench (especially an adjustable one). Meanwhile, more advanced lifters can get incredible mileage out of a bench by unlocking more innovative moves like half-bench single-arm presses and single-arm rows.

Here's a breakdown of the key differences:

A flat weight bench is designed with a fixed, flat surface, whereas an adjustable weight bench allows you to adjust the angle of the bench to different incline or, in some cases, decline angles.

"The adjustable benches that offer a decline setting are a terrific value for anyone who wants to get creative with their core exercises while training at home," says Samuel.

"Adjustable benches give you so many more options for your exercises," explains David Otey, C.S.C.S and Men's Health Advisory Board member. "Instead of just working at flat or upright, all of the angles in between can give you variety and diversity in your training options." Those angles allow you to bias muscle groups in different, more selective ways. A flat weight bench limits you to exercises that can be performed on a flat surface.

Adjustable benches offer more convenience overall (especially well-built ones), offering access to more movements and angles. Adjustable benches also offer support for extra movements, such as overhead presses and lateral raises, which can allow for greater loading of those movements in the long term. But flat weight benches win for convenience in two areas. They're generally lighter, so you can more easily move them around your gym, and they're easier to stow when not in use, too.

Because flat weight benches generally have fewer mechanisms and lack a hinge of any sort, they'll be easier to maintain. Adjustable benches don't require a ton of maintenance, but it's worthwhile every so often to check on bolts and caps, and make sure your hinge mechanism is working smoothly.

We consulted with Men's Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., for the best exercises for beginners to get the most out of a weight bench.

#4679. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.
