#4649. The 10 Best Skincare Brands for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Editor

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Save yourself time aimlessly browsing the ever-expanding men's skincare aisle with these guaranteed winners.

AS A GROOMING editor, I’m constantly testing products from both emerging brands and classic favorites, which culminates in two major outcomes. First, I’m regularly discovering new and exciting ingredients that I’m allergic to (please patch test—do as I say, not as I do, etc.). But more importantly, I’ve come to be intimately familiar with which brands are consistently putting out the best-feeling and overall most effective products to include in your daily skincare routine.

In recent years, the men’s grooming industry has been exploding, with new options dropping every week. As a result, there have never been more brands available, and choosing which to try has never been more overwhelming. The shelves are packed with a selection of skincare products which, let’s get real, can feel a little daunting.

The good news is that there are now plenty of options out there for every guy, but cutting through the noise to find what actually works can be a hassle. To ease this decision-making tension when choosing serums, moisturizers, soaps, or other grooming products, these are the best brands for men.

I love Marlowe products mainly because the brand never overthinks this whole skincare thing. Its products are simple and effective. The creams are smooth and long-lasting without being heavy; the soaps are deeply cleansing with strong lathers, and the deodorants smell great while providing day-long protection.

The brand heavily features natural ingredients (which I love) and never includes any irritating chemicals like parabens or phthalates (which my sensitive skin hates). Not to mention, many of the products are sustainably packaged, including the soap wrappers, which are made of 100 percent recycled materials. Simply put, when I’m browsing the skincare aisle (or more accurately, Amazon’s skincare page), Marlowe is the most reliable brand I can find time after time.

Product Highlight: The Marlowe No. 102 Body Scrub Soaps get a lot of love thanks to their clean formulas backed by always-moisturizing green tea, shea butter, and olive oil, as well as incredible, cologne-quality scents like santal or oud wood. Not to mention, insanely strong lathers that help these bars last for weeks.

But if I had to pick one facial moisturizer to wear for the rest of my life, it’d probably be the No. 128 Daily Face Lotion with SPF 50. Not only is it the best SPF moisturizer around, but it’s also one of the most nourishing, hydrating, and non-irritating moisturizers, full stop, SPF or not.

Read More: Marlowe No. 128 Daily Face Lotion Review

Founded in 1965, Baxter of California is one of the oldest grooming brands on this list. As a result, it has a wide range of skincare solutions, but has really been able to zero in on options for sensitive skin over the years.

The brand’s most notable skincare products are all either fragrance-free, like theOil-Free Moisturizerand Daily Face Wash, or mildly scented so as not to irritate skin, like the Exfoliating Body Wash. And while the latter’s oak moss and cedar scent is certainly subtle, it’s also delightfully woodsy and lasts much longer than its initial intensity would suggest.

Product Highlight: The facial scrub is backed by walnut shell powder, which helps shrink pores and absorb oil, and moisturizing avocado oil to create a gentle, soothing exfoliation. The container is also barely over $20 and lasts forever, as you only need a small dime-sized dose to cover your entire face.

If your skin is prone to dryness, there’s a good chance that you already have some La Roche-Posay in your medicine cabinet. But if you haven’t tried the brand and you often battle flakes, redness, or other issues associated with dry skin, I can say with no hyperbole that I’m about to change your life. La Roche-Posay products heavily feature skin-soothing gems like niacinamide, glycerin, and ceramides, all of which help restore the skin's moisture barrier and promote a healthy microbiome.

The creams feel as gentle as any I’ve tested, and most are fragrance-free to avoid any unnecessary irritation. Not to mention, the brand has more products officially accepted by the National Eczema Association than I can count (I also hate doing math, but that’s beside the point). You simply won’t find better skincare for dry skin than La Roche-Posay.

Product Highlight: Speaking of the brand’s plethora of National Eczema Association-approved products, the Lipikar AP+M Triple Repair Body Moisturizer is specifically designed to combat dry skin with a formula featuring soothing shea butter and glycerin, ceramide-3 to strengthen and protect the skin’s natural barrier, and niacinamide with its anti-inflammatory properties.I’m prone to dry skin pretty much everywhere (especially during the cooler months), but I lather this stuff on twice a day, and it’s barely an issue anymore. Plus, it absorbs faster than any other body lotion I’ve tried.

Read More: La Roche-Posay Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 with BEMT Review

This UK-based skincare brand is heavy on the science and uses its own labs to develop products focused on keeping your skin healthy in the most effective way possible. Built on three pillars—sun protection, vitamin C, and retinol—these products not only help your skin live its best life now, but protect it from signs of aging in the future.

It’s an extensive line with popular favorites like the Crystal Retinal Ceramide Eye Cream, C-Tetra Vitamin C Serum, and the Advanced Night Ceramide Cream to set your skin up for success.

Product Highlight: Of all the best-sellers mentioned, there is none I ride harder for than the Crystal Retinal Ceramide Eye. You may have noticed the retinal in that title, rather than the far more common retinol, but that isn’t a typo. Just like retinol, retinal is a vitamin A derivative with anti-aging and acne-fighting properties. It’s a slightly more potent vitamin A derivative, however, meaning two things.

One, it’ll clear skin and reward it with additional elasticity even more successfully than retinol options. And two, it’s way easier (and more harmful) to overuse than retinol, so take it slow and easy if you’re new to the ingredient. Too much product can result in irritation and drying (been there!), which is not fun.

You’ll likely find this French grooming brand in the medicine cabinet of your coolest, most in-the-know friend. It’s a Parisian-born brand that merges the French sensibility of simplicity with modern natural ingredients.

What started with highly effective and pleasant-to-use face products (try the Mattifying Face Moisturizer and Anti-Dark Circle Cleanser) has now expanded to beard products like luxuriously scented beard oils, body lotion, and hair products (even solid shampoo).

But what we really dig about Horace is the brand’s commitment to offering options for various skin types or unique concerns. In fact, Horace’s website even includes a consultation quiz you can take to ensure you’re set up with a curated list of items to address your specific needs.

Product Highlight: As someone who has struggled with easily irritated skin and redness, I ride hard for Horace’s Balanced Skin Set. It features the Purifying Face Cleanser, which delicately cleanses skin while eliminating excess oil, and the Hyaluronic Acid and Panthenol Serum to then provide immediate moisture, leaving skin feeling softer for longer.

The trio is then topped off with the Mattifying Face Moisturizer to hydrate and protect skin. Not to mention, it doesn’t leave any greasy residue behind. This routine has eliminated facial redness time after time for me.

Horace also has some great, surprisingly affordable colognes, the highlight of which is Horace Vintage Vanilla. It’s leathery and cozy, perfect for cooler weather.

What started with a razor designed to minimize ingrown hairs has since exploded into a full-on grooming empire with thoughtful, solution-oriented products to be used from head to toe. The brand was conceived to provide grooming products to men of color, specifically, but these innovative and effective products can be used by all people regardless of skin color or type, like the soothing aloe vera and coconut water infused face and beard wash, or body wash, which is the body wash which we found to be the most moisturizing option available. Best of all, rarely are these products above $15.

Product Highlight: Obviously, Bevel has come a long way from its ingrown hair-fighting origins, but the brand’s exfoliating toner pads are still hard to beat. Thanks to a powerful combination of green tea and 10 percent glycolic acid, they prepare skin for additional products by deeply cleansing and clearing any lingering gunk on the face, while minimizing the risk of ingrown hairs or other blemishes by exfoliating the skin.

Developed by the former president of Kiehl’s, Chris Salgardo, this men’s grooming brand provides innovative and intuitive products that are deceptively simple. The founder developed all the formulas from scratch using natural, non-toxic ingredients, and used his learnings from his years in skincare to create products that don’t just work, but that you actually want to use.

Similar to Horace, Atwater breaks out products by unique needs. However, it’s a bit more streamlined with three simple options: normal/combination, dry, and oily. While the dry and normal options are also stellar, no other brand nails the demands of oily skin better.

Product Highlight: This is led by the Oil Regulator Facial Cleansing Bar and Oil Regulator Facial Moisturizer. The moisturizer is great, as its gel-consistency is both lightweight and non-greasy, so oily folks can use it without fear of residue; however, the cleansing bar is what’s truly special. Most people with oily skin understand the importance of using lightweight, non-greasy moisturizers and creams, but few pinpoint the importance of soap in this journey.

So many standard soaps and washes strip away skin’s natural oils, causing it to overcompensate and produce more sebum (aka how our skin naturally fights dryness) to restore its moisture balance. Not this bar, though—with hero ingredients like charcoal to target excess oil and sebum, and glycerin to restore the skin’s naturally balanced moisture levels, there are few better options for oily skin.

Bravo Sierra started in 2018 with a simple goal: Create military-grade personal care products that can withstand the most extreme conditions without the use of any harsh ingredients like parabens, sulfates, or silicones.

In just a few years, the high-performance brand was offering upgrades on daily essentials like bar soap, body wash, and deodorant with better ingredients, as well as incredible, elevated scents like orris and santal, and bergamot and musk. Bravo Sierra never forgets its military-inspired roots either, donating over $500,000 to veterans organizations since its inception, according to cofounder Benjamin Bernet.

Product Highlight: I’ve written quite a bit about Bravo Sierra’s incredible deodorant and how its unscented option is the best fragrance-free deodorant on the market, but the scented versions are equally great. Whenever I’m going camping or planning a long hike, I turn to Bravo Sierra’s deodorants because they go on clear, contain probiotics to help control bacteria, and truly withstand the elements.

I once competed in a 10k trail run in the rain wearing the bergamot and musk, and you better believe I was the best-smelling dude there post-run, as the scent was still lingering after all that. The brand’s cleansing bar soaps also deserve a shout-out as one of the most multipurpose soaps (formulated for face, hair, and body) while packing the same stellar scent.

Status skincare is a thing, and Aesop pretty much invented it. Using natural ingredients and elevated scents, these products don’t just look good on your bathroom counter; they actually work to cleanse, hydrate, and fortify your skin, hair, and body.

But anyone who has ever used Aesop products knows that, among the slick designs and soothing formulas, the aspect that really stands out is the scents. From the earthy sandalwood blend of the Moroccan Neroli Post-Shave Lotion to the fresh, citrus-scented Bitter Orange Astringent Toner, it’s no wonder the brand sells its own parfum bottles.

Product Highlight: This product selection is wide, so I’d recommend starting with a bundle that features curated product groupings based on skin type and need. But a special shout-out to the Parsley Seed AntiOxidant Intense Serum, which is a perfect do-it-all serum for daily use, and the Coriander Seed Body Cleanser, one of the best-smelling body washes around.

You probably already know about Harry’s thanks to their hard-to-beat razors and shaving products that revolutionized the cartridge razor game, but if you haven’t explored the brand’s skin, body, and other beard products, you’re missing out. The brand known for inexpensive and easy-to-use shaving solutions now offers an entire range to keep you groomed and fresh from head to toe, including the 2025 Men’s Health Grooming Award-winning black lip balm backed by meadowfoam for lasting moisturization.

Product Highlight: The Exfoliating Face Wash and moisturizing Daily Face Lotion for your mug are a couple of my favorite budget options available. The face wash is especially useful, as it helps minimize any irritation or ingrowns after shaving with the help of hero ingredient, volcanic rock, which works to remove dead skin cells and promote cell turnover.

Being a great skincare brand doesn’t necessarily mean all-encompassing. Not every label offers every product, and this is a good thing. I love a wide selection, but nobody can nail everything, even the greats (further reading: Michael Jordan’s baseball career).

Instead, look for brands that have perfected their corner of the skincare world with key products that are specialized to certain objectives, like Bevel with reducing shave irritation or La Roche-Posay with sensitive-skin-friendly creams. This will result in the highest quality options for every skincare need.

Let’s be honest, for many dudes, this is really the main concern when it comes to buying skincare products. Prices can vary substantially across categories, with one moisturizer costing $20, like Marlowe’s No. 128, and another surpassing $50, like Medik8’s C-Tetra Day Cream. Does this mean Medik8 is $30 better and more effective? Not necessarily, but the pricier you go, typically the more specialized the formulas are. So it really comes down to personal preference, need, and budget.

These are generally the basics. That’s not to say they’re lower-quality, just simpler formulas with more wide-ranging attributes. For example, Marlowe’s No. 121 Facial Cleanser is $14 and is uber effective for all skin types. However, if your skin tends to be especially oily and you want a cleanser with a cologne-quality scent, look to Aesop’s Amazing Face Cleanser for $36, which would find itself in the next cost bracket. Speaking of…

In this range, you’ll find plenty of specialized formulas and quality scents. To combat fine lines and wrinkles, especially if you also have sensitive or dry skin, the La Roche-Posay Hyalu B5 Hyaluronic Acid Serum is ideal. However, to provide that level of additional elasticity to your skin without aggravating it, you have to spend a bit more, which is why it’s $40.

The same goes for Atwater’s Eye Armor anti-aging eye cream. This $32 tube offers nourishment and hydration to fight puffiness and wrinkles at a level lower-priced eye creams might struggle with.

Still, the products you’ll find in this range aren’t the most expensive available. Instead, they’re more mid-tier when it comes to cost. Think of them like a frisky four- or five-seed team that can absolutely make a run in the NCAA tournament, rather than the favorite ones or twos—those would be your luxury options.

Now we’re in the high-end zone. If you’re looking at one skincare product that’s over $50, it’ll either be in a humongous Costco-type container or offering a level of luxury other products simply cannot.

There is no shame in surpassing these options if you’re on a budget or have fairly uncomplicated skin with minimal long-term concerns. Just as there is also nothing wrong with indulging for those who are able. You won’t find many night creams more skin-firming or youth-boosting than the Medik8 Advanced Night Ceramide, which is why it’s $78.

As a grooming editor, I’m constantly putting skincare products to the test and evaluating their feel and efficiency. It is quite literally my job. In fact, I drop a recurring column on the latest and greatest new products in the field, so it’s safe to say that I’m up to date on brands and their skincare offerings.

#4648. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4646. Volkswagen may have just hinted at the name of its next affordable EV

Volkswagen is getting ready to launch a new electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW plans to call it.

The new entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

The new model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

Volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its new MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

Volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

Volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

The VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen previously said the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

Volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

Ah, finally a car in the upper range of being meaningful and sensible.

If someone needs more, then those are obviously special needs people. Being like can't enter and exit such a sensible car. Or like having to move the 15 horses of their 5 daughters. Or being a fieldworker driving a gazillion miles every day. Or requiring a lot of attention from lesser beings.

In March, the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture tested the new SDV architecture on the ID. EVERY1, alongside Audi and Scout reference vehicles, validating over-the-air (OTA) capabilities.

The new architecture will enable “highly automated driving features” and “advanced infotainment solutions,” with continuous OTA updates.

While VW said it will deploy the SDV architecture in “electric vehicles across markets in the Western Hemisphere,” the entry-level EV is not expected to reach the States.

Volkswagen is, however, preparing to launch the ID. Tiguan, which will launch in 2027 as the successor to the ID.4 (and ID.5 in Europe).

#4645. The Courage to Disagree

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

At 23, Mike Soutar was appointed editor of the British teen pop magazine Smash Hits. It was an amazing opportunity at such a young age for someone who had left school and started life as a journalist just six years earlier.

Soutar was much younger than editors working on other titles; in fact, he was younger than almost everyone on his own team. Feeling the need to be seen as a strong, decisive leader, he modeled himself on the powerful authority figures he had seen in Hollywood movies.

His leadership was falling flat, and after a couple of weeks, the organisation’s CEO, Sir Robin Miller, visited him. Sir Robin gave Soutar some advice that has stuck with him to this day: “A great day in the office is when I lose more arguments than I win."

What initially seemed counterintuitive—how can you assert authority if you are constantly shown to be wrong?—became a central mantra for a career that took Soutar to the pinnacle of the media world.

Encouraging disagreement lies at the heart of Soutar’s definition of a great leader. Why, if disagreement can be so valuable, are we often so reluctant to challenge each other?

Many of us naturally like the easy life. It’s tempting to keep our heads down, get on with our work, and avoid being marked as a troublemaker.

In her research into speaking truth to power, Professor Megan Reitz, leadership expert and author of Speak Out, Listen Up, has explored why people remain silent, even when they have something important to contribute.

Reitz told me about a leader who was frustrated that employees weren't speaking up and assumed they needed to become more assertive or articulate. But when she and her colleagues spoke to those employees, one response revealed a rather different problem: "Last time somebody spoke up around here, they disappeared."

The issue wasn't a lack of courage. It was what people believed might happen if they challenged authority. As Reitz explained, our willingness to express an opinion depends not just on our own confidence, but on how the person listening behaves and how safe they make us feel.

Growing awareness of the need for psychological safety has led leaders to tell their teams it’s OK to speak up and challenge. But telling people they have a safe space isn’t enough; you have to demonstrate it. Trust develops through repeated interactions and consistent behaviour.

When Mike Soutar reflected on the advice he took from Sir Robin Miller, he explained how he saw a culture of positive dissent in the workplace evolving.

“It starts with trust so that everybody knows that they can voice their feelings, their doubts, their own opinions.

From there, it moves into constructive dissent, where ideas are challenged rather than individuals attacked. Then it moves into decision-making, where the leader weighs the arguments and reaches a conclusion.

Finally, you move to accountability, where the leader parcels out the jobs, timelines, and deadlines, with everybody getting behind the decision that's been made.

When I understood this, it transformed my capabilities as a leader because it meant I could take people with me.”

Building constructive dissent on a foundation of trust creates an environment where people actively seek alternate opinions to create better outcomes, rather than spiraling into a destructive culture of blame and competition.

Disagreement that leads to better decisions ultimately strengthens working relationships, creating a positive cycle that reinforces a safe space for dissent.

The ability to challenge and dissent doesn’t mean you will always get your way, but you should always be heard. That only works when the leader genuinely engages, listens, and is seen to welcome challenge.

Soutar later moved into his first managing director role at the London dance radio station Kiss FM, where one of his first moves was to change the station’s playlist policy. He wanted the station to focus on playing only "new" music—nothing more than two years old. To mark the shift, he planned a symbolic bonfire of old records in the station’s car park.

The proposal provoked strong opposition among both staff and listeners, who felt that Soutar was destroying a culture they cared deeply about. People warned him, but he dismissed their criticism.

“We didn't end up having a bonfire. I’m glad this happened before social media existed, because I think I would have been hounded out of a job.

All around me, I had people telling me in advance, ‘This is a really bad idea’. And I didn't listen to them because I took it personally.”

Knowing that constructive dissent matters is one thing, but welcoming it when your own judgment is being questioned is quite another. A culture of dissent has to be source-agnostic, focusing on the idea itself rather than the person who suggested it.

Professor Reitz, whose research explores speaking truth to power, warns that leaders often underestimate the signals they send when challenged. They may genuinely believe they are approachable, yet their colleagues experience something quite different.

Reitz calls these behaviours "shut-up signals," the often-unintentional gestures and responses that discourage people from speaking openly. She describes how her own "thinking face" can become a frown when she's particularly interested in a conversation. Someone who doesn't know her might interpret that expression as disapproval.

The danger is particularly acute when someone challenges a leader's judgment. As Reitz warns, "If you respond poorly, you can just forget about ever getting difficult feedback again."

Leaders need to respond to dissent with curiosity rather than judgment. Seek to uncover why someone disagrees and what they might see differently.

We can often react too quickly, shutting down debate without taking time to reflect. Even if the challenge isn’t ultimately accepted, a good leader will return to the person who flagged an alternative approach, acknowledge their contribution, and explain what they have decided.

Demonstrating that their perspective was considered and valued reinforces trust and encourages them to try again.

Sir Robin Miller made a huge impact on the young Mike Soutar when he said, “A great day in the office is when I lose more arguments than I win.” He helped Soutar recognise that effective leaders don’t need to win every argument, but that better decisions come when you invite dissent.

Constructive dissent requires challenge on both sides: the courage to challenge and the courage to invite challenge.

When was the last time someone challenged your thinking, and what did your response teach them about whether they should do so again?

#4644. The Best Men's Boots, Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Blundstone and Tecovas came out on top in our testing.

I DIDN’T START out as a “boot guy.” I always thought they were clunky, poorly stitched and didn’t provide enough insole support like my favorite Nike Air Force 1s. But 15 years ago, I bought my first pair of Timberland 6-Inch Premium Boots because a brutal winter hit the East Coast, and slipping around in sneakers wasn’t going to cut it. I needed something that could survive the rain, snow, and slush. It didn’t take long to realize that once fall hits, having a solid pair (or two) in rotation is a non-negotiable. That first leather lace-up carried me through snowball fights and more than a few questionable bar floors—and it sold me on what a good boot can do.

Since then, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested well over 50 pairs across every silhouette imaginable: cowboy boots, hiking boots, waterproof commuters, dressier Chelsea styles, heritage work boots—the whole lineup. I’ve worn them on shoots, to weddings, on rainy office days, and on long travel runs, and I can confirm: not every boot is bulky. The right pair can feel as clean and sleek as your favorite sneakers. So if you’re looking for something versatile enough to move from the office to the bar or carry you from one event to the next, we’ve got you covered. Our picks deliver comfort, durability, and style, whether you need a tough trail option, something practical for wet commutes, or a sleek pair for a night out.

The iconic Blundstone #585 still reigns supreme for its comfort, durability, and style. Part Chelsea boot, part work boot, its leather feels soft with a pre-distressed texture, while inside is cushy and snug from the moment you put it on. We didn’t feel any tightness or have to wait a couple of wears for it to mold to our feet. Our editor Tim Kohut wears it at his standing desk for seven hours straight, and his feet never give in or develop blisters. He even took it on a weekend hike and felt comfortable the whole way, hills, dips, and all. The pull tabs also make it easy to slide your foot in and out.

I’ve worn warmer boots in my testing, but they were much bulkier. This pair has a lighter, slimmer build, yet works for general fall and winter gear. The boot’s leather upper dries in minutes, whether I get caught in light showers or trudge through three inches of snow. Yes, the material can scuff if you’re not careful, but a quick wipe with a damp cloth brings it right back. After months of near-daily wear, the elastic panels haven’t stretched out, the sole hasn’t flattened, and the leather has developed a natural patina versus looking beat up. Underfoot, the synthetic polyurethane midsole feels like a thick layer of cushioning, softening every step, especially on New York’s uneven sidewalks.

In the toe area, my feet have wiggle room instead of feeling cramped. Whether for style or performance, this boot works in a variety of settings. I’ve worn mine with a sweater and dark denim for dinner as well as chinos for the office, and it pairs seamlessly with any casual staples like a flannel overshirt, tee, and jeans under a fall jacket. The price tag may give you pause, but most boots that I’ve spent over $100 on are worth it. You don’t have to baby this one. It looks good as new after being worn everywhere, so it’s a reliable option for work, travel, and trail.

Read More: Blundstone 585 Chelsea Boot Review

When our senior fitness and commerce editor Brett Williams slipped into the Beckett Simonon Bolton Chelsea, he immediately called out how sharp it looked. This Chelsea boot—a style originating in 19th-century Britain as a close-fitting riding boot with elastic side panels—elevates whatever you’re wearing. The super premium, full-grain calfskin leather has a natural sheen and structure, and the almond-shaped toe box gives it a sleek profile that reads dressy. Inside, the Vachetta leather lining helped keep his foot cool and surprisingly comfortable after hours at his standing desk.

Brett wore it with suits, dress pants, and black denim on shoot days, and it held up across the board. And yes, Chelseas aren’t strictly “formal only” anymore, but the Bolton proves that a dress-leaning Chelsea can still be incredibly versatile. The stitched construction makes it lighter and more flexible than the typical Goodyear-welted options. It’s easily one of the best leather Chelsea boots on the market because it nails every detail: premium calfskin, a breathable lining, a sleek silhouette, and real comfort. Plenty of Chelseas look the part but feel clunky or overly stiff, so the $279 is justifiable.

Our grooming editor, Sean Zucker, took the Amberjack Chukka for a proper test run, and he came back raving about how wildly comfortable it felt from the jump. The full-grain leather upper and sheepskin lining give it a polished look, but the real magic is underfoot: the heat-activated insole that molds to your feet after a few wears. Plus, the lightweight outsole feels closer to a cushy sneaker than a traditional boot.

Sean wore it on rainy commutes, into the office, and around the city on weekend errands. He didn’t have any sore arches or slips on wet sidewalks. The leather ages nicely over time, and the overall vibe lands squarely in that “smart casual” sweet spot. It works with chinos and slim trousers, and can stretch to dark denim, but it’s not meant to stand in for a dress boot.

If you’ve dismissed cowboy boots as too costumey, Tecovas offers a sleek option that balances rugged style and pairs with a bunch of casual and dressy fits. The round-toe design features a tough, beautiful cowhide leather that wears well whether you’re dressing up or down. The cowhide leather gives the Cartwright a durable feel, while its classic round toe and signature stitching keep the design recognizable.

Surprisingly, I didn’t have to break this boot in. From the first wear, it felt comfortable without any pinching or stiffness. To coincide with the theme, I wore it to Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter concert in New Jersey, and I stood the entire three hours. During the first half of the show, it started lightly raining, but the leather dried in seconds. While it’s not as grippy on slippery surfaces as the Merrell and Timberland boots, it’s stable enough for most city sidewalks. Our editors found it to be suitable for the office, the bar, or even a wedding. It’s one of those boots that you can wear year-round. Tecovas offers a few different colors, but we’re especially into the hazelnut, which looks great with dark jeans or dressier pants.

What really makes this Tecovas pair stand out is how approachable it feels, especially if you’ve never owned a cowboy boot before. The 12-inch shaft—the part of the boot that rises from your ankle to your lower calf—isn’t overly tall or stiff, so it slips easily under straight or relaxed-fit jeans. Also, the 1½-inch heel is low and manageable, so you get a classic cowboy shape without feeling like you’re walking on a block. Fit-wise, it runs true to size and feels secure without squeezing the instep, which is often the biggest concern with Western-style boots. If you want the look without committing to something flashy or trend-driven, this is a smart, low-risk entry point that still feels elevated.

Timberland’s classic work boot has outlasted trendy styles for decades because it’s durable, has a timeless design, and goes with everything. Aptly named the “Butters”, it’s one of the most recognizable boots because of its signature cut and proportions: the high top, thick lug sole, and warm wheat-colored nubuck leather. It’s become a staple across music, streetwear and sports culture. I’ve had it in rotation since I was a teen and still weave it into my casual fits to this day. Yes, it takes one to three wears to break in, but after that you get a snug, customized fit that you can fine-tune with the laces.

The Timberland boot’s cultural relevance hasn’t slowed down, either. A lot of fashion gents like Timothée Chalamet have been spotted wearing Timberland off-duty and even at red carpet events. It also taps into today’s men’s trends, especially the ongoing ’90s-Y2K revival, where baggier denim, boxy jackets, and easy, layered knits are back in rotation.

This boot has full-grain and nubuck leather uppers that can handle scuffs and are fully waterproof, so rain and slush never ruin the look. It's sturdier and heavier than most fashion boots, because it was originally built for work, but it doesn't feel like you’re lugging around bricks all day. The bulk is part of the style, and why it pairs so well with relaxed denim, cargos, and winter fits. Whether I’m walking on wet sidewalks or cobblestone, the lug sole feels stable underfoot.

If we’re judging purely on trail performance, the Merrell Thermo Chill 2 is the best pick for hiking. The mid-height design gives your ankles the extra support they need on uneven terrain, so you’re not wobbling around. Most hiking boot outsoles rely on standard rubber compounds that work well, but they usually sacrifice grip for durability or flexibility. With 200g insulation, this style makes for a perfect winter boot.

It’s fully waterproof, so puddles, rain, or soggy grass aren’t going to slow you down. The main draw here is the exclusive footbed, which molds to your foot, over time, giving each step a cushioned, natural feel. Brower wore this boot on a weekend camping trip, splashing through soggy trails and wet grass, and by the end of it, his feet were dry and comfortable. The mesh on the tongue keeps things breathable, too, so when the sun comes out, your feet don’t feel like they’re baking. While it’s not as sleek as the Danner boot, it’s still a solid-looking boot that you can wear off the trail.

Most rugged boots are kind of ugly, but Danner delivers a trail-ready option that actually looks sharp. The rich tan color paired with red laces gives it a bold yet unique look for the trail. Outside of hikes, our Tech and Gear editor Ryan Brower likes to style it with a flannel shirt and jeans. He’s been wearing it consistently over the last couple fall seasons. It’s not the warmest option in freezing 30-degree temps, so it might be wise to wear with thicker socks. It’s made with full-grain leather uppers, which age beautifully and bead off rain. Plus, the waterproof liners keep water from getting inside.

Full-grain leather is also tougher and more durable than corrected grain or split leather (found in cheaper boots) that have been sanded or split down, losing their outer layers. The break-in period takes a little patience, but after a few wears, this boot feels comfortable and natural. The Vibram outsole grips especially well on uneven terrain, whether you’re climbing trails in the Oregon mountains or navigating slick city streets in New York. Between the outsole and insole, there’s a fiberglass shank—a thin, supportive layer that reinforces the midfoot. It helps keep your feet stable, prevents the boot from twisting, and reduces fatigue on long walks.

Red Wing has been crafting durable, American-made workwear for more than a century, supplying tradesmen, factory workers and miners with boots built to last. The Classic Moc Boot continues that tradition with a roomy moc toe, weatherproof leather construction, and a comfortable wedge sole that makes long hours on your feet far more manageable. (A moc toe is a stitched toe design where the seam wraps around the front of the boot, giving extra room and durability.)

Men’s Health designer Jason Speakman broke it in on a hike in upstate New York. Since the leather is a bit hefty, it did take some getting used to. But after about two or three wears, he said it didn’t feel as cramped as other moc toe boots he's tested. There was no strain on his feet after going from rocks to packed trails, and they stayed comfortable even on uneven terrain. Aesthetically, it has the rugged, All-American vibe that works on a job site, weekend trail, or just rolling up to the beer hall in jeans. The full-grain oiled leather is super premium, so this option will last years and develop a cool, worn-in patina.

After doing some work in the yard for hours on end, Speakman found the EVA midsole—which is a foam material that’s both lightweight and strong—makes this boot the most comfortable option for raking leaves and pushing a lawnmower. It also handles hard surfaces like concrete or brick, keeping your feet cushioned and protected from constant pounding.

If you’re looking for a hiking boot that won’t make your wallet flinch but still performs like something far more expensive, the Nortiv8’s offering is an easy win. On the trail it proved, while affordable, that it’s not cheaply made. Right out of the box, the waterproof synthetic leather and textile upper felt surprisingly substantial—not floppy or flimsy like some lower-cost boots. The material stood up to brush and rocks on a muddy forest loop, and after hours of hauling gear and setting up camp in wet grass, it still looked crisp with no signs of fraying.

The waterproof membrane lived up to its promise during shallow creek crossings and soggy morning hikes; my socks stayed dry every time, even when water pooled around my feet. Underfoot, the rubber lug outsole delivered dependable traction. I tested it while fishing and the grip felt stable and sturdy. The midsole’s cushioned EVA foam struck a nice balance too: supportive on long miles but soft enough that my feet didn’t feel trashed by day’s end. It’s not an ultralight trail runner, but for hiking, camping, fishing, and general outdoor wear, the way these materials work together is impressive for the price.

Not many boots can pull off a tailored suit, but Frye’s luxe ankle style is the rare exception. I’ve been wearing mine for the past couple months, and it instantly makes any semi-formal fit feel sharper. The design is simple but polished with a premium leather upper and is stitched around the edge for extra durability. I wore it in light rain and the material dried in seconds. I also found the inner-side zipper makes life so much easier when I’m slipping it on and off after a long day. It was refreshing that it didn’t require an annoying break-in period. When I first tried it on, I realized I had wiggle room in the toe area right away.

After five wears, the leather starts to crease naturally, but that adds personality to the boot without it looking worn. I’ve tested it on city streets and light rain, and the grip is solid enough to feel confident walking anywhere without slipping or scuffing the leather. The ankle height is flattering, the shape is not heavy-looking, and the richness of the leather colors pairs with different outfits. You can rock jeans and a sweater for a casual lunch, or dress it up with slacks and a blazer.

Sure, this boot isn’t cheap, but the quality, durability, and timeless design make it worth the investment. You’re paying for a boot that will remain in good condition for years, look better as it ages, and feel comfortable from day one.

Leather is a reliable choice for everyday boots because it can be durable and develop character with wear. Full-grain and nubuck each have their own look and feel, but neither guarantees waterproof protection on its own. If you’re regularly walking through rain or slush, look for a waterproof membrane or specifically waterproof construction.

EVA foam midsoles are lightweight and cushioned, perfect for long days on your feet. Some boots use polyurethane midsoles, which are a bit heavier but offer more durability and stability, especially if you’re on rugged terrain.

Your traction and durability depend on this part. Vibram outsoles are often considered the gold standard for their grip and long-lasting wear. Rubber outsoles are common on everyday and outdoor boots because they can provide traction and abrasion resistance. Grip varies by rubber compound and tread pattern, so look for an outsole designed for the surfaces and conditions you’ll encounter.

Goodyear-welted boots can be a good investment because their construction often allows the outsole to be replaced when it wears down. The welt can also help limit water intrusion, although the construction alone doesn’t make a boot waterproof.

Our fashion team, led by longtime boots enthusiast and Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, found the most comfortable and durable options out there. We put more than 50 pairs of boots through the wringer, wearing them across cobblestone New York streets, rainy city commutes, long-distance hikes, and casual weekends around town. In each test, we looked closely at grip, how the soles handled slick surfaces, insulation to keep feet warm in cold weather, and waterproofing to make sure soggy socks weren’t part of the deal. We also rewarded boots that could pull double duty: looking sharp with dress pants or a suit while still holding up for more rugged, off-duty wear.

#4643. Rinnai’s new heat pump water heaters get smarter – and easier to install

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

The new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

#4642. F1 Academy Is Coming to Apple TV, and Its Drivers Are Ready for Their Close-Up

The all-female racing series is getting a bigger platform in the U.S.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Starting in 2027, Apple TV will become the exclusive U.S. streaming home of F1 Academy, the all-female racing series developing the next generation of talent.

Fans will be able to watch every qualifying session and race on Apple TV, bringing more visibility to a series that is quickly gaining momentum. It also expands Apple's partnership with Formula 1, which began its five-year U.S. broadcast deal with the streaming service in 2026.

For Austrian driver Emma Felbermayr, who represents the Audi Revolut F1 team in F1 Academy, the announcement is particularly exciting.

“Apple TV is such a big platform, and it's all about F1 Academy getting more attention,” Felbermayr told Women's Health in Las Vegas ahead of the Grand Prix. “It just makes the interest into the sport much bigger, and that's what we need. We need to have more girls interested in the sport so that we get more attention. In the end, we want to get seen by people."

Launched in 2022, F1 Academy is a Formula 4-level development series designed to create more opportunities for women in motorsport. And its impact extends beyond the racetrack.

At a private dinner in Las Vegas celebrating the Apple TV announcement, F1 Academy managing director Susie Wolff reflected on the series' rapid rise.

“It's incredible how the sport has shifted in the last five to seven years,” Wolff said. “Women have a huge part to play in that shift, and that has been part of the reason why F1 Academy has had so much success in the short space of time.” The dinner event, co-hosted by Wolff and F1 Chief Commercial Officer Emily Prazer, brought together women from across the worlds of sports, entertainment, and advocacy, including activist Malala Yousafzai and model Kelly Piquet.

That growth is personal for Felbermayr, who says F1 Academy has helped her become more confident both in and out of the car. Once a self-described shy person, the 19-year-old has learned to navigate interviews, limited track time, and the pressure of competing at a high level.

“I got so much better in the language of English. That's maybe just a small part of it, but just getting more confident in front of the camera, but also in the car,” says Felbermayr, who just signed on for a third F1 Academy season with Audi. “Every challenge grows yourself as a person, and I think that's something I really saw in the last two years.”

With seven race weekends on the 2027 calendar, including stops in Austin and Las Vegas, American fans will have plenty of opportunities to get acquainted with F1 Academy's rising stars. And with Apple TV bringing their races to a wider audience, more young girls will have the chance to see what's possible behind the wheel.

#4641. Cheating on Food Intake: How, Why, and What to Do

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

At any given time, millions of American adults (and some younger) are on a diet. That means they are watching their weight. Or trying to. Some diets actually incorporate “cheat days” or “cheat meals.” Some people on diets institute their own cheats—as in, “I’ll just splurge on this tonight, and get back to my diet tomorrow.”

Unfortunately, food cheating can lead to weight gain, failure to lose weight, and diet-disease consequences.

Where does this come from? Is cheating a “thing” in its own right or does it have more to do with food cravings, impulse control, metabolism, brain function, gut health, and any number of other body and brain processes?

To take a closer look at this, we can check out research on people reporting their food intake. After all, that is the only way we can find out what people are eating. Or think they are eating.

How is this tracked? There are a variety of ways, including self-report questionnaires, 24-hour recall forms, recording food intake in the moment on an app, taking pictures of food being eaten, and wearing cameras throughout the day. There are some problems with all of these methods. For example, people may report differently when they are part of a study that watches what they eat. Still, there have been some discoveries that are fairly consistent.

People are not great at reporting what they eat. They typically underreport snack foods, readily available foods, and foods that are high-calorie and feel more rewarding than vegetables. Most commonly, people tend to forget the snacks they grab between meals. Interestingly, people also tend to overreport their intake of healthy foods, like proteins or vegetables.

Social pressure can work both ways. If someone has announced to their family and friends that they are on a diet or following a certain plan, they may feel pressure to eat only healthy items when in that group. On the other hand, some may just go along with a group if they are enjoying some party foods. Being observed versus not being observed may also be part of the mix.

Distraction can cause people to grab a food and forget about it.

Negative affect can be associated with emotional eating and giving in to the impulse to seek highly palatable foods, and then have it slip from their memories.

Memory and judgment issues: One study (2020) discovered that negative affect is associated with decreased memory suppression in the hippocampus of palatable food cues. In other words, palatable food cues become more salient and can lead to wanting those items.

Another study (2019) noted that the Western diet, which includes processed foods, can impact the hippocampus and several other areas to impair judgment.

The hippocampus is a center of memory and can be implicated in confirmation bias. An article in the Washington Post (2022) noted that “one of the biggest problems to correcting information is the fact that hearing the truth doesn’t delete a falsehood from our memory.” Our brains store the original piece of misinformation, and it takes a different tagging system to get at the truth. To put it in the context of cheating with food, perhaps the eating was unconscious, or perhaps the person just doesn’t want to identify as a person who sneaks food. Either way, there is the memory that the cheat didn’t happen. The memory can become part of an identity or even a system of belief.

Metabolism: Excess weight can affect leptin signaling, so that hunger signals are inhibited, leading to food consumption unrelated to hunger signals.

Excess weight can lead to diabetes and insulin resistance. A study (2019) showed insulin resistance to be associated with deficits in episodic memory.

One study (2023) used a trial of supervised machine learning, which did, in the end, mitigate food underreporting. Unfortunately, this is not a sustainable process, or one that could be used widely.

Another study (2015) used Inhibitory Control Training with some success. However, the gains they made were only short-term.

A study (2016) noted that accurate monitoring is “synonymous with the most weight loss.” However, studies that provide opportunity to do so are necessarily time-limited. The process needs to nurture long-term skills to maintain success.

Irregular eating patterns have been associated with cheating. So, one strategy would be to encourage people to eat regular meals and double down on planning.

Another strategy includes education or coaching. Awareness of the potential areas where pitfalls can happen and presenting other options may give people a strategy they can use long-term.

Education could include some of the reasons why cheating is so prevalent. It’s not a moral failure. It’s human nature, and it’s the way our bodies work. Knowledge can start to make some inroads.

Monitoring is a good tool. It is an external process that can lead to awareness. However, the strategies above point to an overarching process that is internal—changing attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors. These are changes that can be realized over time and can be lasting.

Zhang, R., Yang, X., Yang, R., Xu, Z., Sui, N., Gao, X. (2020). Wanting to eat matters: Negative affect and emotional eating were associated with impaired memory suppression of food cues. Appetite. Vol. 150, 104660.

Davidson, T.L., Jones, S., Roy, M., Stevenson, R.J. (2019). The Cognitive Control of Eating and Body Weight: It’s More Than What You “Think.” Frontiers in Psychology. 10:62.

Sima, R., (2022). Why do our brains believe lies? The Washington Post. Nov. 3.

#4640. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required.
