#4619. The 11 Best Deodorants for Women in 2026, Tested by a Beauty Editor

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Real talk: Deodorant isn't a sexy beauty product, but it's arguably one of the most important. Imagine plopping down on your exercise bike, pounding the pavement in your favorite running gear, or even just commuting to the office without one. Scary thought, right? Growing up in notoriously humid South Florida, I was always hyper-aware of body odor and well-acquainted with underarm sweat—and I knew that deodorant was the way to keep me dry and stink-free.

I've no doubt that one of the products below will get the job done beautifully for you (so please, scroll!). But here are a few expert pointers if you want to shop for the best deodorant on your own.

"Keeping underarms fresh involves two main goals: controlling sweat and eliminating B.O.," says dermatologist Blair Murphy-Rose, MD. That's where deodorants and antiperspirants come into play. The only problem? People often use the terms interchangeably, but they're actually very different.

Deodorants help mask or neutralize underarm odor caused by sweat mixing with skin bacteria, while antiperspirants use aluminum to reduce underarm sweat by blocking sweat glands, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose. "One potential downside with antiperspirants is that they can dry out surrounding skin, leading to irritation, itching, and rash for those with sensitive skin," adds Alicia Zalka, MD, a dermatologist and associate clinical professor at Yale University School of Medicine.

Controlling sweat and masking bad odors are both important, but you'll have to be honest to decide which is a higher priority for your needs. If you're a heavy sweater and want to stop underarm wetness, opt for antiperspirants. If excess perspiration isn't as big of an issue for you, stick with deodorants. My daily go-to is deodorant, but I swiped both types to share the full scoop on the best women's deodorants and antiperspirants in the game. And the best part? Everything starts at just $9.

You've probably seen a variety of deodorant and antiperspirant formulations, and Dr. Murphy-Rose says your choice should be based upon personal preference and your unique issues. That said, there are some differences between the different types, so here's a quick rundown to think about.

Solids and sticks typically have a waxy consistency, are generally well-tolerated, and usually are the best for sensitive skin. Dragging on the skin is usually the primary source of irritation with these, so "try warming the stick on your skin first before swiping to minimize friction," advises Dr. Murphy-Rose. They also tend to leave behind annoying powdery white streaks on dark clothes and stickiness on the underarm area, adds Dr. Zalka. (All of these featured solids and sticks did not leave behind any residue on my clothes.)

Gels are convenient roll-ons and are typically light or clear so naturally, they leave behind less residue than solids. The only downside is that they tend to feel wet on skin—so if you're already dealing with excess perspiration, you may not love that sensation.

Creams feel moisturizing and soothing with application, but are a bit more messy and not as easy to apply. They're totally worth using, especially if you're looking to concentrate the application to a specific area or want full-body coverage (think between skin folds or under your breasts). Creams are typically more hydrating than gels and are a good option for those prone to dryness or irritation, notes Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Spray deodorants are quick to use, lightweight, and typically fast-drying, so they're practical for days you're in a rush. "They feel light and dry quickly with fewer ingredients," says Dr. Zalka. However, some may contain alcohol, which can be dehydrating or irritating for sensitive skin. Sprays can also be messy because you can't fully control where all of the deodorant particles land.

In general, you'll want to use deodorants made with moisturizing ingredients like humectants like hyaluronic acid or glycerin for hydration and occlusives like shea butter or beeswax to help protect dry, itchy underarms, recommends board-certified dermatologist Hadley King, MD. There are also deodorants made with bentonite clay, powders, or baking soda to help combat moisture. Important to note: "None of these ingredients blocks sweat ducts—they work by absorbing moisture," she says. Dr. Murphy-Rose is also keen on deodorants made with low concentrations of alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) to minimize underarm discoloration and baking soda.

That's slightly different from antiperspirants, which use aluminum salts to stop perspiration by creating plugs that block sweat glands, using aluminum, says Dr. Murphy-Rose. She adds that most over-the-counter antiperspirants contain 12 to 25 percent aluminum, while prescription-strength formulas can go up to about 30 percent.

I'm our resident scent-obsessed beauty editor and have tried a slew of deodorants and antiperspirants throughout my nearly decade-long journalism career. For this story, I kept the above dermatologist-approved guidance in mind and carefully researched hundreds of women's deodorants and antiperspirants.

Next, I went to the Women's Health beauty closet and revisited products in my personal collection until I eventually narrowed down my list to 24 potential contenders that seemed promising. I tested these deodorants after showering and, on weekends spent indoors, I delayed showering my underarms to see how these products held up against smell and sweat. I also considered how much odor and sweat protection they provide while exercising, running errands across New York City, and wearing them on special occasions and nights out with friends.

I also considered their ease of use, how they feel on my underarms, whether they leave behind any residue (a major pet peeve of mine), and how frequently I needed to apply to remain confident in how I smell.

With that, I give you: the best women's deodorants of 2026. They are all loved by me, and some are even well-known among the dermatologists I spoke with for this story. Regardless of which deodorant you order, they all earned major snaps from me, a very hard-to-please beauty editor. The best part? They all start at just $9 and don’t leave behind embarrassing white marks on clothing. Sign me up for bulk orders!

When it comes to selecting the best overall deodorant for women, it's tough to find a winner that doesn't include aluminum. As mentioned above, aluminum is the only active ingredient approved to stop perspiration in its tracks—a major consideration. What's more, the powdery texture works double duty to absorb moisture and leave skin with a silky finish.

And like most Dove products, this stick is chock full of moisturizing ingredients so you can rest assured that this one won't dry out your skin. “I feel like this is a deodorant you can’t go wrong with," says Women's Health beauty writer Danielle Jackson. "I recently switched back to this after using some aluminum-free formulas with more subtle scents, and I’ve just found that I’m much more confident about any sort of odors being blocked when I wear it."

But the ultimate test is, Can this hold up to activity? Jackson says this Dove stick passes that test with flying colors. "I also realized that I don’t have to worry as much about it doing its job when I’m being active or working out," she says. "It lasts all day and has a powdery scent that smells great but isn’t overbearing.”

When it comes to usage, Jackson assures that the Dove antiperspirant stick glides on easily without pulling (a major downside for most other sticks) and won't leave any white marks on my skin or clothes. Talk about an A+!The one potential downside (if you can even call it that) is that some of the other products on our list have a longer-lasting dryness promise (this one will only keep you dry for 24 hours as opposed to, say, the 48 or 72 hours promised by some other brands). But if you're like me and shower frequently, that won't be an issue.Read more: Best Natural Deodorants

A Women's Health Beauty Award winner for best deodorant, this heavy-duty antiperspirant leaves me with fresher-smelling pits from the second I swipe and up to 48 hours later. Obviously, I'm not going two days without showering, but I do notice that whenever I wear this antiperspirant while enjoying HIIT exercises or on the treadmill I'm less sweaty. Now that's pretty amazing.

Secret swears their antiperspirant helps camouflage sweat caused by activity, nerves, and heat—and I think it does a solid job, especially for heat. I wore this deo regularly back when I practiced martial arts, swam, rode horses, and attempted to play tennis. I don't normally sweat heavily, but in the summer I'd definitely reach for this antiperspirant especially when commuting underground on the New York subway system. It’s still helpful during the fall and winter season when I’m bundled up in several layers.

The only thing I don't enjoy about Secret is the packaging design. It's shaped like your standard stick deodorant where I twist the bottom to help push up the creamy formula, but I noticed the turn mechanism on mine requires a little more effort than others on this list. But if you're a heavy sweater, that's a fairly minor downside—and you shouldn't let this small con deter you from this one.

I learned about this deodorant years ago through my mom, who has been using Tom's forever. I tried it during the pandemic, but stopped using it in favor of other deodorants. But, I wanted to revisit Tom's for this story—and I'm so glad that I did.

The brand recently reformulated their line of natural deodorants, and I'm obsessed with the chic new packaging and all the incredible new scents available, like Wild Lavender, North Woods, and Mountain Spring. Tom's swears the formula is still as long-lasting as ever though, with this deodorant keeping odor at bay for 48 hours. That's pretty impressive for a natural formula. Like I said earlier, I won't ever skip my daily shower (occasionally twice daily in the summer because it's that humid along the East Coast) but Tom's keeps up with my daily activities. Think long daily commutes to the office, full workdays, after work shenanigans, and so much more.

To be frank, this level of protection isn't the norm for natural deodorants, but this stick is formulated with a generous dose of glycerin and aloe to condition my skin. It's also free of artificial fragrances that can irritate sensitive noses like mine.

All this being said, this is not the formula for you if you're a heavy sweater. I'd also say the biggest bummer about this deodorant is that it doesn't glide as easily as other alternatives on this list. There's a light dragging on my underarms, but it's not a huge problem, rather a minor annoyance that shouldn't deter you from enjoying this pick.

Is anyone else flashing back to middle and high school gym class just looking at this deodorant? I know I am, but there are several reasons every girl in my PE classes all used this roll-on antiperspirant—it's so easy to use and it's virtually invisible.

Since it's an antiperspirant, Ban keeps me sweat- and odor-free and embarrassing sweat marks on my clothes are nonexistent when I roll this onto my underarms (its clear formula doesn't transfer or leave behind any marks). What I really appreciate about Ban, though, is how it's lightweight on my skin. Sometimes creamy sticks feel like they're leaving behind a clump of product onto my pits, but that's a non-issue with Ban.

One important thing to note is that this gel roll-on doesn't dry quickly. It's not a huge drawback—the waiting period is minimal—but if you're in a super rush in the morning, keep that in mind. It's also not quite as long-lasting as some of the other formulas at 24 hours, but that's not a problem for me since, again, I shower daily.

I've always preferred stick deodorants and antiperspirants because it's what I'm used to. But this Dove formula makes a compelling case for anyone who's also shopping for weightless odor and sweat protection. So how does it work? “They create a flexible film of active ingredients on your skin and remain dry,” says cosmetic chemist Perry Romanowski. Dove relies on finely milled aluminum for invisible protection, plus a special masking oil to prevent any marks from getting on my clothes.

But similar to spray sunscreens, spray deodorants and antiperspirants can get a little messy and feel hard to control, and this one is no exception. So, it's probably best to skip buying this one for someone who isn’t super clean or a preteen who might spray this a little too liberally.

As we've said before: Whole body deodorants are hugely popular right now, with all the major players getting in on this trend. It's a smart idea—just 2 percent of our sweat glands exist in our underarms, so it's clear the need for all-over odor solutions is great.

This formula, with tapioca starch and mandelic acid, works to acidify skin’s pH, preventing odor-causing bacteria from proliferating. Rub a pea-sized amount into smelly areas, including the vulva, under-boob, thigh folds, and underneath the butt cheeks. A little goes a long way here, and you can always add more as needed.

Since its launch, Lume has expanded its portfolio to include stick deodorants, wipes, body creams, body washes, and acidified cleansing bars that are pH-optimized to control odor.

You deserve a deodorant that can keep up with your active lifestyle. Who better than tennis star Sloane Stephens to create a high-performance natural whole B.O.dy deodorant. I’m a huge fan of this spray and previously named it one of the best whole body deodorants of all time.

This is one of the best natural deodorants I’ve used in the last two years. I’m not the only fan. Tester Brigitt Earley is impressed by the texture of this deodorant, which she describes as almost like a body butter in stick form—and I agree. It doesn’t skip or tug on my skin, which has been an issue with other competitors.

The cylinder shape does take up a decent amount of space in my cosmetic pouch, but TBH, the formula and longevity are worth it for me. Still, if you’re a seasoned traveler who keeps things minimal, then you should consider the Anti Odorant pads instead.

Meet my favorite deodorant launch of 2026. I recently crowned it the best deodorant of the year in our annual Beauty Awards package. However, that might easily irritate very sensitive skin types and those with sensitive noses. And honestly, the current mild scent isn’t bad—just natural and fresh, which I appreciate. Plus, it won’t accidentally clash with my perfume collection.

I've spent four years wearing this deodorant on and off and can confirm that evolvetogether hits all of the factors I look for in a deodorant. For starters, it’s made with natural ingredients. Instead of potentially harsh baking soda, aluminum, and talc, this deodorant uses tapioca starch to soak up sweat and moisture. There's also DeoPlex, a plant-based sugarcane that neutralizes bad odors, while glycerin moisturizes and prevents underarm irritation. Panthenol hydrates my underarms and helps the stick glide on easily.

Most importantly, the odor protection is on point! If you are from the South like I am then you know that even if we shad our underarms sometimes it's so hot and humid out that we inevitably get a little smelly. Not the case with evolvetogether. I've worn this deodorant walking 5Ks around my neighborhood, on the treadmill, during long cross-country flights, and I've never felt self-conscious about my smell. (My mom is also very honest and would have told me if I ever have an odor issue, so I know evolvetogether works well for me.)

As for the cons, it’s really minimal. Heavy sweaters like runners will likely need a traditional antiperspirant to keep their pits truly dry. However, for daily activities this is one of my long-time favorites.

Look, there are studies that have investigated potential links between aluminum-based antiperspirants and breast cancer or Alzheimer’s disease. "To date, no conclusive evidence supports these claims, and aluminum-based antiperspirants are generally considered safe for daily use. There is no clear evidence that they pose a significant health risk," says Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Want more proof? Well, the American Cancer Society says "there are no strong epidemiologic studies (studies in people) that link breast cancer risk and antiperspirant use, and very little scientific evidence to support this claim." Plus, this report in the National Library of Medicine details a study conducted on 130 people regarding the potential exposure to aluminum through antiperspirants, antacids, and Alzheimer's disease (AD). "For all antiperspirant/deodorant use, regardless of aluminum content, there was no association with AD,” according to the study.

#4618. The Psychology of a Hippopotamus's Passing

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Last week, the death of Fiona, a hippopotamus residing at the Cincinnati Zoo, resulted in a massive outpouring of grief. As a Cincinnati resident, I was caught off guard by the magnitude of concern expressed not only locally but also around the world. This episode led me to ponder the psychology underlying why Fiona's death had such a profound impact.

As a member of the Cincinnati Zoo myself, I felt very sad to learn of Fiona's passing. In Cincinnati, this hippo had become a community icon. Fiona was born prematurely nearly 10 years ago, weighing about half as much as a typical newborn hippo (Cincinnati Zoo, 2026). Over the weeks that followed, the public watched zookeepers keep Fiona alive through round-the-clock monitoring in a makeshift ICU, feeding her by hand and celebrating each milestone she reached on her path to survival. When Fiona died, buildings throughout Cincinnati were illuminated in purple to commemorate her passing, and news outlets around the world covered her death and its impact.

Below, I outline several psychological processes that help to explain how this zoo animal touched so many people, both during her rise to celebrity and following her tragic and sudden death.

Anthropomorphism involves attributing human qualities to nonhuman entities, and people often anthropomorphize animals with whom they feel a close connection (McConnell et al., 2025). When people see a baby hippopotamus being bottle-fed by caregivers holding her in their laps, it evokes associations with parents caring for their own babies. Even her name, Fiona, was inspired by Princess Fiona, a character from the movie Shrek, because her fluted ears reminded zoo patrons of the animated princess (ironically, we're dealing with two layers of anthropomorphism here!).

As people anthropomorphize nonhuman entities, they often attribute humanlike emotional capacities to them, which can increase their moral concern and desire to care for those entities (Waytz et al., 2010). Thus, seeing similarities between Fiona being bottle-fed by zookeepers and human babies likely increased people's concern for Fiona and, consequently, intensified their grief following her death.

Moreover, the frequency with which people encountered Fiona throughout her life (e.g., numerous news updates about her progress, t-shirts and ice cream flavors featuring Fiona) may have increased their positive feelings toward her through the classic mere exposure effect (i.e., we tend to like things that become familiar to us through repeated exposure; Zajonc, 1968).

One of the striking things about Fiona's introduction to the world was that she was an underdog. Fiona was premature, underweight, and needed round-the-clock care from zookeepers just to survive. In other words, Fiona faced extraordinary odds from the moment she was born.

People are often drawn to underdogs and root for their success. Research shows that when individuals or groups are not expected to succeed and appear to face substantial disadvantages, people are more likely to support them in contexts ranging from Olympic competitions to geopolitical conflicts (Vandello et al., 2007). Thus, Fiona's helplessness at birth and the challenges she faced may have encouraged people to take her into their hearts and root for her survival, making her unexpected passing all the more crushing.

Research on parasocial relationships shows that people can form strong emotional attachments to individuals, such as celebrities, with whom they have no direct, reciprocal relationship. Indeed, people often feel meaningful psychological connections with professional athletes, movie stars, and even fictional characters, such as those in the Harry Potter series. Research also shows that such symbolic social connections can contribute to people's sense of belonging and well-being (Gabriel & Young, 2011).

Thus, even though many people grieving Fiona's passing never visited the Cincinnati Zoo, and those who did typically only "interacted with her" from the other side of a large glass window, people experienced a genuine connection with Fiona. Consequently, they can experience meaningful grief following her unexpected death.

Moreover, when communities share emotionally significant moments, they can experience collective effervescence, powerful feelings of social connection and shared significance that can make an experience feel special or even sacred (Gabriel et al., 2020). Thus, the collective mourning of Fiona may have made her loss especially poignant while simultaneously bringing people together through their shared grief.

Fiona died on November 19, 2026, from complications after swallowing a child's knit hat that, through a freak accident, landed in her enclosure. Her death led to a surge of anger from internet commenters calling for "justice" (Contrera et al., 2026). Why couldn't people simply accept Fiona's death as a very sad and tragic accident?

One important contributor to these feelings of anger may be counterfactual thinking, or people's tendency to imagine alternatives to events that take place. When trying to make sense of the world, people often engage in "if only" thinking to imagine how things might have turned out differently (e.g., "Would I have made my flight on time if there hadn't been an accident on the expressway?"). The unusual circumstances of a child's hat ending up in Fiona's enclosure make it especially easy to imagine alternative outcomes in which Fiona never swallowed the hat and would still be swimming in her zoo enclosure today.

Indeed, people often experience particularly strong negative emotions when it is easy to mentally "undo" a heartbreaking outcome. Under such circumstances, people may find it difficult to accept an outcome as simply a "bad break" or a matter of chance (Sherman & McConnell, 1996).

It's not surprising that Fiona's death had such a profound impact on people, both here in Cincinnati and around the world. Yet, animals die in zoos every day with far less (and often no) public attention.

Fiona's story illustrates how several psychological processes can converge to make an animal especially meaningful in people's lives. Anthropomorphism encourages us to extend moral concern to animals (McConnell et al., 2025), underdog narratives give us someone to root for (Vandello et al., 2007), parasocial relationships allow us to feel connected to individuals we do not personally know (Gabriel & Young, 2011), and counterfactual thinking can make an unexpected loss feel especially tragic when it seems so easily avoidable (Sherman & McConnell, 1996).

McConnell, A. R., Folmsbee, J. R., & Aldstadt, K. M., (2025). Furry friends: Direct and indirect benefits of human-animal relationships on well-being. Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 19(10), e70091.

Cincinnati Zoo (2017, Feb 12). Caring for preemie hippo Fiona. https://cincinnatizoo.org/caring-for-preemie-hippo-fiona/

Gabriel, S., & Young, A. F. (2011). Becoming a vampire without being bitten: The narrative collective-assimilation hypothesis. Psychological Science, 22, 990–994.

Contrears, J., Tumin, R., & Williams, K. (2026, Nov 20). Fiona the Hippo died after eating a hat. Some want justice. The New York Times. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/us/fiona-hippo-internet-justice.html

Gabriel, S., Naidu, E., Paravati, E., Morrison, C. D., & Gainey, K. (2020). Creating the sacred from the profane: Collective effervescence and everyday activities. The Journal of Positive Psychology, 15(1), 129-54.

Sherman, S. J., & McConnell, A. R. (1995). Dysfunctional implications of counterfactual thinking: When alternatives to reality fail us. In N. J. Roese & J. M. Olson (Eds.), What might have been: The social psychology of counterfactual thinking (pp. 199-231). Hillsdale, NJ: Erlbaum.

Vandello, J. A., Goldschmied, N. P., & Richards, D. A. R. (2007). The appeal of the underdog. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 33, 1603-1616.

Waytz, A., Cacioppo, J., & Epley, N. (2010). Who sees human? The stability and importance of individual differences in anthropomorphism. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 5, 219-232.

Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 9(2, Pt. 2), 1-27.

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

#4616. The 10 Best Walking Shoes for Men, According to Men’s Health Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our experts recommend shoes from Hoka and Asics.

WALKING IS A great way to keep a steady exercise routine, even when you're not in the mood for more intense workouts. Engaging in walking not only provides a gentle form of physical activity, but can also promote post-workout recovery and overall blood circulation. What can motivate you to get out for a few extra weekly walks? A pair of ultra-comfortable walking shoes that keep your feet happy long after you've reached your target.

"All [walking] shoes should feel snug around your foot, have good arch support, the heel shouldn’t slip around, and there should be adequate room in the toe box," recommends Mark J. Mendeszoon, DPM, a board-certified podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon.

Since walking shoes can wear down quickly with everyday use, having one (or two) solid pairs in rotation is a smart move. Below, we’ve rounded up the best men’s walking shoes of the year—tested, podiatrist-reviewed, and chosen for comfort, support, and all-day wearability.

One crucial lesson we've learned from Mendeszoon is not to focus only on shoe length when determining your ideal fit. According to him, it's equally essential to consider shoe width—much like with running shoes. Many brands now offer a range of widths, so understanding your foot anatomy is key to the right fit. "Wear the same socks you wear when you walk when trying them on and remember that our feet expand while walking."

Once you find the right pair, keep in mind to replace them after you've racked up some miles. "It is important to realize that shoes are generally good for 500 to 600 miles," says Mendeszoon. Even when you're primarily sporting them for walking. Ready to step into action? Then check out our guide to the best walking shoes for men below.

The Hoka Clifton 11 continues the franchise's tradition of plush comfort and podiatrist-approved design—earning another nod from the American Podiatric Medical Association. This version builds on what made the Clifton 9 and 10 favorites by refining the jacquard knit upper for a more adaptive fit, while still delivering the high-stack CMEVA foam that gives each stride a cloud-like feel.

The Clifton remains one of the lightest max-cushion shoes in its class; this version is even a little lighter than the 10. Its signature Smooth Metarocker geometry helps roll you forward with less effort, ideal for long walks, recovery days, or standing for hours. While it's technically a running shoe, walkers and all-day wearers have gravitated toward the Clifton for its smooth ride and day-to-night versatility.

I personally have had a lot of friends who love the Hoka Clifton 11 and are on their feet all day working in retail and hospitals. If you liked the 9 and 10, the 11 stays true to the formula—with subtle tweaks that make it feel just a little softer, a little smoother, and still seriously easy on the feet.

If your walking routine takes you through city streets, sidewalks, or even the gym, the On Cloud X4 is built to keep pace with style. This newest version of On’s beloved crossover trainer retains its signature featherweight feel but adds key comfort upgrades that make it better suited for all-day wear. The breathable mesh upper stays cool and flexible, while plusher materials around the heel and tongue provide a more dialed-in, cushioned fit than the X3.

The real update lies in the underfoot tech: the Hellion superfoam midsole delivers soft landings, and the X-shaped Speedboard adds forefoot flex and energy return, whether you're walking forward or moving side to side. A midfoot cage adds extra structure, while a grippy rubber outsole gives you confident traction on pavement or polished floors.

This is still a firmer-feeling shoe, so don’t expect the plushness of a max-cushion trainer, but the Cloudtec pods adapt nicely to your stride and deliver a responsive feel that’s great for quick city walks or active errands.

This newest version of the Glycerin, the Glycerin 22, leans into what the series does best: plush comfort and a dialed-in neutral fit. The nitrogen-infused midsole foam has been fine-tuned for even better softness and smoother transitions, making it ideal for long walks when comfort is a top priority.

Unlike traditional stability shoes, the Glycerin 22 doesn’t use any rigid support posts. Instead, it relies on a wider platform and balanced midfoot geometry to provide a naturally stable base without feeling corrective. The result is a super-soft, highly neutral ride that feels consistent from heel strike to toe-off, whether you have 2 miles or 12 miles ahead of you.

The upper remains breathable and accommodating, and the shoe's durable outsole is built to handle high weekly mileage without wearing down quickly. It’s not flashy, but it’s reliable, and that’s exactly why people keep coming back to it.

It's worth noting that the Brooks Glycerin 23 was recently released, with minor design updates that make it a heavier yet more cushioned shoe. Personally, I prefer the lighter version, and with the price drop, the 22 is a great value.

If you’re looking for a reliable walking shoe that won’t wreck your budget, the Asics Gel-Pulse 17 builds on the success of the 15 with a few key upgrades to comfort and breathability. The FF BLAST midsole and signature GEL cushioning are still here. Meaning you get a soft, responsive ride whether you’re walking city blocks or putting in time on the treadmill. What’s new is the jacquard mesh upper, which offers a lighter, more ventilated feel than last year’s engineered mesh. It helps your feet breathe better on warm days or longer walks without compromising the structure you need for all-day support.

One standout design feature is the elevated midsole through the center, which enhances support and impact absorption across key pressure points. While the foam leans on the firmer side, the added GEL insert softens landings, making it a strong pick for steady-paced daily walks. Stability gets a boost too—thanks to strategic bumpers along the heel that cradle the foot, paired with a rigid heel counter that helps limit excess movement.

If you liked the 16, this one feels like a natural upgrade—just a bit cooler and more dialed in for summer.

The Kuru Atom 2 is designed as a comfort-focused athletic shoe that blends performance features with orthopedic support, making it also one of the best new shoes for stability on the market. The minimalistic style behind the shoe appeals to me, especially when opting for the white or black colorways. I’ll also say that I was impressed at how easily the shoe slipped on, which is a bit of a non-negotiable for me unless I’m doing a trail run or putting in a lot of miles.

The first thing I noticed was how comfortable the shoe was, with its cushioned midsole and KURUSOLE heel shock absorption still providing a solidly responsive ride. This makes it a perfect pick for anyone looking for a daily trainer for low mileage or full days of walking. The Atom 2 offers a moderate improvement over the shoe’s previous energy return, but it still isn’t a running shoe you want to hit the pavement with for long distances.

The Kuru Atom 2 is a little heavy on the foot, which comes from the stability and durability that it provides. And thanks to the clean aesthetic, it fits in almost any setting, from the track to the grocery store.

The Brooks Ghost 17 proves why this Seattle-based brand remains a household name in performance footwear. Founded in 1914, Brooks has built its reputation on reliability, comfort, and a no-frills design approach—and the Ghost line is the perfect example of that. While the brand has recently taken steps to modernize its look and appeal to a younger generation, the Ghost 17 still leans traditional in the best way: It’s well-cushioned, durable, and consistent from mile one to mile 100.

The Brooks Ghost has long been a go-to for runners and walkers alike—and the Ghost 17 kept that reputation alive with subtle but smart upgrades. This version uses an air mesh upper for breathability, along with a redesigned kickback collar that cradles the heel without rubbing or slipping. The biggest change from the Ghost 16, though, is underfoot: Brooks added nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam in the heel and forefoot, giving the shoe a softer, more cushioned feel than previous versions. We should note that the Ghost 18 just released, and while we’re still in the early stages of testing it, it still uses that DNA Loft v3 foam but gets a fully rebuilt upper and tongue.

What makes the Ghost 17 such a standout is its adaptability. Whether you're on your feet for hours, squeezing in a quick power walk, or just want something that holds up across daily mileage, this is an easy choice. It’s not flashy—but that’s kind of the point. It’s durable, balanced, and built for comfort, making it an ideal “one-shoe-fits-most” option. And with the Ghost 18 just releasing, the price drop on the 17 still makes it worthwhile.

Asics has refined the Gel-Nimbus line year after year, and the twenty-eighth iteration is one of its most luxurious yet. Known for max cushioning and long-wear comfort, this model upgrades the upper with a premium, breathable knit that feels as good as it performs. The toe box is also more spacious than in previous versions. A welcome relief for walkers who often feel squeezed in standard neutral shoes.

Underfoot, the Gel-Nimbus 28 still delivers a soft and stable ride, thanks to its combo of lightweight foam and added gel (FF Blast Plus ECO) cushioning in the forefoot and heel. The 8mm drop subtly rolls the foot forward, creating that ideal balance between protection and propulsion. The flexible knit tongue and solid heel lockdown add to the premium feel, making it a go-to for long walks, recovery days, or even light runs.

Men's Health Deputy Editor Paul Kita enjoyed how they felt structured, but not restrictive. Plus, Asics beefed up the outsole for better traction and longer wear. This pair will keep pace with more use. And while it's built for a neutral gait, it plays nicely with custom insoles if you need more arch support or pronation control.

Two defining features set Altra shoes apart: a roomy toe box and a zero-drop platform. This combination ensures an anatomic fit and promotes a natural gait. Your feet enjoy greater freedom to move naturally, allowing your toes to flex and bend as you walk, which encourages better biomechanics and can reduce strain on your foot's structures.

Compared to other Altras, the Via Olympus 2 leans more toward plush than performance. The wide-base footbed adds stability, while the rocker-shaped sole still promotes a smooth forward roll with each step—even if it’s more subtle during walking than running. That extra room in the toe box and midfoot also comes in handy during longer efforts, giving your foot space to swell without feeling cramped.

"I love super high stack shoes like this, and Altra’s dedication to extra-roomy toe boxes makes the Via Olympus 2 even more comfortable," notes Williams. "The rocker shape is less pronounced on my walks than when I run in them, but it’s still noticeable for turnover on each step."

If you're planning long walks, you'll appreciate how the shoe's roomy toe box accommodates the natural expansion that occurs during extended physical activity.

Fashion meets function with this shoe. It showcases a stylish design while seamlessly integrating waterproof features, exceptional durability, and a rocker bottom that ensures a buttery-smooth walking experience. It not only performs well, but looks good doing it.

It's explicitly designed for outdoor activities, making it an ideal choice for those who do most of their walking in nature. Thanks to its waterproof properties, my feet stay snug and dry, even in challenging weather conditions. Whether I'm trudging through rain-soaked paths or navigating puddles, these shoes provide unwavering protection for my feet.

Let's talk about Keen's newly patented "constant curve" construction. This design is engineered to encourage forward momentum in the wearer's stride, similar to most Hoka models. The rocker bottom facilitates a smooth transition from heel strike to toe-off, which Keen hopes can make walking more enjoyable for wearers. Based on my personal experience with these shoes, I'd say Keen has succeeded. I find myself walking faster and expending less effort, especially during long or uphill treks.

Although some reviewers have noted a rubbery off-gassing scent when the shoes are fresh out of the box, I didn't find it particularly noticeable (and I'm pretty sensitive to smells).

The Kuru Atom Trail is a purpose-built trail walking shoe designed to protect your heels, support your stride, and keep you moving confidently over rough ground. Its standout feature is the brand’s proprietary Kuru Sole, a dynamic midsole system that flexes with each step to cup and cradle the heel. Compared to traditional heel cradles, this one offers more adaptability and a locked-in feel. This is especially helpful for walkers who deal with heel pain or plantar fasciitis.

On the trail, the Atom Trail holds its own. A synthetic upper with rugged TPU overlays adds structure and durability, while the gusseted tongue helps block out debris. The outsole is aggressive and grippy, built for varied surfaces. It’s not the lightest or most responsive option out there. Which is why we wouldn’t recommend it for trail running but rather for long hikes, uneven terrain, and daily dog walks on gravel or dirt paths; it’s an excellent pick.

Mendeszoon puts it best: "This is a true traditional trail shoe that provides great support, comfort, and protection against the elements and uneven and challenging terrain." Our only qualm is that it's a little heavy and not particularly responsive, which is why we wouldn't recommend running it. But it excels in what it's meant for—trail walking.

Bonus points: it’s made with fully vegan materials and has enough breathability to handle summer hikes without overheating your feet.

Look for walking shoes with support and stability features labeled for your specific foot type. "Consider your foot type and [walking] gait," says Dr. Bradley Schaeffer, DPM. "The goal is to keep your lower body in alignment as much as possible." Features such as a firm heel counter, a supportive midsole, and a secure lacing system can provide the stability you need for comfortable walking and to keep your feet properly aligned.

When it comes to classification, if the shoe is stable, it is designed to help offset pronation, which is the inward rolling of the feet after landing on the ground. When a shoe is neutral, it lacks the stabilizing features, allowing your foot to fall more naturally. When a shoe is moderate, it is somewhere between those two worlds.

"Cushioning absorbs shock and helps to avoid tissue irritation and damage," explains Schaeffer. It's important to choose walking shoes with sufficient cushioning to absorb impact and shock with each step. Look for shoes with cushioned insoles and midsoles made from materials like foam or gel to ensure a comfortable walking experience, especially for longer walks or on hard surfaces.

Decide if you prefer soft cushioning for impact absorption and comfort or a more responsive feel. Some shoes offer a balance between the two, so choose based on your preferences and walking style.

If you're in the market for a walking shoe to take you long distances frequently, be sure the models you're considering are relatively lightweight. Unless we're talking about a stability or trail shoe, which feature additional materials for added durability and support, that means under 11 ounces.

Pay attention to the upper material of the walking shoes, as it can impact comfort, breathability, and durability. Opt for shoes with breathable and flexible uppers made from materials like mesh or knit fabric to help keep your feet cool and comfortable. Additionally, keep an eye out for features like padded collars and tongues for even more comfort and support.

I’m a certified strength and conditioning specialist based in New York and a fitness writer who loves trying the latest gear and raving to my loved ones about his latest discoveries. I have a dog, and I take him for walks twice a day. I also trek through the city from Queens to Manhattan five to six times per week. I have a pretty full roster of clients that I see in-person for training sessions and hit about 15,000 to 20,000 steps per day. Needless to say, I am on my feet A LOT, so I need to be on top of my game when it comes to comfy footwear.

I also got some assistance from Men’s Health fitness editors and medical advisors. We spent months of testing and researching to create this guide. Over the past few years, we’ve logged miles in more than 40 pairs of walking and running shoes from top brands like Asics, Hoka, Brooks, On, and more. Led by Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM and Fitness Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, along with expert input from podiatrists Schaeffer and Mendeszoon, we evaluated each shoe for fit, comfort, cushioning, support, durability, and value. We also considered real-world feedback from testers who wore these shoes during daily walks, commutes, and all-day wear.

From minimalist trainers to max-cushioned picks, we curated this list to meet a variety of foot types, walking styles, and comfort preferences—so you can find the pair that’s right for your stride.

Understanding your foot type is essential for finding the right walking shoes that offer optimal comfort and support. There are three primary arch types based on arch height: neutral, high, and flat. To determine your arch type, you can start with a simple "wet test," Mendeszoon recommends. Wet your feet and stand on a surface like concrete, sand, or a flattened paper bag. Examine the imprint left by your foot.

If your foot leaves a complete, flat imprint, you likely have low arches and would benefit from arch support or stability shoes. If the imprint shows the heel, outer side of the foot, ball of the foot, and toes, but not the arch, you might have a neutral or high arch.

While the wet test provides a basic idea, factors such as weight, biomechanics, and overall fitness also help determine your arch type accurately. For a more detailed analysis, consider visiting a local chiropractic clinic, podiatry practice, or high-quality running shoe store. Some locations offer foot scans that provide intricate information about your feet and arches.

Todd Sinett from Tru Whole Care in New York highlights a special machine called the Foot Levelers Digital Foot Scanner, which identifies specific pressure points on your feet that could be linked to back pain. This advanced tool offers precise measurements for customized orthotics, ensuring tailored support for your unique foot structure.

Yes, running shoes can absolutely be worn for walking, according to Mendeszoon. In fact, they may offer some added benefit compared to conventional walking shoes.

Running shoes are designed to absorb the impact of running, which means they can also provide good shock absorption when walking. Many people choose to wear running shoes for walking because of added support and flexibility, too.

One downside: Running shoes tend to be heavier and less breathable than walking shoes because of their more durable design. So, it's important to note that they may not be the best choice for long-distance walking.

It's important to replace your walking shoes regularly to ensure adequate support and cushioning, probably more frequently than you think. As a general rule of thumb, it's recommended to replace walking shoes every 300 to 500 miles (or every 3 to 5 months for those who walk for at least 45 minutes at least 3 times per week).

The specific lifespan of a shoe depends on several factors, including the frequency and intensity of use, the shoe's quality, and the type of surface you typically walk on. There are a few signs to look out for that may indicate it's time to replace your shoes:

Ultimately, it's important to listen to your body and pay attention to any signs of discomfort or pain when walking. If you notice any of the above signs, it's a good idea to start looking for a new pair of walking shoes.

Powerlifting legend Mark Bell is a huge fan of walking for weight loss, as is Will Smith. This guy lost 60 pounds with walking and bodyweight workouts. And this guy lost 200 pounds by walking and eating a CICO diet. It's all about starting to add to your daily step count, and really sticking with it.

"Starting slow and working your way up is better than overdoing it and giving up," Chris Gagliardi, a certified personal trainer at the American Council on Exercise, previously told Men's Health. An easy way to approach it: Commit to a quick 10-minute walk after dinner, and gradually increase the duration as you become more comfortable with daily movement.

Step counting also helps. "If you’re only getting 3,000 steps on a typical day, don’t try to get 10,000 steps the next day. That can be really discouraging. Aim for 5,000 every day for a week. Then go up to 7,000 the next week," walking coach Michele Stanten, founder of MyWalkingCoach.com and author of The Walking Solution, previously told Men's Health.

Eric Sung, CSCS, is a New York City–based trainer and a member of MH’s Strength in Diversity Initiative.He specializes in athletic training and recently completed his first triathlon.

Dr Mark Mendeszoon is a board-certified podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon at Precision Orthopaedic Specialties in Chardon, Ohio and owner of Achilles Running Shops in Willoughby , Ohio and Erie, Pa. He  still enjoys working out, running  and coaching runners of all ages.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

#4615. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4614. Never Fight a Pig? Why Sometimes You Have To

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

Never fight with a pig. You'll just get dirty, and the pig likes it.

You've heard that line. It sounds high-minded, and it's a relief not to have to fight anyone. You keep your hands clean, you deny the pig its satisfaction, and you get to mutter "pig" as you walk away.

It's the same comfort as "When they go low, we go high" or "Love trumps hate." These claims soothe because they're conclusive, flattering, and easy. They take the pressure off engaging in conflict and flatter us as high, not low; loving, not hateful. We rarely kick the tires on such proud proclamations from a safe distance. We should, because they leak.

Never fight with a pig? Even a pig who harms your family, or sells your country for parts and pockets the profits? I say never say never. Sometimes you have to fight. You will get dirty, and the pig will like it, at least at first. The real question is how to make the fight less fun for the pig. Not how to strut off triumphant, but how to get a pig to stop being a pig and admit they're human.

Here's a poke at a definition. A pig blames all of their mistakes on others, and does so with the preening pretense of God-like authority. Their logic is circular: "Since I deem everything I do perfect, I'm the supreme authority, and so qualified to deem everything I do perfect." It's the same circularity as claiming a sacred text is the word of God because the text says so.

That isn't "playing God" in the sense of changing the world. It's playing God by pretending you're the authority on which changes are permissible. It's the sneer at moral relativism from someone who declares their own subjective morality the last word, so anyone who challenges them is the devil.

A pig acts like they can do no wrong and so feels free to do endless wrong. They like getting dirty because, in their minds, they can't get dirty. They're sadistic narcissists, elevated through theatrical contempt for rivals. When someone contemptible dirties them, that proves they're clean.

Pigs are self-winding. Praise proves they're perfect. Condemnation proves they're perfect too, because they've already decided that anyone who condemns them is contemptible. Pigs don't go low. They go low from on high, nasty to anyone who triggers them yet entitled to be nasty because they've declared themselves saints.

How do you yank them off their high horse without mounting it yourself? The best answer I have so far: Get comfortable being dirtied. Stop trying to win battles with them. Stop trying to get them to dismount and be nice. They're addicted to playing God, so they won't just quit.

Stop trying to win arguments, too, and stay off your own high horse. Skip the morality lectures and the fact-checking, because you can't beat them at that game. The only rule of their game is that anyone who challenges their authority is beneath contempt.

Instead, expose the game, over and over. Interpret their contempt as nothing more than the game. Point out that they'll say anything to pretend they're the authority, and when they respond as though they're the authority, thank them for proving you right.

I've been doing this online for a while, holding up a mirror to the game. I get thousands of responses, all true to formula. Nobody shares an opinion; they make pronouncements. Anyone who challenges their authority is dismissed from their supreme courtroom. I get called every insult in the book, over and over. It doesn't make me flinch. It's boring, a broken record preening as an unbroken one.

I never defend myself, as if appealing in their courtroom. That would be enabling. I never take the bait, because they don't mean it. Their output is inconsistent nonsense on stilts, so I don't feel dirtied. I keep my own counsel on whose counsel I keep, and it isn't theirs.

I've even come to enjoy it. It's fun tangling them up in their own nonsense. They always respond with a defensive pronouncement that they are never triggered, and I tease them right back about how defensive and triggered they sound. It's a taste of their own medicine.

That's all you can do, and all you need to do. You won't want to, but it's a civic duty.

#4613. The Best Shampoos for Every Hair Need and Budget, According to Experts

From L’Oréal to Oribe, these shampoos are worthy of a spot in your wash day routine.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

From sweaty runs and heat styling to product buildup, our scalps and hair need proper TLC—and that starts with a great shampoo. Our scalp is an extension of the skin on our face—it sheds dead skin cells, collects dirt and bacteria, and secretes oil and sweat, says trichologist Anabel Kingsley in our guide on how often to shampoo your hair. While the beauty community has mixed opinions on the cadence of shampooing, dermatologist DiAnne Davis, MD, recommends doing so at least once a week. The frequency varies based on your lifestyle, how quickly your hair gets greasy, your scalp health, and hair type. Since the experts advise regular shampooing, I asked the pros about how we can upgrade our healthy hair routines to preserve the expensive chemical and color treatments we enjoy at the salon.

“I always tell my clients that shampoo is mainly for your scalp, so I would start there,” says trichologist and hairstylist Courtney Foster. “You can have curly hair with an oily scalp, fine hair with a dry scalp, or color-treated hair with buildup. Hair type matters, but it doesn't tell me everything I need to know.” Choose hydrating shampoos that nourish a dry scalp, or use a lightweight shampoo with fewer moisturizing ingredients for an oily scalp.

For an oily scalp or buildup, ingredients like salicylic acid can be helpful, along with gentle cleansing agents like coco glucoside. For mineral and hard water buildup, look for chelating ingredients, as regular shampoo alone may not remove these deposits, according to Foster.

Now it’s time to think about your hair type, advises Foster. In addition to your hair texture, you’ll want to find a shampoo that’s suitable for your dry, chemically treated, damaged, or breakage-prone mane.

For dryness, humectants and conditioning ingredients such as glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and nourishing oils are your new beauty best friends. They help the hair retain moisture and feel softer and more manageable, says Foster.

For damaged hair, you’ll need shampoos packed with amino acids and bond-strengthening ingredients. “These are good for hair that has been chemically treated or excessively heat-styled,” she says of components such as hydrolyzed proteins, which can improve the feel and strength of damaged hair.

Now, if you’re dealing with frizz like I am, it likely means the hair is lacking moisture, says Foster. We’ll benefit from conditioning ingredients like polymers, silicones, oils, and humectants that help smooth the cuticle and improve manageability.

As our hair-obsessed beauty editor, I own a sizable shampoo collection. It’s 24 shampoos strong. So I started there and narrowed it down to 12 contenders. In addition to expert guidance—ingredients for a healthy scalp and cosmetic concerns like frizz—I factored in everything from their cleansing power, lather, fragrance, and feel. Did they leave my scalp parched like I just went swimming in the pool? Or did they help rebalance my scalp and prevent embarrassing flakes on my black clothing?

To help whittle down potential recommendations even further, I recruited the Women’s Health team, including beauty director Brian Underwood and deputy editor Carina Hsieh, to test these picks. Ouai Fine Hair Shampoo and Leonor Greyl immediately caught our attention and kept it. The latter even won a Women’s Health Beauty Award, and we don’t take giving out that accolade lightly.

Still, I wanted to tap into other expert picks and asked hairstylists and trichologists about the products they use at the salon and at home. Their suggestions range from a drugstore pick to a de-brassing shampoo to keep your color-treated hair looking as fresh as possible after washing.

While it sounds obvious, I factored in your budget. While my best overall pick from Oribe is on the higher end, there are several under $20 picks. And if your wallet is also looking a little tight during fun holiday adventures, I totally get it. We tested several of these shampoos, and each full-size bottle lasted us at least six weeks, with some lasting our team up to four months.

Ultimately, these are solid jumping-off points for your healthy hair routine. “One shampoo doesn’t necessarily have to do everything,” says Foster. If you use a lot of styling products, you may occasionally need a clarifying shampoo and a moisturizing shampoo for your regular wash days. “The goal is really to create a routine that keeps the scalp clean without stripping the hair.” Since you’re here, consider checking out our guides to healthy hair, including our favorite editor-tested hair masks, vitamins for hair growth, and red light therapy for hair growth. Yes, it’s a legitimate technology that’s backed by research, and dermatologists are on board.

I’d normally roll my eyes at anyone recommending a high-end shampoo as their best overall pick, but Oribe is the only shampoo I have on auto-refill. Despite its upfront cost, a single bottle of Oribe lasted me nearly four months, so it really helps stretch my cost per use.

My scalp has never been this clean with a single wash before. It helps wash away my silicone hair serum and dry shampoo buildup, and even sand from the Caribbean Sea that recently got stuck in my hair. It also softens my dry tresses before I even apply conditioner, which is incredible, given how parched my mane is.

Cleansing with Oribe really brings that luxurious feeling of being at the salon’s shampoo bowl from the comfort of my bathroom. Plus, it smells like Calabrian bergamot, white butterfly jasmine, and sandalwood. The blend is so enticing that Oribe even created a perfume inspired by this iconic scent. The chic black bottle pops in my otherwise boring gray bathroom.

And don’t just take my word for it: Foster appreciates that it combines gentle cleansers with conditioning ingredients, such as panthenol, amino acids, proteins, and oils. “It cleanses while still giving the hair a polished, conditioned feel,” she says.

You don’t need to splurge to enjoy a great shampoo, argues Foster. “L’Oréal gives you an elevated experience at the drugstore price point,” she says. “It produces a substantial lather and has more of a fragranced, salon-product feel than many inexpensive shampoos.” She especially likes it for anyone dealing with dryness or color-treated hair, or who wants a gentle daily shampoo without the luxury price tag.

“I love this product. It's available everywhere, which means I can travel light with just hand luggage and pick it up wherever I land,” says celebrity hairstylist and Kennaland salon owner Kenna Kennor. “The results are instantly better than most hotel shampoos.”

A combo of Cécred’s Bioactive keratin ferment and hyaluronic acid gently cleanses my hair while leaving it nourished and detangled, which is not exactly the norm for my dry curls. It works equally well on my natural hair and extensions, and it’s so gentle that you can use it on color-treated hair.

Foster especially likes this one for dry hair because it’s formulated with hydrating ingredients and is sulfate-free. “It is designed to provide slip while cleansing, which is especially helpful for dry, textured or highly manipulated hair,” she says. “If I'm shampooing dry or textured hair and it immediately feels tangled and rough, I know I'm creating more work for myself later. This has a richer, more luxurious lather than people sometimes expect from a hydrating shampoo, and it leaves hair feeling clean without that squeaky, stripped feeling.”

Leave it to tennis star Sloane Stephens to create one of our team’s favorite shampoos. After a sweaty Rumble boxing class, Doc&Glo helped bring that fresh salon feeling to features director Rachel Epstein's shower. The first thing she noticed was the gel-like consistency of the shampoo, which easily lathers in her hands—she only needs two to three pumps. But her favorite part was the calming peppermint-and-eucalyptus scent that lingered for the rest of the night. “None of that fruity garbage over here,” she says.

Epstein has used the shampoo and conditioner twice a week for the last month, and her scalp has consistently felt balanced. Her waves are fresher and fuller the next day. “Because I have dandruff, I still need to use a medicated shampoo here and there, but I’ll definitely continue using this duo,” she says.

Chlorine and hard water can fade your color-treated hair and make neutral and cool tones look warm. This de-brassing shampoo reduces yellowing and brassiness in blonde, highlighted, silver, and gray hair. “I have seen great results with this, and there's no purple buildup,” says Kennor, who especially likes this one for double-process blondes.

Foster appreciates that Virtue isn’t relying solely on heavy purple dye. The tone is actually synthetic color-free and dye-free. De-Brassing Shampoo pairs botanical ingredients with Virtue’s signature Alpha Keratin 60ku protein, a proprietary protein that mimics the hair-strengthening, damage-repairing benefits of keratin.

When you want a splurge-worthy shampoo, opt for this recent Women’s Health Beauty Award winner. “If you color your hair, you need a shampoo that protects your investment,” says beauty director Brian Underwood. “With a sulfate-free formula that ensures your scalp won’t become irritated, this one contains ingredients that soothe, repair, and rejuvenate like grapeseed sterols, chia seed, and hook seaweed.” It also contains a trifecta of quinoa extract, chamomile extract, and amaranth extract to soften, smooth, hydrate, and condition hair.

A bonus: It gently foams up while strengthening and hydrating your highlighted, bleached, or color-treated hair, adds Foster.

K18 is beloved by everyone from Foster and me to the legendary Simone Biles. Peptide Prep is pH-optimized and contains the brand’s signature K18 Peptide along with plant-derived surfactants. “It cleanses without adding stress to already compromised hair,” says Foster. “That's important because damaged hair doesn't need to be babied to the point that it's not being properly cleansed, but it also doesn't need an aggressive shampoo every wash day.” It’s also made with salicylic acid, which gently exfoliates and removes excess scalp oil.

After using this shampoo, I experienced less flaking and less product buildup from heat protectants and scalp oils. My hair feels lighter and bouncier, and I can get away with shampooing once a week instead of twice a week since using this product.

Redken's Acidic Bonding Concentrate is another product Foster likes for chemically processed or damaged hair. “Citric acid is a key component of the formula, designed to help reinforce weakened bonds while maintaining an acidic pH,” she says.

I tried this one during its launch in February and continued using it for several months afterward. My scalp felt so incredibly clean, without that pesky tightness and dryness. When paired with the matching conditioner, I noticed less shedding in my shower. My strands felt more resilient, conditioned, and rebalanced. I also noticed that my hair’s balayage took longer to fade, which is a major win.

Caring for fine hair is tricky because it may need moisture and strengthening but can become flat very quickly if the formula is too rich, says Foster. Ouai contains hydrolyzed keratin, biotin, and chia seed oil to leave your fine hair bouncy without that heavy, overly-conditioned feeling.

This shampoo also suds up in a rich, satisfying way, adding a luxurious touch to the mornings of deputy editor Carina Hsieh. “My hair has more lift at the roots—almost the way it used to, pre-30s,” she says. “My bangs are banging again (physically, emotionally, and, of course, spiritually), and my hair no longer separates into the same three sad little strands it seemed to automatically separate every 2 PM.”

To Hsieh, it only faintly smells of rose and musk. It’s the same fragrance as Ouai’s pet shampoo, but she swears the pet shampoo smells better. “But honestly, that’s me really looking for a negative as I sit and twirl my hair all day,” she says.

“Design Essentials is my absolute favorite shampoo,” says Foster. “The brand has been working with textured hair long before it became a trending topic, and that experience shows with Honey Crème.” This shampoo cleanses while providing slip and helping with detangling. As its name implies, it’s enriched with honey, a moisture-preserving, quick-lathering ingredient that helps soften and smooth the cuticle, says Foster.

You can also use this shampoo if you don’t have curly or coily strands, though you might not need the extra help with detangling. Still, it’s an enjoyable experience at a fantastic price point. “The best shampoo isn’t necessarily the most expensive one. It's the one that cleanses your scalp effectively while respecting what your hair needs at that particular time,” says Foster, and Design Essentials proves that with Honey Crème.

I’ve been using Design Essentials since I was in high school. It’s a truly reliable brand that hasn’t compromised on ingredient quality, smell, or feel. My hair is truly softer and more manageable every single time I use this shampoo.

Joico’s Detox Shampoo does just that—it combines a proprietary chelating agent and activated charcoal to remove product buildup and hard-water deposits. This color-safe shampoo also removes trace minerals and salts.

While it’s tough on unwanted components that can compromise my hair's integrity, it also contains moringa seed oil to help prevent dryness. There are also veggie proteins intended to help strengthen weak hair bonds, leaving me with a noticeably cleaner scalp and healthy-looking hair.

Whenever I use this shampoo, my hair feels super clean, but still hydrated. With each wash, my hair is noticeably bouncier, giving me a fresh-from-the-salon look. I also appreciate that this shampoo is compatible with all hair types. My hair is thick and coily, while my mom has fine, color-treated straight hair. This formula worked for both of us, and it has recently become a must-have for her since moving to a new city with hard water.

#4612. Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ new electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.
