#4602. The 10 Best Fitness Trackers for Women, Tested and Reviewed by Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Finding the right fitness tracker is less about buying the most advanced wearable out there and more about choosing the one that will actually work for how you’ll use it to help you meet your fitness goals. You may want a smartwatch that can handle calls and texts along with fitness data tracking, or maybe you’re looking for a distraction-free screenless band that quietly tracks your metrics in the background. If running is your thing, you may want a smartwatch with GPS accuracy and real-time training metrics that are easy to read during a run, and if you’re focused on improving sleep, you may prefer a smart ring that won’t feel bulky overnight.

For this guide, we considered a range of fitness trackers for different training styles and tracking needs, from simple bands for everyday activity tracking to running watches, smartwatches, screenless wearables, and smart rings, all designed to monitor sleep, recovery, fitness, and health trends over time.

Whoop earned the top spot for the best overall fitness tracker because it provides deeper understanding of your data while also giving context of what all that data means. I’ve been using a Whoop for the past several years, and of all the fitness tracker options I’ve tested, it remains my hands-down favorite. It delivers some of the most useful recovery, sleep, and strain insights in a distraction-free design that’s so comfortable I often completely forget that I’m wearing it. The battery life is impressive, and I only have to charge mine twice a month.

Whoop 5.0 is built on the foundation of an app that offers analysis of your metrics paired with context, so you actually learn what all the numbers mean for your health and training. The screen-free design means that instead of buzzing constantly or encouraging you to check another display, it quietly tracks your metrics in the background and turns that data into recovery, strain, sleep data to give you an overall picture of your fitness within an app.

The sensor platform uses multi-wavelength optical heart rate sensors, skin-temperature sensing, blood oxygen monitoring, and accelerometer and gyroscope motion sensors to collect data continuously, tracking your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, sleep stages, strain, and recovery.

The app then interprets those numbers, in a way that feels more actionable than raw data alone, to generate a daily readiness score that indicates how much physical exertion your body is up for on any given day (00033though it’s always important to listen to your body regardless of what a wearable says). If you wake up with a low recovery score, for example, Whoop may recommend reducing workout intensity. If your sleep debt is climbing, it will show how much rest you need to get back on track.

It also offers other behavior change suggestions that could improve how you feel based on the data it collects about you and your habits over time. In fact, the in-depth habit tracking feature offers some of the most valuable insights into how day-to-day behaviors affect us physiologically. As a trainer, this has been one of the features I've seen make the most long-term impact with clients, as it really helps them connect the dots and understand how everything is interrelated.

Whoop 5.0 does require a membership and there are three different tiers, the main difference being the level of insights and analysis. Whoop One covers the core Whoop experience, including sleep, strain, recovery, steps, activity monitoring, heart-rate tracking, and women’s hormonal insights, which helps us see how menstrual cycle phases may relate to sleep, recovery, and performance. Whoop Peak adds a broader health and wellness layer, including health monitor, stress monitor, healthspan, and more advanced coaching-style insights for users who want to connect daily habits with longer-term performance and recovery trends (this is the tier I personally go with). Whoop Life is the most advanced tier, adding heart-health features such as ECG, irregular heart rhythm notifications, and blood pressure insights where available. Ultimately, the difference between the tiers is less about the tracker experience itself and more about how much interpretation, health context, and advanced monitoring you want.

The tradeoff is cost. Since Whoop uses a membership model, it will end up being more expensive over time than a tracker that doesn’t require a subscription. It also is not the best choice if you want live pace, distance, or workout stats on your wrist during a run. For that, a Garmin, Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch, or COROS watch will be more practical.

The Google Fitbit Inspire earned its spot as the best budget pick because it gives you the core fitness-tracking features most people want in a slim and approachable design. It’s not trying to be a full smartwatch or a performance running watch. Instead, it focuses on the basics: steps, heart rate, workouts, sleep, active minutes, and general wellness trends.

That simplicity makes the Fitbit Inspire a good entry point for someone who wants to become more aware of their fitness data without getting buried in advanced metrics. It can track walks, gym workouts, casual runs, and sleep, while the Fitbit app makes the data easy to understand. You can quickly see how much movement you got throughout the day, how long you slept, and how your habits are trending over time. Additionally, you’ll get a stress management score, guided breathing sessions, and reminders to move.

It is also one of the easiest trackers to wear all day. The band is slim enough to feel less bulky than a smartwatch, and the display is small but still easy to use for checking basic stats. If your main goals are walking more, staying accountable, improving sleep habits, or getting started with activity tracking, the Inspire offers strong value.

The main limitation is that it’s not necessarily built for serious training. Depending on the model, the GPS may rely on your phone rather than being fully built into the device, and runners who want advanced pace analysis, training load, recovery guidance, or race tools will likely outgrow it. But for the price, it’s one of the most practical fitness trackers for everyday use.

The Apple Watch Series 12 blends health tracking, workout features, smartwatch convenience, and safety tools better than almost any other wearable. If you already use an iPhone, this is the most seamless option in our guide.

The Series 12 features more advanced sensor capabilities, including an upgraded optical heart sensor that measures heart rate every five seconds, and tracks HRV more frequently. WH associate fitness editor Addison Aloin wrote in her review that the Series 12 has “a great baseline of health and fitness features.”

The Series 12 tracks a wide range of workouts, including running, walking, cycling, strength training, HIIT, yoga, Pilates, swimming, hiking, and many more. During activity, the display is bright and you can easily view data like pace, distance, heart rate, time, and workout zones during runs and workouts. It also integrates smoothly with Apple Fitness+, the Health app, and third-party training apps.

One of the most meaningful updates the Series 12 got is a new readiness score, which uses recent activity, training load, your sleep score, and overnight metrics like heart rate, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and recovery HRV to estimate how prepared your body is for exertion. The score runs from 0 to 10 and gives you a recommendation for your day, such as Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. “My only complaint is that it’s kind of hard to find the readiness score on the watch and in the Health app,” Aloin says.

Since it’s so much more than just a tracker you wear during workout, the Apple Watch also offers a lot of versatility. It can handle notifications, calls, music, maps, timers, contactless payments, fall detection, and emergency features, making it a strong option for anyone who wants one device that can move between workouts and everyday life.

It is also a good pick for people who like motivational nudges. Apple’s activity rings are simple, visual, and surprisingly effective if you respond well to daily goals. If you want coaching-style feedback without digging through complex training dashboards, the Series 12’s newer software can translate health and fitness data into easily digestible prompts.

The Series 12 offers up to 24 hours of everyday battery life, and Apple says 15 minutes of charging can add up to 12 hours of battery. That makes it more manageable for overnight sleep tracking, but it still requires more planning than fitness trackers that last several days or longer on a single charge. “I’ve found the battery life is awesome for everyday use, but usually does need a charge every other day or so,” Aloin says.

Read More: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Ultra 4

The Google Fitbit Air gives you the quiet, distraction-free experience of a screenless wearable at a more approachable price point than premium recovery bands. The Fitbit Air tracks core metrics like activity, heart rate, sleep, and wellness trends over time, then sends that information to your phone.

Since there’s no screen, you’re not checking your wrist throughout the day. That makes it a strong option for anyone who wants to be more mindful about movement and sleep but doesn’t want a smartwatch. It’s also a good fit for people who are curious about screenless tracking but are not ready to commit to a more expensive platform. It offers a simpler, lower-pressure way to see whether passive health tracking actually helps your routine.

The Fitbit app is another advantage. Fitbit’s platform is approachable, especially for beginners, and tends to present health data in a way that feels less intimidating than more athlete-focused apps. That makes the Air a strong choice for casual users who want guidance without performance overload.

The main limitation is that a screenless budget tracker will not replace a running watch or smartwatch. You will not get the same real-time workout stats, app support, phone features, or advanced training analysis. But if you want affordable, low-distraction tracking, Fitbit Air is a compelling pick.

The Coros Pace 4 is our best lightweight pick because it delivers serious training features in a watch that feels easy to wear. After testing the watch for two months, MH deputy features editor Carina Hsieh said that it feels so lightweight that you forget it’s there. It’s especially appealing for runners and fitness-minded users who want more data than a basic tracker can provide but don’t want a bulky smartwatch.

Coros has built a strong reputation among runners because its watches tend to offer excellent battery life, practical training tools, and reliable GPS. The Pace 4 continues that tradition. “I was pleasantly surprised by how responsive and quick the GPS signal was on runs,” Hsieh said. She also noted that the watch had an exceptionally long battery life during her testing, and that she only had to charge it twice in two months.

For runners, the Pace 4 can track pace, distance, heart rate, route data, workouts, recovery, and training trends. Features like race predictions, virtual pacing, breadcrumb navigation, and personalized training tools make it feel like a strong contender for anyone who is a serious runner. It is also useful for people who cross-train, since it can handle gym workouts, cycling, walking, and other activities.

A big reason to choose the Pace 4 over other smartwatches is that it feels purpose-built for fitness. You’re not paying for a huge app ecosystem or phone-like features. Instead, you’re getting a lightweight training watch that can help you understand your fitness, recovery, and progress.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 is the best fitness tracker for Android users, especially anyone with a Samsung Galaxy phone. It offers a polished smartwatch experience with robust health and fitness tools, making it a bit like an Android equivalent to the Apple Watch. WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders, who has tested multiple wearables over the years, says she usually struggles to wear trackers consistently because the bands were uncomfortable overnight. But the Galaxy Watch 9 changed that. “The band is surprisingly comfortable to wear and, dare I say, actually looks good,” she said.

This smartwatch tracks everyday activity, steps, heart rate, workouts, stress, sleep, and recovery-style metrics. It also includes Samsung’s Vitals feature, which monitors overnight patterns including heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and other sleep-related signals, then compares them against your personal baseline. Saunders says it took about a full week for her baseline to set up, and anything outside of her normal range appeared in orange in the app, making it easy to compare metrics and spot subtle changes over time.

It also tracks a wide range of exercise modes, and its running features are useful for people who want coaching-style tools. Samsung’s body composition measurement feature can also be helpful for observing trends over time, though the numbers should be treated as estimates rather than medical-grade measurements. Saunders also liked the sleep features, including sleep quality tracking and snore detection, which she found both funny and potentially useful for better understanding nighttime habits.

The watch pairs easily with Galaxy phones, and the Samsung Health app organizes fitness and wellness data in an approachable way. If you want a tracker that can monitor workouts in the morning, handle notifications during the day, and track sleep at night, the Galaxy Watch 9 is a strong choice. In her testing, Saunders found it to be stylish and effective, adding that it would make a great gift for someone starting a health journey or looking for more detailed insights.

The Oura Ring 5 offers robust health and sleep tracking in the most discreet package of all the fitness trackers in this guide. If you don’t like wearing a watch around the clock or simply prefer jewelry over a wristband, Oura is the easiest fitness tracker to live with. In her review, WH associate editor Olivia Luppino said it’s the only fitness tracker she’s ever used that she hasn’t wanted to take off.

The Oura Ring’s biggest strength is passive health tracking. It’s designed to unobtrusively monitor your body in the background, and then translate that information into readiness, sleep, activity, stress, temperature, and recovery insights in an easy to use app. It can be especially helpful for people who want to understand how sleep, illness, stress, menstrual cycle changes, and daily habits affect energy.

For sleep tracking, the Ring 5 is one of the more comfortable options since a ring is less bulky than a watch, and many people find it easier to wear overnight. The app also makes sleep data easy to understand, showing not just how long you slept but how restorative that sleep may have been.

The tradeoff is workout tracking. Oura can track activity and has improved its fitness features, but it’s still not the best choice for people who want real-time stats during runs, strength workouts, or cycling sessions. It can also interfere with grip during weightlifting and kettlebell training. If you want to glance at pace, heart rate, or intervals mid-workout, choose a watch. If you want discreet, all-day and all-night health tracking, choose a smart ring.

For runners, the Garmin Forerunner 570 sits in a sweet spot between advanced training watches and an everyday wearable. Garmin makes several excellent Forerunner models, but the 570 offers a mix of running metrics, GPS tools, recovery insights, smartwatch features, and comfortable wearability for runners who want more than the basics without jumping straight to flagship option.

The Forerunner 570 is designed to be useful for structured training with its capability to track runs, intervals, long runs, tempo sessions, races, recovery runs, and cross-training workouts. It also gives runners access to Garmin’s broader training ecosystem, including performance metrics, suggested workouts, recovery guidance, HRV status, sleep data, training readiness-style insights, and race-related tools. For someone training for a 5K, half marathon, marathon, or simply trying to become a more consistent runner, those features can be super useful.

It has a bright AMOLED display, touchscreen support as well as physical buttons, a feature that’s especially notable for runners since touchscreens can sometimes be frustrating with sweat, rain, or gloves. Battery life varies from 8 hours to up to 10 days depending on how many features you’re using.

The biggest drawback is price. Though it’s not the priciest Forerunner offering out there, the Forerunner 570 is not inexpensive, and newer runners who only want pace, distance, and heart rate may be perfectly happy with a more affordable Forerunner model. But runners who want a capable watch they won’t outgrow, the 570 is a great option.

The Garmin Cirqa is the best screenless tracker for lovers of the Garmin fitness ecosystem, since it integrates seamlessly with Garmin’s other tech. It delivers health and activity tracking without adding another display to your life, and is especially well suited for anyone who wants to use Garmin Connect but doesn't want to wear a full Garmin watch all day long.

That makes Cirqa especially useful for athletes who already own a Garmin running, cycling, or outdoor watch. You may want to wear your Forerunner for workouts and during runs, but prefer something smaller and screen-free for sleep, recovery, or everyday tracking. The Cirqa fills that gap.

It also has a cost advantage over some screenless competitors because it doesn’t require a subscription. That makes it appealing for Garmin loyalists who want ongoing tracking without committing to a monthly membership.

The Cirqa isn’t the best choice if you want live workout stats, on-wrist coaching, or a display for pace and distance, and a Garmin watch would be better for that. But as a low-distraction daily tracker that complements Garmin’s training platform, Cirqa is a welcome addition to the category.

The Google Fitbit Edge bridges the gap between a simple Fitbit band and a full smartwatch, making it a strong choice if you want a display but don’t want a bulkier smartwatch. It gives you a screen for checking stats, starting workouts, reviewing progress, and seeing basic information at a glance.

Compared with the Fitbit Air, the Edge is more interactive, compared with the Inspire, it’s a more advanced option, and compared with a Pixel Watch, it’s simpler to use and more fitness focused. It offers enough features to be useful throughout the day, tracking activity, workouts, sleep, heart-rate trends, and daily wellness data, while still keeping the overall experience lighter than a smartwatch. If you want a compact Google Fitbit tracker with a screen and stronger features than the entry-level models, the Edge is the best fit.

A good heart rate monitor is one of the most important features to look for in a fitness tracker, whether you’re training seriously or just getting started. Heart rate data can help you better understand exercise intensity, track effort during workouts, and monitor resting heart rate over time, which can be a useful marker of cardiovascular fitness. While wrist-based trackers typically aren’t as precise as chest straps, they can still offer a helpful read on exertion levels during moderate to intense activity, according to a 2019 study in Cardiovascular Diagnosis & Therapy.

Sleep tracking can be a useful feature because sleep plays a major role in recovery, energy, mood, and overall performance. By tracking patterns like sleep duration, consistency, and overnight restlessness, a fitness tracker can help you spot habits that may be affecting how you feel the next day. Many models also break down sleep stages, show trends over time, and offer recovery or readiness insights based on your nightly data. While the numbers aren’t always perfect, they can provide a helpful starting point for understanding your routine and making small changes, like adjusting bedtime, limiting late caffeine, or improving sleep consistency.

Weight may not seem that important at first, but it matters when you’re wearing a fitness tracker all day and night. A larger, heavier model can feel more noticeable over time, especially during sleep or long workouts. There’s no single ideal size, and the best option will depend on how you plan to use it.

If you run, hike, or spend a lot of time outdoors, it may be worth choosing a more durable model, even if it’s slightly bulkier. For everyday wear, walking, strength training, or mostly indoor workouts, a lighter, lower-profile tracker may be more comfortable. Ultimately, the right fit comes down to your activity level, wrist size, and what you’ll actually want to keep wearing.

Many of the best fitness trackers can run for days or even weeks on a single charge, such as the Whoop 5.0. But battery doesn't always equate to quality, given that an option like the Apple Watch Series 12 needs to be charged every day and it’s still one of our absolute favorites. Ultimately it comes down to how a trackers charging needs will fit into your routine.

As with all tech, you want a fitness tracker that’s easy to use. If your new tracker isn’t intuitive for you to set up or use daily, you’re far less likely to use it consistently. Ultimately, the only way to know for sure is to try it out yourself to see if it works for you. That's why it’s smart to buy a fitness tracker with a generous return policy.

I’ve been a certified personal trainer for more than a decade, and together with other Women’s Health editors, I’m constantly testing the latest fitness trackers across key factors like durability, comfort, features, and accuracy. We tested them during our workouts, on our runs, in Pilates class, and more. And of course, we tested them during sleep. Whether you’re training regularly or just want something for everyday activity tracking, the models we tested for the latest update range from basic fitness trackers to powerful smartwatches and everything in between.

#4601. Spirituality and Awe in Animals: Dancing in the Rain

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

One of the most frequent requests I receive from readers deals with the spiritual or mystical lives of animals and whether they feel awe and wonder, and how they might express it.

Physically and behaviorally, humans and chimpanzees are almost the same. We share more than 98 percent of genes and around 90 percent of expressions and gestures—like kissing, shaking fists, swaggering, back slapping, and holding hands. As anthropologist Frans de Waal has said, chimpanzees are “equally evolved,” and “their socio-emotional lives resemble ours to such a degree that it is unclear where to draw the line.”

One line some people draw between human animals and nonhumans is spirituality. However, in their own ways, might they feel an urge to celebrate and express the miracle of being alive? And if they do, how would we recognize it?

Chimpanzees are known to drum. Researchers think they do this to define territories or attract a mate and that these patterns might be precursors to musical rhythm. But what if chimps also drum for the same reason we make music—to express our passions through rhythm, vocalization, and movement?

Biologist Caitlin O’Connell describes the strange ritual called “accumulative rock throwing.” This behavior has been observed only among male chimpanzees in West Africa. O’Connell says that, after the chimp carefully selects a fig tree with a hollow, resonant trunk, the performance begins:

Suddenly, the chimpanzee stands and picks up a rock the size of a melon. His shoulders start heaving and his lips purse as he emits a soft moaning sound. The moaning gets louder and louder, shorter and sharper in a buildup that reaches an open-mouthed climax—the chimpanzee’s signature pant-hoot vocalization.

At the height of this intense call, the chimpanzee reveals his intention and hurtles the rock against one of the buttresses of the tree with a bang. He then climbs onto the buttress and briefly beats at it with his feet as if he were playing a drum…. After a good drumming, he runs off into the forest, screaming.

At Gombe National Park in the 1960s, Jane Goodall watched chimpanzees eating in a fig tree on a dreary spring day:

At about noon the first heavy drops of rain began to fall. The chimpanzees climbed out of the tree and one after the other plodded up the steep grassy slope toward the open ridge at the top…. As they reached the ridge the chimpanzees paused. At that moment the storm broke. The rain was torrential, and the sudden clap of thunder, right overhead, made me jump. As if this were a signal, one of the big males stood upright and as he swayed and swaggered rhythmically from foot to foot, I could just hear the rising crescendo of his pant-hoots above the beating of the rain. Then he charged off, flat-out down the slope toward the trees he had just left. He ran some thirty yards, and then, swinging round the trunk of a small tree to break his headlong rush, leaped into the low branches and sat motionless.

One after another, the other six males followed: running downhill, breaking branches and hurling them, then swinging themselves into trees. Meanwhile, the audience of females and children watched from the ridgetop. Then the males trudged back up the slope and did it again—and yet again—as, Jane said, “the rain fell harder, jagged forks or brilliant flares of lightning lit the leaden sky, and the crashing of the thunder seemed to shake the very mountains.”

This “rain dance” lasted for 20 minutes, and the performance was as dramatic as the storm. As Jane later discovered, individual chimps often do this, but group displays are rare, and rain dances are reserved for those sky-opening deluges when, as we might say, “the heavens part.”

Whatever the chimpanzees are thinking, uncontained nature clearly evokes a swirl of uncontainable emotions, inspiring behavior that mimics a deliberate, self-aware ritual.

As the group finally left that day, Goodall said, “One male paused, and with his hand on a tree trunk, looked back—the actor taking his final curtain. Then he too vanished over the ridge.”

Goodall witnessed another remarkable chimpanzee ritual that, as much as any, seems to embody a genuine nature-related spiritual experience. Here she described a chimpanzee approaching a waterfall in a heightened state of arousal:

As he gets closer, and the roar of the falling water gets louder, his pace quickens, his hair becomes fully erect, and upon reaching the stream he may perform a magnificent display close to the foot of the falls. Standing upright, he sways rhythmically from foot to foot, stamping in the shallow, rushing water, picking up and hurling great rocks. Sometimes he climbs up the slender vines that hang down from the trees high above and swings out into the spray of the ﻿falling water. This “waterfall dance” may last ten or fifteen minutes.

Goodall asked, “Is it not possible that these performances are stimulated by feelings akin to wonder and awe? After a waterfall display, the performer may sit on a rock, his eyes following the falling water. What is it, this water?”

From the outside, a spiritual experience can look like nothing. For a period of time, someone lies down, kneels, sits, or stands, yet inside they feel moved in ways that are hard to explain.

Might that very stillness be another sign of awe? Like us, chimpanzees are known to admire the sunset. For 10 minutes or more, individuals may pause whatever they are doing. Groups will gather, greet, and sit on a particularly good lookout as the sun signs off for the night.

Are the chimpanzees admiring beauty? Are they enjoying a peaceful connection to nature? Or are they thinking about what to eat for dinner? These chimpanzees aren’t doing anything, but something is going on inside. And we’d be foolish to assume that an animal’s curiosity can’t lead to the biggest questions of all.

We need more research on this fascinating topic, and scientists must feel comfortable trespassing into what most frequently is assumed to be an arena reserved only for humans—the having of spiritual or mystical experiences and asking what the animals are feeling. Studying possible relationships among science, sentience, and spirituality is a most fascinating and forward-looking topic that awaits and demands more transdisciplinary attention.

All in all, research shows the line between humans and animals is thinner than we ever supposed. Most likely, we are not alone in occupying the spiritual or mystical arena and should welcome in other animals.

Many thanks to Jeff Campbell for helping to research and write about this topic in Love in Their Hearts: A Celebration of Animal Emotions and a Guide to Compassionate Action.

Bekoff, Marc. The Emotional Lives of Animals, Revised Edition. New World Library, 2007/2024.

———, editor. The Smile of a Dolphin: Remarkable Accounts of Animal Emotions. Discovery Books, 2000.

de Waal, Frans. Mama’s Last Hug: Animal Emotions and What They Tell Us about Ourselves. W. W. Norton & Co., 2019.

Goodall, Jane. The Chimpanzees of Gombe: Patterns of Behavior. Belknap Press, 1986.

———. In the Shadow of Man. Mariner Books/Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 1971/2010.

———. Jane Goodall: 50 Years at Gombe. Stewart, Tabori & Chang, 2010.

Krulwich, Robert. Holy Baboon! A 'Mystical' Moment In Africa. NPR, RadioLab, December 22, 2009. https://www.npr.org/2009/12/22/121713610/holy-baboon-a-mystical-moment-…

O’Connell, Caitlin. Wild Rituals: 10 Lessons Animals Can Teach Us About Connection, Community, and Ourselves. Chronicle Prism, 2021.

Safina, Carl. Becoming Wild: How Animal Cultures Raise Families, Create Beauty, and Achieve Peace. Henry Holt and Company, 2020.

#4600. The 92 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 13 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4599. China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

#4598. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4597. ‘I Started Strength Training at 74. At 78, I Can Deadlift 132 Lbs—Here’s How.’

“While I love lifting weights and hitting new PRs, the greatest reward is how much easier everyday life has become.”

If there’s one thing I’ve learned as I’ve gotten older, it’s that being active and being strong aren’t necessarily the same thing. For most of my life, I’d been recreationally active, and had loved kayaking, swimming, and taking my dog on long walks. I’d never done any kind of structured strength training, until right before my 75th birthday. One day, I was sitting on a curb outside my house, and when it was time to stand up, I couldn’t. I felt embarrassed, and the idea of falling and not being able to get up or being in a situation where I couldn’t take care of myself was scary.

I wanted everyday activities, like climbing stairs, carrying groceries, and getting up off the floor, to feel easier. I also wanted to trust my body more, and feel confident in my ability to handle whatever life threw my way. So, I joined Aspire Athletic Club, a gym near my home in Schenectady, New York, and began working out once a week with the owner, Chris Wertman. In the beginning, even simple movements were challenging, so I started with basic bodyweight exercises like the box squat, step-up, and bird dog. The focus was on learning proper form and getting comfortable with the movements.

After a few weeks, I gradually incorporated 5- to 8-lb dumbbells into the movements, and a month or two later, I noticed a real difference in my strength: I could do more repetitions, lift even heavier weights, and move with greater confidence. It was so encouraging to see the hard work pay off, and it motivated me to keep going. About a year into consistent training, I was feeling stronger and ready to take on more. I began training full-body twice a week and incorporated more challenging exercises like squat variations, the walking lunge, weighted glute bridge, and chest fly to build overall strength.

I’d never deadlifted before, so seeing someone my age lift with that kind of strength was incredibly inspiring. That decision marked the beginning of a new chapter in my strength training journey—I told my new trainer of about six months, Jack Tyree, that I wanted to lift heavier weights and try deadlifting. I even began training for my gym’s upcoming annual deadlift exhibition, which was in eight months.

Since I’d just been training with dumbbells, I tried working with a kettlebell while I got comfortable with the movement and proper technique. As I got stronger and more confident, I graduated to the barbell and continued adding more weight each week. Then, this past May, I deadlifted 132 lbs for a single rep at the exhibition, setting a personal record. I never imagined I’d be able to do something like that, but I was so proud of how strong I’d become—and I was excited to see how much further I could push myself.

Six months after the exhibition, I now strength train three days a week: one day focused on upper body, one on lower body, and one dedicated to mobility and balance. Jack still programs all my workouts, and every session includes six to eight exercises, with 3 or 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps each. I use a mix of free weights and weight machines, and some of my go-to moves include the farmer’s carry, curtsy lunge, lat pulldown, scapular pushup, squat, and bench press. Deadlifts are still my favorite; I can now do three reps at 132 lbs, which I’m really proud of.

Outside the gym, I love getting outside and staying active, so I walk a few miles with my dog every day for my cardiovascular health. In addition to mobility and balance work at the gym, I also try to stretch at home whenever I can to ease muscle soreness and improve my range of motion, especially in my shoulders and hips.

I know nutrition is an important part of recovery too. Although I don’t follow a strict nutrition plan or count macros, I try to eat protein at every meal to support muscle growth. Usually, it’s chicken, red meat, or a scoop of protein powder mixed into my morning oatmeal. I also prioritize whole foods and aim to incorporate a variety of fruits and vegetables throughout the day.

When I first started strength training, I didn’t know where to begin. So, having someone guide me through the movements, teach me proper form, and help me build strength safely made all the difference. My trainers have helped me recognize what I’m capable of, push beyond what I thought was possible, and progress at a pace that feels right. They also create workouts that challenge me while keeping my goals in mind. Having their support and encouragement has given me the confidence to try things I never imagined I could do. Whether it’s deadlifting heavy weights, bench pressing a barbell, or taking less rest between working sets, my trainers have taught me not to put a ceiling on what I think I can accomplish.

Before I strength trained, I felt weak and unsteady, but I didn’t give up and accept that I’d feel like that for the rest of my life. In some ways, I completely started over with exercise at 74 because I tried something brand new—and that’s affected my life outside of the gym.

Now, at 78, I feel stronger than ever; I can get up off the floor with ease, carry my own groceries into the house, shovel snow, garden, and play sports with my grandchildren. These are things I want to keep doing independently, and having the strength to do them confidently means the world to me. While I love lifting weights and hitting new PRs, the greatest reward is how much easier everyday life has become.

Learning to lift in my mid-70s wasn’t easy, and building that strength didn’t happen overnight, but I kept showing up, putting in the work, and gradually accomplishing what I once never thought was possible. Now, as I approach 80, I’m still getting stronger, and I want other women to know they’re never too old to get started, and they may be capable of far more than they realize. If I can go from struggling to get up from a curb to deadlifting 132 pounds, who knows what else is possible?

#4596. Why Language Makes Us Absolutists and Jerks

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

My research spans the physical origins of life, the evolution of human language and what it is like to live under its influence, and the emotional psychology of absolutists and jerks. The theme throughout is to better understand what we actually are. I have been at it for 35 years. For decades, I was dogged by the question "What's wrong with me?" I simply broadened my focus to "What's up with us?" Me included.

For 30 years, I have studied and collaborated with Terrence Deacon, a UC Berkeley biologist. I met him after reading his book on the physical evolution of human language. I call his approach physical philosophy. He is a lab scientist who tackles big questions, such as what life and consciousness are, or how purpose-driven behavior emerges from nothing but purposeless chemical phenomena.

He does not take abstractions like "information" as givens. Most scientists simply assume information exists, treating DNA as an "information-bearing molecule." Deacon holds that anything can become information, but only when it is about something for some being trying to achieve something—most fundamentally, trying to stay alive. The burden is on us to explain how beings struggling for their own existence emerged before DNA, such that molecules could become information for them.

Likewise, most social scientists simply assume motivation. If someone makes an effort, they assume the person is motivated, without explaining what motivation is. That is little better than assuming life is a soul installed in matter. Deacon explains motivation from the ground up, starting with the first chemical system motivated to keep itself going.

Meanwhile, much of my work, especially around Trumpism, has been about humans driving drunk under the influence of language. Language makes us a visionary, anxious, delusional, and dangerous species. We can imagine real and unreal threats and missed opportunities, past, present, and future, that no other creature can. We trudge through a sandstorm of confidence-eroding possibilities, and we can compensate for the anxiety with language, too, buying into all sorts of delusional and dangerous nonsense.

Organisms traffic in two basic kinds of information: icons and indexes, resemblances and pointers. Your buddy today resembles your buddy yesterday. That is iconic. Hearing your buddy's voice on the phone makes you think of him. That is indexical: a trait pointing to what it belongs to, the way smoke points to fire.

Humans add a third kind of information: symbols. As a toddler, you heard your parents repeat words while pointing at things. Eventually your ability to talk achieved lift-off from things. You did not have to point at Mommy to say she was sad. You could say it even if she was not around. Symbols have no built-in significance. The word "dog" neither looks nor sounds like a dog. It is a social convention. So you can talk about dogs nowhere in sight, or about gods who do not exist.

That freedom from present reality makes us creative and visionary, but also anxious. We can imagine our own deaths and haunting memories, and then reassure ourselves with unreal, self-soothing delusions. Recognizing how much language shapes us would fill us with compassion for ourselves and others, and help us manage our anxieties and delusions more effectively.

Language also amps up our capacity to rationalize and moralize in defense of anything we have done or want to do. Though we have language, we are still driven mostly by feelings, the urgent need to feel comfortable in our own skin. The more intense the feeling, the more it seems like reality itself: I feel it, therefore it is real. Then, since it feels so real, we assume away the feelings that drove it. You hear it in absolutists who speak intensely about what they love and hate while acting like neutral judges. You hear it in their hypocrisy: If I do it, it feels good and is therefore virtuous; if my rivals do exactly the same thing, it feels bad and is therefore evil.

Almost all organisms are parasites and predators. Only humans can become absolutists or jerks, thanks to language. We can spin words to see ourselves as superheroes and our enemies as the devil's spawn. With words, humans can rationalize anything, even killing people at the command of an imaginary God who likes us best.

A jerk is a self-absolving absolutist, certain they are right about everything. "Absolute" originally meant dissolved away from any influences. Nothing and nobody can give them a reality check. They barge through life spinning everything they do as perfect and anyone in their way as evil. They are disgusting, but we should not overlook how satisfying that feeling must be. It is the obvious cure for the anxiety of living vulnerable lives.

And it is not just absolutists. It is all of us, to some degree.

First, if you can admit that you are human, prone to trafficking in language, with high anxiety and a tendency to reassure, rationalize, and moralize, you can manage that tendency more effectively. If you deny it, or assume only the other guy has the problem, you will not manage it. You cannot manage an appetite you deny having. An alcoholic cannot manage alcoholism by saying, "I'm no alcoholic. Other people are alcoholics. They disgust me, which proves I'm not one."

Second, watch out for how feelings make ideas feel true and make us forget they were driven by feelings. Whenever you or others speak with passionate insistence on rational moral arguments, you are likely rationalizing and moralizing, spinning convincing feelings into words that make them feel absolutely true.

#4595. High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

#4594. 9 Bodily Changes That Happen a Month After Taking Testosterone

TRT can bring big changes fast—and some might surprise you.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

TESTOSTERONE GOES BEYOND building muscle. T helps you maintain muscle mass, facial and body hair, sex drive, and red blood cell production. So when your T levels start to decline—which happens naturally in your thirties—there’s a whole range of symptoms like low libido or just feeling blue.

Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can help raise T levels. After a couple of weeks to a month, you’ll start to see some changes, some big and small. Some pleasant and not so pleasant. Below, urologists explain what happens to your body a month after taking testosterone.

IF YOU HAVE low T, your doctor will conduct some tests to see if you’re a good candidate for the therapy. Ryan Smith, MD, urologist specializing in men’s health at the University of Virginia Health, says a doctor will perform two blood tests in the morning (on different days) when testosterone is at its highest.

Low is considered under 300 nanograms per deciliter (ng/dL) by some accounts and under 264 ng/dL by others. Doctors also factor in any symptoms you’re having, like trouble getting erections or orgasms, fatigue, or just feeling blah.

Nowadays, testosterone is more accessible without a prescription, with many people only having to complete an online assessment. Leaving out a doctor’s approval and supervision, however, can be harmful, says Justin Dubin, MD, urologist at Baptist Health.

In a 2022 study that Dr. Dubin co-authored, researchers found that many online platforms are not providing testosterone therapy in accordance with the American Urological Association and the Endocrine Society guidelines. Using a secret shopper, the researchers found that the platforms offered therapy to men who didn’t meet the guidelines and didn’t mention the risks or benefits of testosterone therapy.

Working with a doctor ensures that you’re prescribed testosterone only when you need it and that you’re taking the right dose. Then, they can work with you to make sure your testosterone levels respond appropriately. Doctors like to recheck everything every six months to make sure you’re not having any negative side effects.

A number of testosterone options are available. You can choose between injectables, topical gels, creams, under-the-skin pellet therapy, pills, and nasal sprays. You can learn more about them here.

Each comes with its own set of side effects, so it all comes down to your personal preference, health situation, and what your insurance covers. You can read about the real-life experiences of guys of different ages and body types and their experiences with taking testosterone.

IT CAN TAKE a few weeks to a month or two to see your symptoms improve after starting testosterone replacement therapy, says Dr. Smith. Here are some of the side effects—some obvious and some not—that come with testosterone therapy.

When you’re low on testosterone, you might notice your sex drive dip. But when you take TRT, the treatment reactivates the androgen receptors in the part of your brain that controls desire, says Abraham Morgentaler, MD, associate clinical professor of urology at Harvard Medical School and author of Testosterone for Life. Regaining a healthy sex drive is one of the biggest benefits of testosterone replacement therapy, he says.

TRT may also make your erections more satisfying, though this isn’t the only piece of the puzzle. Erections also rely on healthy nerves and blood flow. That means that testosterone therapy by itself won't always help erectile dysfunction.

Muscles respond to testosterone and starting TRT can increase muscle mass, says Dr. Morgentaler. That’s because testosterone activates the androgen receptors in muscle tissue to stimulate growth.

The effect of a testosterone replacement dose on your muscles, however, is fairly minimal. To make the most of this muscle-building benefit, you’ll need to be doing your part through strength training and possibly raising the amount of protein you consume (depending on your current intake). Don’t know where to start? Check out MH’s four-week muscle building guide.

Some men also report fat loss. While testosterone doesn’t directly incite fat loss itself, part of it may be thanks to the uptick in muscle mass. The more muscle you have, the higher your basal metabolic rate (BMR). That means your body will burn more calories at rest.

Another indirect way testosterone can help with fat loss is motivation to keep pushing once you see results. Jed Kaminetsky, MD, urologist at NYU Langone Medical Center, testosterone can increase your energy levels, making it easier to get up and sweat it out.

Fatigue is a common symptom of low T. “When we treat them, a lot of men will say that their energy has improved,” says Dr. Morgentaler.

Scientists studying testosterone aren't sure exactly how the hormone plays a role in energy—just that it does. One of the prevailing hypotheses Dr. Morgentaler can get behind is that testosterone somehow affects your mitochondria (that organelle you learned in high school is the powerhouse of your cells). The theory is that “testosterone turns them on, so they're more productive in terms of creating the energy that the cells need.”

Ronald Tamler, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, says changes in energy may also be tied back to androgen receptors. “If they don't get sufficient input, that can cause fatigue,” he says. Bringing testosterone levels back up can help reverse this.

Experts don't have a definitive answer to why testosterone impacts mood so deeply—after all, “the brain is a complicated thing,” says Dr. Tamler. But the positive effect of TRT on mood is a potential life-changing benefit.

An old but highly referenced clinical trial in 2003 looked at how testosterone gels affected middle-aged men with treatment-resistant depression and low T. After 8 weeks, the men showed greater improvements in the psychological aspects of depression (sadness, guilt, and anxiety) than those given a placebo. The men taking testosterone gels also showed nearly the same rate of improvement in somatic aspects of depression (improvements in sleep, appetite, and libido). A more recent review of 27 clinical trials involving 1,890 men with low T found that TRT provided a significant reduction in depressive symptoms, especially at higher doses.

One of the most important things to know before starting TRT is that the treatment decreases sperm production and may cause infertility.

Testosterone might affect the size of your testicles, too. "Most of the size of the testicle is dedicated to making sperm, so when you're making less sperm, the testicles get smaller," says Dr. Morgentaler.

Sperm production may or may not go back to normal even after stopping treatment, says Dr. Kaminetsky. One study found increasing age and longer TRT linked to lower chances of normal sperm recovery.

Some people notice a little swelling in their feet and ankles because testosterone can encourage your body to hold onto excess fluid, says Dr. Morgentaler.

This isn't a big deal for most people, he says, and swelling is more common if you're taking a non-daily treatment like an injection, when you're getting a higher dose of T in one sitting.

Testosterone replacement therapy may change your skin type—for better or for worse, says Dr. Morgentaler.

Testosterone can increase oil production, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. Oil production is important for healthy skin, so you may actually end up with a better complexion. However, too much oily buildup can lead to breakouts.

While Dr. Morgentaler says testosterone-induced breakouts aren’t common, they are more likely to occur in men with a history of acne. Skin changes may also be more common if you’re taking testosterone injections versus other modes of administration since you're getting a higher dose all at once.

In all men—whether you’re taking T or not—some testosterone is converted into the hormone estradiol, a form of estrogen. In men who naturally have more breast tissue, testosterone can be converted into estradiol, which may stimulate breast tissue to grow.

This is called gynecomastia, says Dr. Morgentaler, and it's not as common as other side effects. If gynecomastia does happen, your doctor will likely stop treatment for a month or two to allow your breast tissue to go back to normal. Then, you’ll resume T along with a drug that blocks the conversion of testosterone to estradiol.

If you’re going the topical testosterone therapy route, one issue to watch out for is transference with women and children.

Darshan Patel, MD, assistant professor of urology at the University of California San Diego’s Men’s Health Center, says testosterone from gels or creams can be transferred through skin-to-skin contact or from clothing and absorbed by someone else.

“You really have to be careful to wash your hands well and not expose others,” adds Dr. Smith. Contact with excess testosterone can affect children’s genitalia and cause premature pubic hair development and aggressive behavior.
