#4570. 7 Running Shorts for Women That WH Editors Love

Editor-tested picks built for comfort, pockets, and sweat control.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s nothing more humiliating than having a huge sweat stain on your butt after strenuous mile repeats—been there, done that. A good run is supposed to lift your mood, not bring you down, so finding the best running shorts to keep the endorphins flowing (and your butt dry) is essential.

Not all workout shorts are made the same. Some offer more compression, while others are less restrictive and have convenient features like pockets—the holy grail! “You need a place to carry all your resources—pockets are a non-negotiable for running gels, electrolytes, phone, wallet, and keys,” says New York-based running coach and personal trainer Amanda Katz, NASM-CPT.

While many athletic shorts can be used for different purposes, running shorts usually have a built-in interior liner, sweat-wicking material, and a nonconstrictive design to keep you cool and comfortable as you rack up mileage in your sleek running shoes.

I researched and gathered the best running shorts from a running coach and editors who’ve personally tested them. Whether you’re training for a marathon or are a hobby jogger, all the shorts I picked are from trusted activewear and athleisure brands that will benefit you in the long run (literally). Ready to find out more about the best running shorts for women? Keep scrolling.

After testing countless pairs of running shorts over the years, the Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short from Lululemon is my fave for its sweat-wicking fabric and comfortable fit. The polyester blend wicks away sweat, prevents cling, and promotes airflow while running. The loose, flowy fit keeps me cool, while a built-in interior liner adds lightweight coverage and support without bulk.

The side pockets are small, but hold small essentials like a credit card, key, or energy gels for long runs. The leg openings are spacious, allowing for a full range of motion, and an adjustable drawstring secures the waistband for a customizable fit. Want to hit the road at the crack of dawn or at night? No sweat; reflective detailing improves visibility in dark or dim light, making early morning or evening runs safer.

I appreciate the 4-inch length, given I prefer more coverage, but a 2.5-inch length is available if you prefer a shorter fit. WH associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, is also a fan of the fit and vast color palette. “They never ride up or move around, which is hard to find in a running short,” she says. With tons of colors and sizes to choose from, you can't go wrong.

New Balance is a top brand in the running world, and the RC Short is one of my faves. It runs slightly big, but I love the extra breathing room during a sweat session.

The lightweight, flowy construction uses the brand’s quick-drying tech fabric (a polyester and spandex blend) to wick moisture from the skin. The breathable design promotes tons of airflow, creating a cooling effect while I run—especially ideal during scorching hot summer runs.

The seamless, interior lining reduces chafing and irritation, while the waistband features an adjustable drawstring to customize the fit. It’s also not too tight—some liners can feel like you’re wearing a diaper (hate). As for storage, there’s a back pocket for securing small running essentials and even tiny snacks like a granola bar when you’re on the move.

A pair of high cut shorts, such as the Alo Match Point Short, is a running staple. The high-cut at the thighs keeps things perfectly airy and flowy for optimal coolness when I get overheated, more so than the Lululemon Hotty Hot Short.

This construction, paired with its moisture-wicking polyester fabric, creates the perfect breathable running shorts. While it’s a bit short at just over two inches, there’s still great coverage with a built-in brief, and I find it doesn’t show too much skin.

WH style contributor Lily Wolhner also appreciates this loose style for various workouts. “My favorite part about this short is that it’s never clingy, so it doesn’t ride up the thigh or need constant re-adjusting while you’re working out,” Wolhner says. “I’ve worn it for months and recently tested it during a 45-minute strength and HIIT workout, as well as an hour-long cross-training workout—I never felt over-exposed or uncomfortable in it.”

By the looks of the elastic waistband, I expected it to dig into my skin—wrong. It felt comfortable, although it’s important to note this short does run big, so I suggest sizing down.

We love a two-for-one, and this short from Brooks is ideal for both trail running and running at the gym. It has light compression with a built-in tight liner that doesn’t sacrifice mobility.

The mega-durable polyester fabric resists tears and moisture, which makes it ideal for trail running in tough terrain. “I love the high waist, the zipper pocket to carry my keys, and the tight shorts under a looser short aesthetic,” Katz says.

Two waistband pockets are impressively large and can even fit a water flask, so you can always stay hydrated during your jogs.

I personally don’t love compression-lined shorts because I like to feel totally free, but if you prefer extra coverage and double layers, this short is ideal.

If you want a no-frills pair of shorts at an affordable price point that will stand the test of time, the Under Armour Play Up 3.0 belongs in your running gear collection. I’ve owned multiple pairs for years in eye-catching colors, and they’re still in good condition with no pills—even after dozens of runs and wash cycles.

The lightweight knit fabric made from smooth polyester has an anti-pill finish for extra durability, and is impressively comfy. Plus, it hides embarrassing sweat stains post-run, despite the slightly thicker material.

The waistband uses a wide elastic band that provides a secure fit without any adjustable features. However, I find it still fits roomy and allows for a full range of motion.

It includes deep side pockets but no enclosure, so I don’t recommend stashing anything super important besides fuel, like energy gels. I wear it the most for shorter, mid-distance runs and whenever I want to add a pop of color—it has 21 color options!

I usually don’t gravitate toward compression shorts since I don’t like feeling constricted, but the Athleta Salutation Stash 5-Inch Short offers the perfect amount of tightness. It hugs my thighs with gentle compression, while the high-rise waistband distributes pressure evenly for a secure fit without digging in. Plus, the two deep side pockets offer convenient storage for longer runs.

The smooth, double-knit fabric is buttery-soft and offers great coverage. While on the thicker side, it conceals sweat stains well—a huge win during long-haul runs. I wouldn’t say it feels the most breathable compared to other shorts in this guide, but the nylon and lycra blend wicks away sweat and dries fast.

Another huge selling point? The fabric’s UPF 50 protection, which prevents UV radiation from scorching your thighs. This is my favorite feature as someone fair-skinned and prone to nasty sunburns (IYKYK). Aside from its fabric, I love that it has a matching jacket for a coordinated workout set.

Tracksmith’s Van Cortlandt Shorts combine retro styling with a performance-driven design that makes them a winner both on and off the track. It’s made from a lightweight mesh fabric to maximize airflow, paired with an antimicrobial finish to help combat odor by wicking away sweat and limiting bacteria buildup during intense runs.

After summer runs when I’m dripping with sweat, I noticed zero smell—and that the short dries at the speed of light.

Like our best overall, it’s quite short at 2.5 inches, so if you prefer a longer style, you should look to other styles in this guide. On the flip side, it doesn’t disrupt my range of motion during speed work or long runs. As for fit, I found it runs true to size, but make sure to consult the size chart as always.

Running shorts with sweat-wicking fabric are the way to go, Katz says. Most shorts use a blend of polyester, spandex, and/or nylon, which lifts moisture from the skin while staying flexible during movement. Based on testing, it’s best to avoid cotton since it doesn’t dry nearly as fast and clings to the skin when wet.

It’s important to determine what kind of rise and inseam you desire. High-waisted running shorts offer more coverage and tummy control, while a mid-rise waist sits right at the hips. Ultimately, what you find most flattering for your body type is the best option.

The inseam is the length from the crotch to the bottom. A longer length will show less skin but may disrupt the range of motion, while some running shorts favorites, like the Lululemon Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short, offer a 2.5-inch option if you like a mini fit.

As for an interior liner or compression, this will make running shorts fit more snugly. “Compression is a matter of preference, but the goal in this material is to boost recovery,” says Katz. If you want a less constrictive fit, it’s probably best to avoid that feature.

In addition to my own testing, Women’s Health associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT also extensively tested tons of running shorts to determine whether or not they’re the real deal. Each pair was worn during training runs or races for anywhere from three weeks to even three years to see how they performed and held up.

Essential features considered were materials, inseam, pockets, durability, and adjustability. Additionally, I asked a running coach for their go-to running shorts and guidance on how they should fit.

#4569. Is Cheating in Marriage Ever Justified?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

“Yes, cheating can damage a marriage,” a couples therapist I interviewed a few years ago told me, “yet it can also make the marriage stronger.”

This approach is playing with fire. Most of us generally would not recommend such an activity, as we know that while fire can warm your home, it can also burn your house down. Instead, we would more likely suggest learning how to use fire responsibly—for the warming and cooking, not the burning.

We could also compare cheating on your spouse with taking care of your health. Living through cancer can become the catalyst for making better decisions about how to live your life. Yet I wouldn't recommend smoking two packs a day to attempt to induce this appreciation—as it can also lead to another outcome.

It’s the same with relationships. Betrayal can become the catalyst for candid discussions about what hasn’t been working, open conversations about intimacy, and a renewed appreciation of what you have. Alternatively, it can lead to the loss of the relationship—the scorched-house equivalent of playing with fire.

After infidelity, both people become aware that the other person was willing to take this risk. All the post-cheating epiphanies do not erase this awareness, and it feels extremely painful and difficult to assimilate for the person who was betrayed.

Why is this? Cheating is the ultimate form of narcissistic validation. It’s a trade: your short-term validation for your partner’s long-term suffering.

And suffer they will. “I will regret it for the rest of my life,” shares one woman in a recent survey. “My marriage was already falling apart, but I will never forget the look of hurt on my now ex-husband's face when he found out. He forgave me many years ago, but I still struggle to forgive myself some twenty-plus years later.”

To understand the problem with betraying your intimate partner, consider the words of Afghan-American novelist Khaled Hosseini. “There is only one sin, only one, and that is theft. Every other sin is a variation of theft,” shares Hosseini in The Kite Runner. “When you kill a man, you steal a life. You steal his wife’s right of a husband, you rob his children of a father. When you lie you steal someone’s right to truth. When you cheat, you steal the right to fairness.”

To make matters worse, when you betray another human being, it’s not just the right to fairness you are taking from them. You also take their right to believe in love, in acceptance, in belonging.

In other words, you take everything that most matters to them. “There is no more wretched act than stealing,” Hosseini concludes.

“At the end of the day, it wasn’t the cheating that hurt the most,” confides another woman, “it was the betrayal. Someone I trusted so much didn't trust me enough to simply say, ‘Hey, I'm unhappy, and I want out.’”

Despite the harm we do to others, in our fragile, volatile search for validation, many of us are capable of seeing past how infidelity will affect the other person. We often don’t see the forest when standing right in front of a tree. We don’t think about the trust that will be eroded, and almost always never fully recaptured, if we cheat.

Why? Trust in a relationship is like air. You don’t think about air unless you don’t have it. Then it becomes the only thing you think about.

When you convince another human being to build their life around you and then take that safety and security from them through betrayal, you dispel the closest approximation to sacredness you will ever experience in your life.

It is at this point that you learn that when you destroy what is sacred, you destroy the sacred within you.

Cheating, then, is not only an ethically flawed form of validation; it also injures ourselves. We need to find better ways to express our relationship dissatisfaction.

If your partner is unable to listen to you or adapt with you for a protracted period, separation may be a recourse. It’s very simple: If you can’t continue your commitment, tell them rather than going down the road of pretend. They deserve as much from you.

Once you’ve come clean, you can move in another direction in your intimate life—and seek the Holy Grail of external validation you’ve been craving—knowing you were honest and did what you could to preserve the sacred within your relationship.

#4568. The 15 Best Jeans for Men, Tested and Reviewed by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FEW MENSWEAR PIECES nail durability and easy style in one package like a great pair of jeans. For me, it’s the starting point for most of my outfits. But once you start paying attention, you realize how wide the gap is between pairs that just look good and pairs that can go with a bunch of different looks. Some are so stiff like a straitjacket, others stretch out so much they feel like leggings rather than denim.

Over the past five years, I’ve tested more than 60 pairs across seasons—winter layering, dead-of-summer heat, and everything in between—alongside Men’s Health’s fashion team. We looked at different fits, washes, and cuts across a range of builds and style preferences. Skinny fits are out. Instead, go for relaxed, straight, or straight-slim cuts that fall at the widest part of your legs for a flattering drape.

The Levi’s 501 is the blueprint of jeans—the one that every other pair takes notes from. I’ve had the straight-leg style in my closet for some years now and it fits comfortably every time. It has an easy fit through the hip and thigh, with a slight taper below the knee that doesn’t stack over my shoes. The 501s is made with 100% cotton, that’s sturdy and substantial but still breathable, even in the subway where things feel stuffy.

Levi’s offers five different inseams, which is not standard for most retail denim brands. There’s also plenty of washes and different levels of stretch including low and high stretch as well none at all. In other words, whether you’re tall, short, or somewhere in between, there’s an option for everyone and you can skip wasting money at a tailor. I found that the low-stretch pair gives you enough flex to move around without any stiffness. The no-stretch version broke in nicely after a few wears, and the high-stretch ones felt more laid-back without losing shape, but just a tad less breathable.

I’ve washed the 501s a million times and the fit always held up. It hasn’t become too baggy or too tight. Though I’ve machine dried mine before and only saw minimal shrinkage, I still recommend air drying to keep the fit where it’s at. The button fly took a minute to get used to, but it adds to that vintage feel. Out of all the washes I tried, the medium stonewash was the standout. It’s soft straight out of the box, with just the right amount of fading. It works with everything in my closet: t-shirts and hoodies, oxford shirts and loafers, boots and sneakers.

This pair of travel jeans from Bonobos is the most flexible jean I’ve tested. Honestly, they wear more like athletic pants than traditional denim. The brand uses a stretch cotton blend with a generous dose of elastane, which gives you full range of motion to handle all kinds of airport chaos: twisting and turning through TSA, sprinting to your gate, or squeezing into a tight middle seat.

I usually fly in sweatpants because I can’t stand feeling restricted on long flights, but these jeans completely changed that. On a 13-hour flight back from Japan, I stayed comfortable the entire time. No pinching, no stiffness, and I wasn’t overheating, either. The fabric is super breathable and lightweight, so even during hot layovers and road trips, I didn’t feel like I was melting.

Another big win: they hold their shape. A lot of high-stretch jeans get that saggy, baggy-knee look after a few hours, but not these. I’ve worn and washed them multiple times, and they still bounce back. And despite the gym-pant-level flexibility, they still look like real jeans; clean, tailored, and polished.

They’re also extremely low-maintenance. I packed them tightly into a carry-on for hours, pulled them out, and didn’t see a single crease. That wrinkle resistance is impressive. They looked crisp and ready to wear, no steamer or iron needed. And in true Bonobos fashion: they come in more waist sizes and fits than just about any brand we’ve tested, so no matter your build, you’ll find a version that works for you.

Abercrombie has one of the strongest takes on the baggy jeans right now. This style of denim in general has fully made its comeback, showing up on runways all the way down to everyday streetwear. The brand’s offering is easy to wear: lightweight, super relaxed through the leg, and has that slight “puddle” at the shoe—meaning the hem stacks a bit over your sneakers instead of hitting right at the ankle.

I like that it comes in multiple inseams, so you can actually control how much stacking you want depending on your height or how you like your jeans to sit. And with 20-plus colorways, it’s easy to find a version that fits your vibe, whether you want something low-key and neutral or a little more standout. I personally love the vintage black wash that reads clean and modern, even with the looser shape. In terms of fabric, it’s made from 100% cotton that already feels broken-in, so you’re not dealing with anything overly structured out of the gate.

I put on the Ford Standard Jean from Buck Mason, and could instantly feel how durable this pair was. Not only is this denim as tough as they come, it’s built to last and looks damn good doing it. It’s sourced from Japan’s Kaihara mills, which is known for blending traditional shuttle loom techniques with modern innovation. In other words, this fabric has that rich, textured character you expect from premium Japanese denim, but with a level of consistency that ensures long-term durability. At 14 oz, these jeans sit in that sweet spot—not too heavy, not too light—so it feels sturdy but won’t take forever to break in.

Unlike classic 100% cotton, this pair has a hint of stretch that lets me move freely from the jump. The mid-rise sits perfectly at my waist and I noticed the cut is straight through the thighs, giving ample room to breathe and take big, confident strides. If you’ve got some serious quads, that’s not a problem. These jeans can handle your muscles without compromising your style. It tapers neatly down below the knee, laying right on your sneakers for a clean, sharp finish. Whether I’m keeping it casual with a tee or dressing it up with a crisp button-down and blazer, it has that versatile edge to switch things up.

Most selvedge denim is super stiff like cardboard, but that’s not the case with this pair from 3sixteen. Since the cotton fabric blend is infused with a hint of spandex, it's wearable out of the gate. I didn’t go through an annoying break-in period, so I could actually sit down, bike to the bodega, or bend down low without cutting off circulation. The straight fit gives me breathing room instead of feeling painted on. It’s tapered in all the right places so you get that clean, tailored silhouette without feeling like you borrowed your little cousin’s pants. And they’re not stacking weird at the ankle or drowning your sneakers; these sit just right, especially cuffed.

This is Japanese selvedge denim from Kuroki Mills: a denim mill famed for its high-quality fabrics and innovative production techniques like indigo dyeing. Yes, the pair is priced north of $300, but you get your cost per wear, it goes with a bunch of different looks, and is built to last for years to come.

If you’re the kind of guy who thinks $15 jeans have to feel like cardboard and fit like a punishment, let me introduce you to the Amazon special that exceeds my expectations.These budget jeans clock in at just $15, but they don’t feel like a throwaway buy. The denim is a cotton-elastane blend, so while it’s not that stiff, 100% raw denim people love, it looks like classic denim and feels way more forgiving. That hint of stretch allows me to sit, squat, and climb stairs without any restriction. Honestly, the pair is also comfortable enough to travel in, which is not something I say lightly about most cheap jeans.

The fabric has a decent weight to it, too. It’s not paper-thin, not overly rigid; just that sweet middle ground that feels broken-in without looking flimsy. Now, are the jeans perfect? No. The zipper jammed on me a couple of times during the first few wears. Not a dealbreaker, because it loosened up and zipped smoothly after a bit, but worth noting. They’re functional, but they don’t have that tank-like durability you’d expect from a $200 pair.

Uniqlo’s straight jeans from its JW Anderson collaboration are a really clean, easy take on everyday denim. It’s got that classic straight-leg silhouette that’s not too baggy or too slim, so it feels wearable right away. I don’t feel like I’m fighting the jeans, but I also don’t feel swallowed by them. One of the standout qualities is the pre-washed finish. You get a subtle, broken-in fade straight out of the box that doesn’t feel stiff or raw.

Another thing to note: the inseam is 32, and on me this pair runs a little long, so there’s some stacking at the ankle. I’ve found it looks better cuffed. For taller guys, it creates a nice break over the shoe. When it comes time to style, it pairs nicely with oversized tees, structured outerwear, and pretty much anything you’d wear year-round. This pair just sits well, doesn't feel restrictive, and holds up as a reliable “grab-and-go” pair. Plus, it’s more affordable than most options on the list, meaning you can stock up on the three colorways without blowing too much money.

When you’re spending good money on denim, it should be built to last and AGOLDE’s jeans fit the bill. The moment I pulled one leg through, I could tell it was rigid yet surprisingly smooth. It’s made from non-stretch sustainable cotton, which breathes well and softens over time without losing structure. It also has some heft, so I wouldn’t wear it in high-80- or 90-degree temps, but I’ll be reaching for it from fall straight through spring.

Style-wise, it’s a nice departure from your classic blue denim, with a washed-out grey hue that looks sharp with a plain tee or lightweight flannel and boots. My only gripe is the fit: the jeans are already baggy and only come in a 32-inch inseam, which creates more stacking than I’d like at 5 '8". I had mine hemmed slightly to clean up the break. If you’re 5 ‘11” or taller, though, it’ll drape over your shoes or boots the way it’s intended without looking overly bunched.

If you’re looking to lean into the Western workwear trend without going full cowboy, AG’s classic bootcut Jean is an easy place to start. I wore this pair to the Beyonce Cowboy Carter concert to coincide with the album’s theme, but it also works just as well for everyday wear when you want to keep things more understated. For the office, you could wear it with a crisp button-down, simple tee, and minimal sneakers. From a fabric standpoint, the cotton-elastane blend has enough give to move with you, while the premium stretch denim from Japan’s renowned Kaihara mill still feels substantial.

It tapered through the thigh before opening slightly below the knee and sits naturally over cowboy boots. Though it looks just as sharp with clean leather sneakers if boots aren’t your thing. AG only offers one color, but I love the medium-blue wash, which has a clean, lived-in look that adds character without looking overly faded, making it easy to dress up or down. I’d throw it on with a plain white tee and overshirt for the weekend or a denim shirt and leather boots when I want to lean into that classic Americana vibe. Like AGOLDE’s jeans, this pair also only comes in a 32-inch inseam. In this case, it works for guys who are closer to 5’11” or taller.

Wrangler makes one of the most iconic cowboy jeans out there for decades. These were originally made for working cowboys and riders, but this timeless silhouette works for a casual office day or weekend outings. The denim is heavyweight cotton, so right away you feel that structure with a broken-in-over-time feel.

Fit-wise, it sits higher on the waist and runs straight through the leg with room where you actually need it—seat and thigh especially. That’s why guys with thicker legs tend to gravitate toward them. They don’t squeeze you or taper too hard, so you actually get comfort without losing that classic straight-leg Western shape. It’s not chasing trends or trying to be “updated.” And if you’re looking for a more affordable alternative to the AG Jeans, this is your best bet.

Brooks Brothers may be known for Oxford shirts and chinos, but our fashion editors were thoroughly impressed by the Americana brand’s denim. Its slim fit pair is made with premium, mid-weight denim that’s super robust, but soft enough to wear for hours, with a hint of spandex for extra mobility. The fit is where the pair truly shine—a precise, tailored cut that contours through the hips and thighs for a clean silhouette without being super tight. Although the jeans fit closer to the body, you don’t feel like you’re suffocating.

Every stitch is strategically placed, reflecting Brooks Brothers’ heritage in classic menswear while still feeling fresh and contemporary. Style-wise, these jeans bridge the gap between smart-casual and laid-back cool, so we’ve worn them to a baseball game as well as an office meeting. These jeans are a dream for a lean to moderately athletic build, though if you have a muscular lower body, you might want to size up.

I’ve probably tested over 30 pairs of dark wash jeans in the past few years, and they all start to blur together. But I can confirm that this one from Tommy Hilfiger is an exception. The straight cut is what really sold me. Because it’s regular from the hip to the hem, it doesn’t pinch when I sit down. You know that awful feeling when you’re at your desk or on the train and your jeans dig into your hips like a vice grip? None of that here. I wore these straight through a long shoot day and a subway ride home without needing to unbutton them the second I walked in the door.

The fabric blend is another win: it’s mostly cotton with a hit of lyocell. That synthetic blend softens things up in a way pure cotton denim never does. It almost feels broken-in right off the rack but still has the structure of a good pair of jeans. And unlike stretch-heavy blends, it doesn’t bag out or sag. The deep rich indigo wash makes it easy to dress things up with a blazer, but casual enough that I can throw on sneakers and a simple tee without it looking too forced.

Our style editors did some research and it turns out that there is no rule saying you can only wear white denim during the summer. Every guy could use a pair in their wardrobe, and make good use of it all year around. The best option we found is this pair from Ralph Lauren that has a pearly white texture, while providing the rugged comfort of a pair of jeans. It’s a straight fit but not too loose, and there was just a hint of stretch for a little boost in comfort.

If you haven’t worn white denim in the past because you’re just not sure how to style it, the trick is to think of something you already know how to work with and just switch this jean in. If you wear chinos in any shade of khaki or brown, a pair of white jeans will give an edgier look without having to change anything else about the outfit. You get the opposite effect when it comes to bluejeans, where swapping them for white elevates the feel of, what is otherwise, the same outfit.

The fit of a black jean is crucial to pulling off dressed up fit, and that is exactly what Lee did here. For starters, I’m 5’8 and the slim-straight cut elongates my profile, giving a sleek, balanced silhouette. This pair is tailored to hug my frame just right without feeling like I squeezed into skinny jeans. When wearing them out on multiple occasions, I still felt like I had enough room to move, thanks to the comforting stretch fabric.

Adorned with branded hardware and the leather logo patch, the aesthetic feels like a nod to the past, while the modern cut still keeps you looking fresh. In terms of style, this pair is the ultimate wardrobe chameleon, working in both casual and semi-dressy settings. It looked just as great with a simple tee and sneakers at a backyard BBQ, as it did with a sport coat and dress shoes at a theater show.

Indigo is the dye that makes most jeans blue. When a brand uses a really rich indigo, like Mavi did here, you get a beautiful range from deep, dark navy and light sky blue. The lighter fades gradually show up and get more pronounced with each wear in a jean like this.

Mavi nailed the modern athletic fit in this jean, providing plenty of room in the hip and thigh, along with a taper in the lower leg that looks clean and stylish. This fit is assisted by a blend of cotton, tencel, polyester, and elastane that is lightweight and stretchy. It was one of the most comfortable jeans for our testers with big quads.

The right fit is the foundation of great jeans. A well-fitting pair should flatter your body type, feel comfortable, and align with your personal style. Here's a breakdown of common fits:

A slim fit jean is slightly tapered from the thigh to the ankle for a modern, streamlined silhouette. It's great for lean, athletic, or average builds who want a sleek, put-together look. Not to get them confused with skinny jeans, they're not nearly as tight, but they are more form-fitting than straight-leg jeans. Because slim fit jeans are so sleek, they pair well with everything—tees, button-downs, and even blazers. In terms of footwear, it can be worn with dress shoes or sneakers.

A straight fit has a uniform width from hip to hem, meaning no tapering at the ankle. It works for all body types, and offers a relaxed but structured look. Offering a balanced silhouette that isn't too baggy or too tight, this fit works great for everyday wear, whether you're pairing it with a flannel, sweatshirt, or polo shirt.

A relaxed cut has extra room in the seat, thighs, and leg, so it’s the most comfortable fit, but it also gives laid-back that’s come back in style. It's ideal for bigger guys, muscular legs, and more breathability. We found it looks great with oversized or relaxed tops to maintain proportion.

A tapered cut is slightly wider in the thighs and gradually narrow toward the ankle. It's a sweet spot between straight-leg and slim-fit jeans—giving you some comfort up top while keeping things clean and tailored below. Ideal for guys with athletic thighs or anyone who wants a streamlined look without going full-blown skinny.

Elastane and spandex (same thing, just different names) are synthetic fibers known for thor serious stretch and bounce-back ability. They’re the secret sauce in modern jeans that makes them way comfier than the stiff, unyielding denim of decades past. A bit of elastane—usually around 1-2%— gives jeans just enough flex to move with you, making them ideal for guys who plan to wear their jeans all day everyday, whether that’s sitting at a desk, running errands, or just kicking back. The trade-off? Stretchy jeans don’t always hold their shape as well as OG 100% cotton denim.

No stretch, no shortcuts. At first, these jeans are stiff. But over time, they mold to your body, creating a custom fit. If you love the idea of breaking in a pair like a well-worn leather jacket, go for this kind—but be ready for a couple uncomfortable weeks.

The holy grail for denim lovers. Selvedge denim is considered top-tier because of its durability, excellent craftsmanship, and the way it develops over time. It’s woven on old-school shuttle looms, which produces a fancy self-finished edge inside the cuff. This means the fabric is denser, less prone to fraying, and typically of higher-quality than mass-produced denim. The real magic? It molds to your body and fades in a way that’s totally unique to how you wear them—no fake distressing needed. The downside? It’s usually stiff at first. Since most selvedge denim is raw (aka unwashed), it starts out rigid, like a thick cotton canvas—but, in the end, it rewards you with some of the best-looking, long-lasting jeans out there.

Your inseam isn't just a number—it dictates whether your jeans stack, skim, or flood. If your denim is too short—you're in capri territory, unless you're purposely rocking cropped jeans. If they're too long, we hope you like puddles of denim at your ankles. For that just-right length, your jeans should either break (gently touch the top of your shoes) or stack naturally if that's your thing.

Most brands offer 30", 32", and 34" inseams, but if you're a shorter or taller guy, look for brands that offer extended sizing or hemming services (Uniqlo and Levi's are great for this). Pro tip: If you like cuffing, go a little longer. If you want a clean, straight-down look, hem them or buy your exact length.

When it comes to denim type in terms of wash and color, you’re choosing between raw vs. washed and light vs. dark vs. everything in between. The right pick depends on how much patience you have, how polished you want to look, and whether you mind a little indigo rub-off. Here’s the breakdown:

This is denim in its purest form: untouched, unwashed, and dark as midnight. It starts out stiff and gradually fades in all the right places based on how you wear them. The trade-off? It takes commitment—you’ll need to break them in, and they might stain your lighter clothes and furniture (hello, indigo bleed).

Pre-washed for softness and color variation, so you get that broken-in look without the break-in period. If you want instant comfort and zero dye transfer, this is your move. If personal fades is your jam, go raw. As for a consistent color and softness from day one, go washed.

The most versatile option—dress it up with a blazer or down with a hoodie. Darker washes are slimming and work in almost any setting. Raw or rinse denim will develop natural fades over time, adding character.

A casual, everyday wash that looks good with everything. Already has some fading, so there’s no awkward stiff phase. Think of it as the sweet spot between too dressy and too relaxed.

Laid-back, retro, and effortlessly cool—perfect for summer or a more relaxed vibe. Looks great with white tees, sneakers, and vintage-inspired fits. Not as dressy as dark denim, but adds character to your wardrobe.

Since 2021, myself and the Men's Health style team have gone full denim detective mode—testing more than 50 different pairs, each worn for at least two weeks at a time, and six hours a day. As someone who’s 5"8" and typically wears 28W/30L, I know what works and what doesn’t. I threw these jeans into every case scenario—casual brunches, city commutes, long-haul flights, running errands, and yes, even squatting for good measure. I took detailed notes on fit, comfort, wash, inseam, and performance (stretch, moisture-wicking, breathability).We checked if they were true to size, how the fabric held up through hours of movement, whether they needed a marathon break-in, and if they could work in a variety of settings. Our testers also include a diverse range of body types to help us ensure an unbiased result for selecting the best jeans for men. We made sure our picks weren’t trendy jeans, but true workhorses that will look great years from now.

As the most versatile article of clothing a man can own, jeans have the ability to traverse many different types of formality. Given that denim originates from workwear, it inherently embodies a casual nature. That's why I suggest throwing in some contrast, like rocking penny loafers with laid-back tailoring.

For a more laid-back look, pair your jeans with a well-fitted tee and canvas or leather sneakers. But when aiming for a smarter appearance, combining dark wash jeans with a crisp button-down shirt or sweater with a pair of boots is a great idea as well.

On the other hand, for a business casual look, throw on a pair of suede loafers with dark denim, an oxford button down, and timeless accessories. Take those same jeans and style your denim with a pair of low-top sneakers like common projects white sneakers, or a heavyweight crewneck sweatshirt and you've got a great weekend look for fall.

100% cotton denim will feel sturdier and often lasts longer—but it can be stiff at first. A cotton-elastane blend adds comfort and mobility. Neither is “better” universally; it depends on how you wear your jeans. If you’re commuting, traveling, or sitting all day, stretch will keep you comfortable. If you want that old-school fade-and-mold-to-your-body experience, go full cotton.

Look at the stitching. Tight, even seams with no loose threads means you have a pair of durable jeans. Check the rivets (those little metal reinforcements at pocket corners), the zipper glide, and the heft of the waist button. Quality jeans often have reinforced belt loops and sturdy pocket bags that don’t feel like tissue paper.

Think about silhouette. The rise—whether high, mid, or low—changes where the jeans sit on your torso and can subtly shift proportions. From there, it’s about the leg shape. Straight-leg jeans are timeless and work on nearly everyone. Tapered cuts offer more room in the thigh with a slimmer opening at the ankle, ideal if you lift or prefer a cleaner line. Slim fits narrow throughout for a sharper look, while flares and bootcuts widen at the hem and are designed to sit neatly over boots (and yes, they’re creeping back into the mainstream). The right combination of rise and fit can make an affordable pair look elevated—or make an expensive pair look completely wrong.

#4567. The Best Fall Skincare Routine, According to Dermatologists

Your cold-weather glow starts with these expert-approved tweaks.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I finally pulled my favorite fuzzy black jacket out of my closet for long strolls around New York City. Many of the leaves in Central Park are turning a gorgeous burnt-orange hue, and hot apple cider is readily available at local cafes and farmers' markets. But like clockwork every fall since moving to New York from Florida, my skin has been feeling dry, tight, and a little itchy. My complexion is also a little flushed after cleansing, which isn’t the norm during the spring and summer.

Turns out that I’m not alone. Dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD, says her patients often experience rough or flaky patches, dullness, and increased sensitivity to products they previously tolerated well after cleansing this time of year. They also notice tightness, itching, and products that suddenly sting. Sure, cranking up my pretty pink Canopy humidifier can help a little, but after talking with dermatologists, it’s officially time to upgrade my skincare routine for fall.

The good news: We don’t need to replace our entire routine this fall. Dermatologists share their ideal morning and night skincare tweaks. Plus, they reveal how to safely exfoliate dry, flaky skin, and weigh in on using retinoids. The best part? Many of their suggestions are drugstore staples from brands like Cetaphil and La Roche-Posay.

“A healthy barrier does not require a ten-product supporting cast,” says Dr. Gohara. You really only need a few key items—and you may even have them in your home already. Here’s a roundup of dermatologist-recommended products the pros agree are worthy of a spot in your skincare routine. I also included my favorite face sunscreen for the morning and eye cream for twice daily use.

Dr. Nazarian swears by this Cetaphil option and calls it her top cleanser because it's, well, super gentle. She highlights the trifecta of glycerin, niacinamide, and panthenol, as a major win for your skincare game. Notably, glycerin is a humectant to hold onto moisture.

Aveeno Positively Radiant Vitamin C Serum

“Glow with a built-in comfort crew,” says Dr. Gohara about this Skincare Award-winning face serum. “Vitamin C is a proven skin-brightening, collagen-boosting powerhouse. The only problem: it’s known to be irritating on sensitive skin. Aveeno has solved for that here, adding a calming concoction of niacinamide and the brand’s famed oat complex,” says beauty director Brian Underwood.

We’ve previously named this the best overall hyaluronic acid serum and Dr. Nazarian agrees. She appreciates that it boasts multiple forms of hyaluronic acid to enhance hydration, adding that it’s a great serum for layering with other products in your routine.

You can slather this budget-friendly moisturizer on your face and body. It earned snaps from Dr. Gohara, who points to the combination of glycerin to attract water and ceramides to support the skin barrier.

Pro tip from Dr. Gohara: Whether you use a lotion or a face cream, apply it to slightly damp skin.

For extra dryness, layer SkinMedica Barrier Calming Cream on top, advises Dr. Gohara. “Just as you double up on clothes, you can double up on moisturizer. Hydration first, a protective outer layer second,” she says. And that’s exactly what the Barrier Calming Cream does. It contains a nourishing blend of moisturizing glycerin, niacinamide to minimize skin inflammation, and calming oat kernel extract.

The experts I chatted with say eye cream is a totally optional step. You can technically get away with just using a plain face moisturizer under your eyes, says Dr. Nazarian. However, since the undereye skin is thinner and prone to dryness during colder months, a separate eye cream can be helpful for dealing with dryness, fine lines, or crepiness.

Neocutis combines human growth factors with a proprietary blend of peptides to target fine lines, wrinkles, puffiness, and dark circles. After about two weeks, I noticed my undereye area was a little more luminous.

Isdin Eryfotona Actinica Mineral Sunscreen SPF 50+

You shouldn’t retire your sunscreen in the fall, argues Dr. Gohara. A broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher sunscreen is a daily staple. My all-time favorite one is the Isdin Eryfotona Ageless—it’s a tinted mineral sunscreen that doesn’t leave a ghastly finish on my face. It contains plankton-derived DNA Repairsomes, which Isdin says help repair existing sun damage. The formulation is lightweight and absorbs quickly and it’s even water-resistant for active lifestyles.

SkinMedica HA5 Hydra Collagen Facial Mist

Spritz your skin with this spray whenever your complexion needs extra TLC. Dr. Gohara calls this your skin’s “hydration intermission.” It moisturizes and helps keep water in, and layers beautifully over makeup.

Before you go to bed and watch TV, you’ll want to do your skincare routine. You can use pretty much everything from your morning routine.

This creamy cleanser is great for seasonal dryness.

Pro tip from Dr. Garshick: Avoid washing with very hot water since it can contribute to dryness. If you have very sensitive skin, consider splashing your face with water instead of cleansing twice daily, she says.

"This eye cream is rich without being heavy so it won’t leave skin with an oily finish,” says dermatologist Joshua Zeichner, MD, in our 2020 Skincare Awards. He loves that it can “help strengthen the skin and improve texture and fine lines—no irritation in sight."

Lock in hydration with this lightweight face serum that doesn’t feel overly tacky on your skin.

SkinMedica makes a slew of impressive products, including a recent 2026 Skincare Award win for the Exfoliating Pads. However, when you’re shopping for a moisturizer for fall, consider this investment-worthy pick. While pricey, you only need a few small dabs of cream all over your face.

Dr. Nazarian suggests Dermal Repair Cream to anyone who wants to use a retinoid product in the fall. “It’s incredibly hydrating and calming—and uses a form of hyaluronic acid combined with vitamins C and E for skin hydration and environmental defense along with a gentle form of retinoid,” she says. Just be sure to gradually introduce it into your routine.

In the fall, it’s all about hydration. Both Dr. Garshick and Dr. Nazarian suggest humectants such as glycerin and hyaluronic acid to attract water, plus skin barrier-supporting ingredients such as ceramides. You might also benefit from slathering on a richer cream packed with fatty acids, shea butter, or squalane if your skin is very dry.

Yes, you can exfoliate in the fall, but only occasionally. TBH, the frequency varies based on your specific needs and the product you’re using. But you can probably start with once a week or even every two weeks if you have more sensitive skin. You should also avoid scrubbing irritated skin and not exfoliate the same night you use a retinoid while building tolerance. “Flakes are not an invitation to scrub harder,” says Dr. Gohara. “You are polishing skin, not refinishing furniture.” Also, don't be afraid to pause exfoliating if your skin ever feels uncomfy. You can just use your classic face moisturizer until your skin feels comfortable again, adds Dr. Gohara.

Look, just because it’s overcast and chilly out doesn’t mean you should skip wearing sunscreen in the fall. And don’t just take my word for it: “Your sweaters have seasonal employment; your sunscreen works year-round,” says Dr. Gohara. That means you should wear a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher on your exposed skin, including your ears, neck, and hands. Follow your sunscreen label for specific reapplication tips, but typically, you can reapply at least every two hours and after sweating or swimming, according to the American Academy of Dermatology.

The experts I spoke with say you can use a retinoid year-round if your skin can tolerate it and if you diligently reapply sunscreen. However, fall is a convenient time to add a retinoid—such as retinol, retinal, tretinoin, or adapalene—into your routine. Regardless of which type of retinoid you select, start using it gradually. Dr. Garshick says two or three times a week is a good jumping off point, then you can increase frequency as tolerated.

#4566. Phenomenological Bioethics: What Does It Mean to Die Well?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Co-authored by Mark Shelvock and Daniel Wyzynski

In the modern fast-paced world, many of us spend little time consciously thinking about our inevitable deaths until we are directly confronted by them. This existential confrontation can occur through a new diagnosis, a loved one’s health declining, an unexpected tragedy, or perhaps when we put on our favourite hospital drama on TV.

According to historian Philippe Ariès, death was once a communal and intimate event within the Western world. People died at home, surrounded by family, within a web of cultural and/or religious rituals.1 Over the course of the 20th century, however, dying became more medicalized; relocated from the home into hospitals and institutions, and transferred from the hands of families into the hands of healthcare providers. As medical interventions progressed and the ability to keep death at bay grew, the location of care shifted to a place where more invasive interventions could be performed — and now a common request that arises in the hospital is for the medical staff to "do everything" to prevent death.

In North America, and across much of the Western world, many people today have little personal experience with dying or death. Alternatively, movies and TV may have taught them to expect a tranquil death that rarely matches reality. This cultural estrangement has real consequences for individuals, families, healthcare providers, and the health system.

One of the most important distinctions in end-of-life care is between disease and illness. Disease is objective; the measurable, diagnosable change in the body that a clinician can identify and treat. Illness, on the other hand, is subjective and deeply personal. Illness is the lived experience of being unwell, which may include experiences of fear, fatigue, grief, and a loss of identity or other personal struggles that no medical chart can fully capture.

Modern medicine has become extraordinarily good at treating disease, but far less attentive to illness, and to dying.1,2,3 Yet for the person who has become a “patient”, illness is what often matters the most: what it means, how it feels, and what it does to a person's sense of self, their life story, and the impact it has on the people they love the most.4

Pain follows the same logic. Many clinicians learn early that pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, and two people with identical diagnoses can suffer in radically different ways. Dying, then, is never simply a medical event. It is a disorienting, multidimensional, and existentially raw time in a person’s life.

The physician-author Atul Gawande put the problem plainly: people facing serious illness have priorities beyond simply prolonging their lives.2 They want to avoid suffering, remain psychologically present, feel connected to the people they love, and they want to reflect on the sense that their lives have been complete and meaningful. The dominant model of technological medical care, Gawande argued, has frequently failed to meet these needs in the 21st century.

What people need at the end of life is not always more intervention, but more presence, listening, psychosocial supports, and more honest conversations about what really matters. This is where phenomenological bioethics enters; it is not just abstract theory, but a practical human philosophy and orientation towards authentic care.

Phenomenology is the philosophical study of lived experience, and grapples with what it is like to be a conscious, embodied, mortal, and vulnerable human being. The philosopher Fredrik Svenaeus invites us to start with a unique person’s experience of suffering.

This approach asks clinicians and caregivers alike to sit with questions that no brain scan or blood panel can answer:

Dying well is not about achieving some idealized exit, or being stoic, entirely peaceful, or free from all fear and suffering. It is about being seen as our own person, dying on our own terms: as a full human being with a history, a body, a web of relationships, and a particular way of making meaning in the world.

These questions are not morbid but generous, and asking them is one of the most profound acts of care available to us.

We also acknowledge that phenomenological bioethics has significant limitations. It is difficult to scale its recommendations when faced with institutional and system-wide limitations; further, existentially informed approaches demand time, humility, and relational skills that constrained budgets and widespread burnout make hard to sustain. Still, it offers what medical treatments cannot supply on their own; a way of approaching dying as a fundamentally human experience, and not merely a set of clinical problems to be managed.

To our readers: the question worth asking now, not at the bedside or in crisis, but here, in the quiet of an ordinary day, is: What might it mean for you to die well, and can you talk about what dying well means to you and your loved ones?

This article was co-authored with Daniel Wyzynski, a Clinical Ethicist, associate scientist, and adjunct research professor at Western University. Daniel specializes in clinical ethics, complex medical deliberation, mental health ethics, and patient-centred and family-centered care within acute and long-term care settings.

1. Ariès, P. (1981). The hour of our death. Knopf.

2. Gawande, A. (2014). Being mortal: Medicine and what matters in the end. Metropolitan Books.

3. Svenaeus, F. (2017). Phenomenological bioethics: Medical technologies, human suffering, and the meaning of being alive. Routledge.

4. Frank, A. W. (1995). The wounded storyteller: Body, illness, and ethics. University of Chicago Press.

#4565. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

She said issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are important windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” said Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they said could reverse these trends. Among them:

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan said women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”

#4564. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

The CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

What stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

We’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?
