#4554. How Italians Cured My Loneliness

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

A couple of years ago, I’d made the painful decision to leave my marriage, and my beloved dog of 13 years had died. Suddenly, I found myself deeply alone.

The life I had always imagined for myself—a long-term stable marriage and a family nested in community—had never materialized.

One day, though, I realized that there was something that I had dreamed of when I was younger, that suddenly might be possible.

I went. And I went again. I discovered a lesser-known town in my favorite area, and an affordable apartment that I could use periodically in the off-season. I committed to going, using airline points, when I had lulls between stretches of speaking engagements.

Because of my youthful obsession with all things Italian, I had studied the language. I’d also had a long-distance Italian boyfriend for a few months in my early 30s.

I brushed up via a language app, and this was the key that opened all doors.

In Canada, I was a solitary woman who had to book appointments to see her busy friends, all of whom had families.

In Italy, I found myself swept up into a large, generous family and their circle of friends, and rarely had enough time to sit and read a book.

The way I learned to live in Italy transformed the way I live at home.

I always thought my phone aversion was due to being an introvert. Even if the name on my screen was a friend, I’d send it to voicemail and text them a little bit later.

In Italy, I discovered the delight of being interrupted.

At least once a day, my friend Vincenza knocked at my door unannounced, calling out my name. My old Canadian self might have pretended not to be home, but I began to associate these unexpected visits with delight. Vincenza usually had a plate of hot pasta or pastries in her arms, or her sister Angela would call to invite me for lunch.

The effect stuck. Today, when a friend or family member calls me, I find myself answering. Sometimes I even call them.

Part of why I wouldn’t answer the phone when it rang was because it wasn’t part of "the plan." I ran a tight ship. Or perhaps not actually that tight, because I was usually already behind on the day’s to-do list. There wasn’t room for an unplanned 15-minute chat with a friend.

In Italy, Angela randomly calls to let me know that they’ll gather in the piazza in 10 minutes “because the sun is so beautiful today.”

An impromptu lunch invitation may stretch into a couple of hours around a table with friends.

When I run into Vincenza’s daughter, Nausica, while out running errands, she often invites me for a spontaneous coffee or aperitivo, or to go to a store around the corner and help her pick out a dress for an event.

In my past life, I believed that because I was doing something (anything) else, the natural answer was, "Sorry, not now."

I’ve learned that unless I absolutely must be doing something else, the best answer is “Sure, why not?”

If you’ve seen the meme of the hyper-independent woman carrying a clothes washer up the subway steps by herself, that’s me.

I don’t like needing or asking for help. I am, however, a professional helper. Literally. I’m a medical doctor, an executive coach, and a professional speaker/educator. Perhaps most importantly, I’m also the first-born daughter of four.

I will help you with things you didn’t even know you needed help with.

Then there are my Italian friends. They don’t need my help. They don’t seem to even want my help.

They stealthily pay for my aperitivo or pizza, sneaking the waiter money while pretending to use the washroom. I once tried to pay for parking, and my friend wrestled me out of the way so intensely that I hesitate to ever attempt it again.

But what about medical help? Surely, there might be potential for heroics. Nope, they already have a doctor in the family.

The thing is, they seem to just enjoy having me around—without me doing anything other than showing up and eating the food they place in front of me, with great enthusiasm. This seems to be all one needs to do to earn permanently adopted status.

I think that was the ultimate blow that broke the chains of my very North American loneliness. In a “What can you do for me?” world, it’s remarkable to discover a collective of people, all of whom seem to live by the same rules: “You’ll always have a place at my table—just don’t argue when I serve you more pasta.”

#4553. Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of new technologies.”

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

The campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

“They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” said Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

“Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is important for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski said. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

“A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he said. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious issue,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he said it was also fulfilling.

“I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he said. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he said.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

Getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

“We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar said. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”

As he embraces his 50s, he said he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” said Gosselaar.

He also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

“[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

“I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar said.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he said.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”

#4552. Trump again orders broken coal plant to stay open, even after court said it’s illegal

The Department of Energy has issued a seventh “emergency” order forcing J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan to remain open, 534 days after the plant’s planned retirement. The orders have cost ratepayers $303 million and counting, causing electricity prices to increase amid a global energy crisis.

One of the Department of Energy’s recent tactics has been to issue “emergency orders” forcing coal plants to stay open, even when nobody wants them open.

The DoE has used this on six coal plants (and one oil-and-gas plant) in six states, claiming that the plants need to be kept open for “reliability.”

The problem, of course, is that coal is the least reliable form of energy we have available to us. It’s also expensive and polluting, which is why coal use has been plummeting in recent years, dropping from a high of around half of US electricity generation in the early 2000s, down to 17% now.

So everyone is trying to get off coal, for good reason. And when I say “everyone,” I mean everyone – even the owners of the plants subject to these orders have made filings opposing the orders.

The only person trying to keep these coal plants open is fossil shill Chris Wright, posing as head of the Department of Energy, whose main goal is to make American energy supply more expensive and less secure, and ensure that Americans suffer as much harm as possible from it, both to their lungs and pocketbooks.

Each of these orders was obviously illegal from the start – there is no emergency that should force broken coal plants to be reopened, at great cost, in order to sit there idle, providing nothing for ratepayers in the region who are on the hook for the hundreds of millions of dollars that these orders will cost.

Thankfully, courts agreed – even if it took them a while. After more than a year of this nonsense, a federal appeals court blocked these “emergency orders,” specifically targeting the order for the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan. The court unanimously found that there was no emergency keeping it open.

The orders for the other plants are all subject to similar lawsuits, and given the ruling for the Campbell plant, it is expected that courts will find similarly for each of them.

However, despite that order, the DoE has continued its illegal actions. Today, it issued another 90-day “emergency order” forcing the Campbell plant to stay open until mid-February. It does this as it requests a re-hearing on the previous decision, which was unanimously found to be illegal.

In the interim, Americans have dealt with skyrocketing energy prices throughout all aspects of life, largely driven by a now 8+ month long war of choice in Iran. This war was started by an ignoramus posing as president who cannot legally hold office in the US, and who was recently widely rebuked by the American public, largely due to his illegal actions to raise their energy prices.

That rebuke wasn’t enough to stop the fossil shills squatting in the White House though, if today’s actions are any indication. The 90 day order will continue to balloon costs, keeping a coal plant open that nobody wants open, even its own operators who had already planned for its retirement.

Who knew that MAGA meant battling the well-documented improvements of modernity, like clean(er) and cheaper energy, vaccines, scientific R&D, etc.?

In a recent filing, the plants owners said “From the date the first emergency order became effective through September 30, 2026, the amount Consumers expects to seek recovery from FERC associated with the emergency orders, including amounts already requested, is $303 million.”

This amount is in addition to the hundreds of millions of dollars of costs incurred by the other six plants subject to these false emergency orders, bringing costs up by over $600 million across the country just from these emergency orders alone. The Campbell plant is the worst of the bunch in terms of pollution – which isn’t accounted for in the $600 million number, meaning American health costs are rising even more in addition to the staffing costs for these broken plants.

In addition, the DoE has channeled nearly a billion dollars in additional subsidies to this dead form of electricity generation, doing so after coal industry lobbyists asked them for these specific emergency orders. Fossil fuel companies have posted record profits as a result of these subsidies and rising prices, channeling money from Americans’ pocketbooks to the pockets of the people who would harm them.

#4551. Gift Guide: 44 Cool, Fun, and Unique Gifts for Motorcyclists

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

We've tested and compiled an array of motorcycle gifts, gear, and accessories to help you find the right gifts for the motorcycle riders in your life.

This article was updated in November 2026.

The best motorcycle gifts don’t have to be flashy. A well-chosen upgrade can make a cold commute more comfortable, a long tour easier to manage, or time in the garage more rewarding. The trick is matching the present to the person: what they ride, where they go, and what gear they already own.

This guide covers a range of options, from protective apparel and useful electronics to compact accessories and garage staples. Whether you’re shopping for a longtime rider or someone still getting used to life on two wheels, you’ll find ideas for different styles, needs, and budgets.

Kriega is the leading brand in motorcycle baggage, and its backpacks are no different. Waterproof inside and with 20 liters of storage space, the R20 backpack is perfect for commuting and features Kreiga's harness-style fasteners. An innovative technology pioneered specifically for motorcycles, the chest clip and straps allow the bag's weight to be pushed forward, making sure that the weight stays centered on the back without disturbing your riding balance.

It's the perfect motorcycling backpack as far as we're concerned.

Give a motorcyclist a gift that makes every ride easier to relive—and can help document the unexpected. The Insta360 X5 Motorcycle Bundle captures 8K 360-degree video, letting riders choose angles later instead of fiddling with framing on the road. FlowState stabilization smooths bumpy footage, while the heavy-duty clamp and invisible selfie stick are ready for bike-mounted shots. It’s a fun way to share adventures and a useful record if a ride takes an unwelcome turn.

This extremely compact starter box is 33% thinner, 27% smaller, and 34% lighter than most portable jump-packs, so it slips right into your pocket. Rated at 1500 amps, it can even jump-start cars, motorcycles, trucks, ATVs, boats, RVs, vans, and SUVs. Best of all, it's equipped with a flashlight and two fast-charging USB ports, both A and C, so it can easily charge your favorite USB devices while it's in your pocket. No motorcyclist should flip up the kickstand without one.

This helmet wall mount is perfect for those who want to save space. It easily mounts on any wall and swivels to display helmets or other items as desired. When not in use, it can be pushed against the wall to take up less space. A bottom hook lets you hang your jacket, keeping all your riding gear together.

Hand signals from your riding buddy can only go so far, especially when a waving arm could mean anything. Communication systems go a long way toward enjoying group rides and Cardo's PackTalk PRO is the perfect communication system for individual and group use. The waterproof model includes a mesh network Bluetooth connection for phone calls, directions, and music while also allowing for rider-to-rider communications. JBL speakers are included in the package and make communications and music crystal clear. Best of all, you can set up voice commands and speed dial to make sure those eyes stay on the road.

Few gifts can improve a rider's safety as dramatically as the Brake Free Helmet Light. This clever wireless device mounts to the back of nearly any helmet and uses built-in sensors to detect braking, downshifting, and engine braking, illuminating bright LEDs at eye level for drivers behind you. With no wiring, no apps, and a weatherproof design, it's an easy upgrade that boosts visibility day or night. For riders who value safety without sacrificing simplicity, this is one of the smartest gifts on the road.

For the rider who owns the gloves, jacket, and boots, give them something that matters most when a ride goes wrong: Alpinestars’ Tech-Air 5 Plasma airbag system. This lightweight, breathable vest slips beneath a motorcycle jacket and deploys to protect the chest, ribs, back, and shoulders. It offers STREET, OFF-ROAD, and RACE modes, up to 30 hours of battery life, and a user-replaceable inflator. It’s an investment in safer miles—and a thoughtful gift with purpose. Available in sizes XS-4XL.

You don't need to be a biker to love this Lego set. It includes a two-speed gearbox and front and rear suspension for realistic movement. The attention to detail is impressive, like the turning handlebar and front and rear disc brakes. A kickstand, exhaust pipe, windshield, and dashboard add the little details that make this model true to the full-size version. Designed in collaboration with Ducati, it's a Technic set, so it's far more than just a toy or model. Still, Lego enthusiasts who want a bigger challenge should try the 1900-piece Technic BMW M 1000 RR ($249.99 at Lego) set.

Quad Lock makes a huge variety of phone-mounting gear, and motorcyclist-specific products are some of the most popular. This particular unit, the Quad Lock Motorcycle Handlebar Mount, includes everything you'll need to install it on any motorcycle and allows for your choice of mounting angle. You'll also need to get one of QuadLock's sleek phone cases to complete the package.

Some riders don't like to wear big clunky boots. Now they can go straight from the bike to the bar with these comfortable moto-specific riding shoes. They're comfortable and easy to wear, with sturdy construction and strong materials around the toe area. They're available in multiple sizes (tip: Know your EU size to get the best fit) and colors including brown and two-tone.

Affordable with no brand or riding style affiliations, this is the perfect fun gift for those riders who are hard to buy for.

Available in black, gray, and tan (shown), this over-the-shoulder sling bag is perfect for riders who hate wearing backpacks. You can keep your wallet, phone, keys, and other valuables inside and secure while riding. We've used this many times; we barely feel it on us and love the convenience.

If your favorite rider is an ADV fanatic who loves to explore off-road, the Garmin zūmo XT3 is the perfect present. Its ultrabright 4.7-inch display is glove-friendly and rain-resistant. It can withstand all kinds of weather, extreme temperatures, and vibrations. They'll get adventurous routes with turn-by-turn directions and topographic or satellite imagery for off-road guidance. Plus, they can manage and review routes, tracks, and waypoints on their smartphone and computer—no subscription needed.

Perfect for motorcycles, this 750-amp, 12-volt Battery Tender is smarter than a trickle charger because it provides a full charge, then switches to Float mode to keep your battery at an optimal level for safe, long-term storage without overcharging. It's compatible with all 12V lead-acid, flooded, AGM, and gel cell batteries.

The ultimate motorcycle gift? Ecuador Freedom offers guided and self-guided tours all over one of South America's most beautiful countries, starting at around $2k. Starting in the central capital city of Quito, these multi-day tours can go on- or off-road (or both!), up to colossal Andean peaks or volcanoes (or both!), and down to the Pacific Ocean to the west or the Amazon jungle to the east (or both!) Freedom also rents Jeeps and other 4x4s. The adventure is yours.

Four carbon fiber heating elements generate heat across the collar, mid-back, as well as underneath. It features two pockets for core-body warmth and three heat settings for comfort no matter where the ride takes you.

Whether your bike is a tool for metropolitan mobility or rural enjoyment, it's never a bad idea to lock it up when parked. Motorcycle theft is a huge problem in major cities around the world, but a simple disc lock will fend off the majority of thieves. Kryptonite makes it simple with the Keeper Disc Lock, blending hardened materials with affordable pricing. And don't forget to use the orange reminder cable; we know from personal experience that trying to ride away with a disc lock on isn't a pretty sight.

A good balaclava is one of those pieces of riding gear you don't appreciate until you ride without one. The Censgo Motorcycle Balaclava is designed with lightweight, moisture-wicking fabric and breathable mesh panels that help keep riders cool, dry, and comfortable on hot-weather rides. It slips easily under a helmet, reduces sweat buildup, and adds a layer of protection from wind, dust, and bugs. Affordable, practical, and useful on nearly every ride, it's a stocking stuffer any motorcyclist will appreciate.

Tired of rolling up those foam earplugs and stuffing them in your ears? Try Earpeace Moto. I was skeptical about these at first, but you get a number of them, along with a handy carrying case. They work as advertised to block out unwanted noise on a long ride, and they don't get your ear canals sore as those foam plugs do after a daylong ride. You can also wear them discreetly at concerts without looking totally uncool. Perfect stocking—or, er, ear canal—stuffer.

Every rider knows that tire pressure can make or break a day on the road, which is why the AstroAI L7 Tire Inflator is a smart gift that delivers real-world value. This compact cordless air compressor packs up to 150 PSI, features automatic shutoff to prevent overinflation, and includes a built-in LED light for roadside emergencies. Small enough to stash in a saddlebag yet powerful enough for motorcycles, bicycles, and more, it's the kind of tool riders will actually use.

Useful gifts include riding gear, luggage, maintenance tools, navigation devices, communication systems, and small comforts such as insulated drinkware. Think about how the recipient rides: a daily commuter may value weather protection, while a touring rider might appreciate route-planning gear or extra storage.

Check the make, model, and year before buying anything that mounts to or fits the motorcycle. Phone mounts, luggage, covers, and electronics can vary in compatibility. If you can’t confirm the details, choose a universal accessory or a gift card from a motorcycle gear retailer.

Yes, but fit matters. Jackets, gloves, boots, and protective equipment need to fit correctly and suit the rider’s needs. For helmets, ask about the recipient’s preferred brand, size, and model first; a gift card may be a better choice than guessing.

Check the rider’s size and preferred fit, plus the weather and conditions they ride in. Ventilated gear may suit warm-weather riding, while waterproof layers and heated accessories can be welcome for commuting or touring. Look for a gift receipt in case the fit isn’t right.

They can be. Commuters may appreciate rain gear, visibility accessories, or compact storage. Touring riders might get more use from luggage, navigation, communication gear, or comfort upgrades. When in doubt, choose something that works across different kinds of rides.

Absolutely. Riders often have specific preferences about brands, fit, and compatibility. A gift card lets them choose gear that suits their bike and riding style while still giving them something to look forward to.
